indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how farmers and ranchers can reduce pricing risk through forward contracts, futures markets or hedging.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Review market terminology such as futures market, bull market, open market, Freight on Board (FOB) pricing, basis, forward contracting, Act of God clauses, and the difference between wholesale commodity marketing and Farmgate or value-added.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research sources of livestock and crop market information (e.g., marketing specialists, business centres, internet and publications) for various commodities, products and services.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate Canada's trade agreements with respect to livestock and crop commodities being traded, their impact on producers and supply management and types (e.g., free trade and tariffs) of trade agreements with various countries.

outcomes.statement: Examine the structure and organization of farm and land management plans for livestock production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17A: Planning for Livestock Production (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 7B, 10B, 11 and 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the annual cycle (i.e., processes followed in a sequence over the course of a year like breeding and culling) and production cycle (e.g., postpartum, conception, mid gestation and late gestation) in livestock production.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the required structures (e.g., buildings, fences and corrals) and land (e.g., land features including soil types and use of that land) of a livestock operation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the rationale for choosing a type of ranching, size of operation and breed of livestock for a given farm location.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate livestock management practices (e.g., percentage as meat processing, pure-bred breeding stock development, crossbreeding, show and aging livestock and introduction of new animals to the herd or operation) including the ability to handle waste (e.g., manure and carcasses) and herd protection measures (e.g., herd dogs and donkeys).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the biosecurity and food safety requirements (e.g., ProAction, VBP+ and Start Clean Stay Clean) for livestock production.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine aspects of livestock nutrition programs including sources of feed, prepared rations, feed storage, method of feeding, grazing methods and sources of water.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the finances of a livestock operation including equipment and human resources, types of products (e.g., meat, eggs, wool, honey and dairy), bedding requirements (e.g., straw bales), outsourcing stages (e.g., feedlot connection), accessibility to markets, cost of input and expected revenue.

outcomes.statement: Examine the structure and organization of farm and land management plans for crop production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18A: Planning for Crop Production (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 7B, 10B, 11 and 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the farming cycle (e.g., seeding, protection and nutrition, harvesting and preparation for next season) in crop production.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the buildings and equipment used for a specific crop production operation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze existing farm soil types and land features to determine the suitability of the types of crops grown.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the planting and harvesting methods used for different species of crop.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain which fertilizers and chemicals are used for specific crops in an operation and the impact that those choices can have on future cropping decisions (e.g., herbicide carryover and what environmental conditions can affect this).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the finances of a crop operation including seasonal and foreign workers, buying or leasing equipment, accessibility to markets, cost of input, crop insurance, cash advance programs, risk management tools such as crop insurance and AgStability and expected revenue.

outcomes.statement: Investigate safe methods of restraining, moving and transporting livestock.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22B: Basic Handling - Restraint, Movement and Transportation · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 22A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore organizations (e.g., 4-H clubs) that teach proper handling of livestock.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the use of basic restraints (e.g., halter, stocks, cage and pharmaceuticals).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss methods of catching a difficult animal.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Catch, halter and lead an animal safely.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe an animal's expected behaviour in various situations (e.g., being led, tying, grooming, bathing, clipping, crutching and mother-baby interactions).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how to appropriately manage unwelcome behaviours (e.g., halter pulling, biting, kicking and striking).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the balance points of a chosen species of livestock.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe preparation, loading and unloading procedures.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how to recognize and use flight zones when handling livestock.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare different types of trailers (e.g., straight haul, angle haul and open stall) and their purpose.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the characteristics of animals that are not fit for transport.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe how to transport a sick animal.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain how to use animals (e.g., horses and dogs) and vehicles (e.g., plane, helicopter, ATV and trucks) to move livestock.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Investigate how technology (e.g., drones) can be used to manage livestock.

outcomes.statement: Explore the regulations governing handling and treatment of livestock.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22C: Basic Handling – Regulations (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 22B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe acceptable and unacceptable aspects of livestock management, such as principles of punishment and reward and physical and psychological abuse.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the laws governing improper treatment of animals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research regulations governing enclosure size for specific types of livestock.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine moral issues of the use of tools that cause pain (e.g., electric cattle prods, whips and electric fences) in livestock handling.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the role of the Animal Protection Service of Saskatchewan (APSS).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore codes of practice (e.g., Code of Practice for the Care and Handling of Beef Cattle by National Farm Animal Care Council [NFACC]) in the handling of specific livestock.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the use of Saskatchewan Premises Identification (PID).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the importance of traceability of livestock (e.g., source of transmissible contamination like E. Coli and proving organic status of meat).

outcomes.statement: Investigate livestock nutritional requirements.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23B: Livestock Nutrition Requirements (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 23A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define feed terminology such as total digestible nutrients, protein content, energy, trace minerals, crude protein, crude fat and feed supplements.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Read and interpret feed labels.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the basic nutritional requirements of various livestock according to breed, age, gender, time of year, reproductive cycle and physical condition.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the importance of calculating dry matter and using a scale to feed animals a specific weight of feed.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the water requirements of livestock, including factors that may affect these requirements (e.g., animal size, growth stage, temperature and humidity).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how feed concentrates, supplements and creep feeding can be used to meet an animal’s unique needs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss why a salt block is used in livestock nutrition.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the advantages and disadvantages of commercially prepared feeds.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the proper mixture of prepared food for nutritional value for a specific purpose (e.g., maintenance, growing and fattening).

outcomes.statement: Explore the equipment used for feed, water and waste in livestock production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 24B: Livestock Feed, Water and Waste Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the ability to read and interpret controls, gauges and indicators commonly found on feed, water and waste equipment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the common types of feeding systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the components and operation of feeding equipment (e.g., silos, augers, feed carts, feed rollers, mechanized conveyors, liquid feed systems and hay feeders).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the operation of feed milling and processing equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the components of a water supply system including pressure pump, tanks with controls, filtration system and distribution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research various waste management systems (e.g., manure sweeper, manure spreader, compost pile, manure pit and lagoon) used in livestock production.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the environmental and safety issues associated with waste disposal.

outcomes.statement: Explore the cause, treatment, management and prevention of livestock injuries, conditions and diseases.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25B: Livestock Health Care - Injuries, Conditions and Diseases (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 25A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of biosecurity in ensuring herd health and production.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe mitigation strategies to prevent new livestock from introducing diseases to a farm.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the contents of a basic first aid kit and the general equipment (e.g., pails, stomach tubes and blankets) used to treat injured animals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the cause, treatment and prevention of injuries (e.g., sprained joints and impaled objects) and open wounds.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research common conditions such as influenza (e.g., bird and swine flu), African Swine Fever and food-borne illnesses (e.g., Escherichia coli and Salmonella).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify common symptoms, nature and the precautionary measures to prevent a chosen disease.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the identification and management of genetic deformations (e.g., mule foot, cleft pallet and beak deformity) in livestock.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the causes and treatment of gastro-intestinal conditions (e.g., consuming foreign objects, bloat and constipation).

outcomes.statement: Investigate pasture maintenance and livestock checks.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 27B: Pasture – Maintenance and Checks (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 10B, 25A and 27A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to use mending tools (e.g., pliers, hammer and post-hole digger) to repair fences and corrals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify personal protective equipment required when mending fences.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the importance of pen and pasture checks.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of a pasture that has been over grazed.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how to calculate animal equivalents to determine the required pastureland for different livestock species.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the effect of climate changes (e.g., drought, deluge and storms) on pasture vegetation and land.

outcomes.statement: Collect and organize livestock data.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 28B: Livestock Record Keeping - Data Collection and Organization (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 28A

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Collect pertinent information into a list or table.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Organize information into a graph or chart.

outcomes.statement: Collect and organize crop data.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 29B: Crop Record Keeping - Data Collection and Organization (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 29A

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Collect and organize information into a chart, graph, list or table.

outcomes.statement: Investigate livestock breeding practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 30A: Reproduction - Breeding (Optional) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the rationale and process of a breeding program.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the methods for controlling animal breeding (e.g., castration and separation of males from females).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the reproductive anatomy and terminology for male and female of livestock species (e.g., bull/cow, rooster/hen and stallion/mare).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the behaviours and characteristics (e.g., behaviours, eating, socializing and physiological signs of oestrous) exhibited by a female animal when in heat.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the operation of common aids (e.g., mount detectors and paints) for heat detection in females.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the different types of breeding technologies such as pasture breeding, hand breeding, artificial insemination, transporting cool semen and embryo transfer.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how to test for pregnancy and egg fertility of different livestock species.

outcomes.statement: Investigate specialized livestock and equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 31: Specialized Livestock and Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify specialized livestock (e.g., bison, wild boar, bees, egg laying chickens and reindeer) in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the benefits and challenges (e.g., market value, disease, marketing of meat, nutritional requirements and facilities) associated with specialized livestock production.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate specialized livestock regulations (e.g., ownership, animal care and export standards).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify associations that support specialized livestock producers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the technology and equipment used for a specific specialized livestock.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how common types of equipment can be adapted to perform tasks for specialized livestock.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate the use of specialized equipment (e.g., honey extractor, tractor attachments and egg sorting machine) designed for a specific task.

outcomes.statement: Explore the diseases, medication and treatment of livestock in an organic operation.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 32B: Organic Livestock Production - Health (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 32A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how diseases can be mitigated (e.g., buying healthy animals) on organic farms.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain why allopathic veterinary drugs are not used in organic livestock operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the exceptions (e.g., antibiotics, hormones and parasiticides) for treatment of livestock with medications.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the necessity of withdrawal periods when medical treatment is unavoidable.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research alternative treatments (e.g., herbal remedies, Brewer's yeast, probiotics and activated charcoal) for sick animals.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain why fewer medical procedures (e.g., tail docking and beak trimming) are used in organic operations than in conventional operations.

outcomes.statement: Explore the management of crops, pests and weeds in organic crop production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 33B: Organic Crop Production - Crops, Pests and Weeds (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 33A

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of buffer zones in organic farming.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify approved organic pest management substances (e.g., dormant oils, pheromone traps and soap).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore organic weed management strategies (e.g., tillage, flame weeding, hand weeding, mulching and seeding date manipulation).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of natural and synthetic organic pesticides.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the use of fertilizers in crop production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 37A: Crop Health Care - Fertilizers (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 3B and 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore sources of information and on crop health research (e.g., Ministry of Agriculture and agronomists).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the macronutrients (e.g., phosphorus, potassium and nitrogen) and micronutrients (e.g., calcium, zinc and boron) found in soil.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how macro and micronutrients in soil affect plant growth.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate soil-sampling procedures for developing an appropriate nutrient application plan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how to interpret a soil test.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how a nutrient application plan is developed.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the types of fertilizer (e.g., granular, liquid, foliar and anhydrous).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the four components of the 4R fertility program.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the numbering method (i.e., nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium [NPK] values) used for fertilizers.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine advantages and disadvantages of technologies (e.g., mid-row banders, spreaders, fertigation and variable rate application) used for different application methods for fertilizer.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze the risks (e.g., excess accumulation in water sources and plant health) associated with the application of fertilizers.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Investigate how fertilizer application may cause issues with water sources like creeks and ponds.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Describe the health and safety hazards to workers and the public of common fertilizer chemicals.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the benefits and application of precision technology in livestock production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 40B: Precision Agriculture - Benefits and Application for Livestock (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 28B and 39A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how precision agriculture technologies impact gathering, storing and interpreting livestock records and data.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the impact of machine learning on the precision of livestock equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how aerial and/or satellite imagery is used in managing pasture vegetation and the security and surveillance of livestock and property.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how precision technology is used to enhance or improve livestock production such as radio frequency identification, biometric sensors and animal management.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the benefits and application of precision technology in crop production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 41B: Precision Agriculture - Benefits and Application for Crops (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 29B and 39B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how applications of precision agriculture (e.g., variable rate application, yield monitoring and weed, soil and salinity mapping) may increase farm efficiencies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how precision agriculture technologies impact gathering, storing and interpreting crop records and data.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the controversy that surrounds who owns the data collected by technology.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the impact of machine learning on the precision of crop farming equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how aerial and/or satellite imagery of a field are used to interpret crop and soil data and for the security and surveillance of farm property.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze how soil type and salinity data are used to determine the inputs (e.g., type and quantity of seed and fertilizer) applied in different areas of a field.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in n The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one's performance during the interview.

evidence.quote: All Practical and Applied Arts curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.

allEvidence.quote: All Practical and Applied Arts curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.
Each Practical and Applied Arts curriculum is composed of modules configured into courses, along with suggestions for modules that are suitable for middle or secondary level survey courses.

allEvidence.observation: Each entry on the course's outcomes page is one module: the entry is titled with the module name and shows a “Module Code” (the outcome code in sk.json); the module's own page prints one “Outcome” with its indicators. The site lists the course levels under “Course Configurations”.

indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in n The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

outcomes.statement: Select, use and reflect on a variety of strategies to interpret American Sign Language messages.
outcomes.printedWith: * For further information and suggestions for additional strategies, see Appendix A.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Use and reflect on a variety of metacognitive strategies* to enhance language learning, such as:
- make a plan in advance about how to approach a language learning task;
- reflect on the communication process, including attending and signing, by checking copied signing for accuracy and monitoring own sign production to check for persistent errors; or,
- keep a learning log to evaluate own performance and identify which language learning strategies are most effective.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate and reflect on a variety of interactive and affective strategies* to enhance language learning, such as:
- work with a friend to identify patterns and relationships in signs;
- summarize the point reached in a discussion to help focus the talk and ask follow-up questions to check for understanding; or,
- recognize facial expressions as an essential component of ASL.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Practise and reflect on a variety of interpretive strategies* to enhance language learning, such as:
- view a variety of video recordings to ensure exposure to regional, cultural and gender signing variations;
- use knowledge of the context to aid comprehension and ask for things to be repeated in order to understand complex ideas; or,
- mentally prepare questions and make predictions about new information based on prior knowledge and personal experience.

outcomes.statement: Select, use and reflect on a variety of strategies to express oneself in American Sign Language.
outcomes.printedWith: * For further information and suggestions for additional strategies, see Appendix A.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Use and reflect on a variety of cognitive strategies* to enhance communication, such as:
- compare and contrast aspects of ASL and students’ other languages;
- group together sets of signs (vocabulary, structures) with similar characteristics; or,
- make information easier to understand and remember by using reference points and initiatives like classifiers and body shifts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate and reflect on a variety of interactive and affective strategies* to enhance communication, such as:
- work cooperatively with peers in small groups to rehearse or role-play language use;
- assess feedback from conversation partner to recognize when the message has not been understood (e.g., squinted eyes, blank look, head shake) and start again using a different tactic when communication breaks down; or,
- use new signs which occur in conversations, making use of them as soon as appropriate and asking for confirmation that a form used is appropriate.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Practise and reflect on a variety of productive strategies* to enhance communication, such as:
- apply knowledge of sentence patterns and ASL structure to form new sentences;
- employ circumlocution and definition to compensate for gaps in vocabulary; or
- practise facial expressions, movement, location and non-manual signals (e.g., facial expressions, mouth morphemes, head nod/shake, shoulder shift/contrastive structure/spatial organization) to assist in effective communication.

indicators.text: Imitate and experiment with basic non-manual features such as common handshapes, movement and location of signs to convey different meanings.

indicators.text: Describe the elements of a signed fictional short story (e.g., character, setting, plot, conflict, theme).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Make inferences by interpreting signed text and identify and justify the evidence on which the inferences were based.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Derive information from signed text and represent it with graphics to assist with comprehension and memory of signs (e.g., word maps, mind maps, diagrams, charts).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate a variety of media (e.g., articles, blogs/vlogs, poetry, film, drama) produced in ASL.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Respond to communication with others by acknowledging requests, granting or denying permission, accepting or refusing invitations and indicating choice from among several options.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify more sophisticated techniques (e.g., play on signs) used to convey humour in ASL.

outcomes.statement: Apply knowledge of American Sign Language, in familiar situations and for a variety of purposes, to impart information, share emotions and personal perspectives, achieve objectives and for enjoyment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Exchange ideas and information using complete ASL sentences in short conversations on a range of familiar topics such as national events and issues or social life.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond appropriately and attentively in conversations by asking questions to gain knowledge and clarify understanding.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Relate a set of instructions with appropriate sequence, rules, conditions and imperatives.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Express thoughts, ideas, opinions and feelings for specific purposes and audiences using signed text and visual media in guided situations.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Narrate a personal experience, event or situation with supporting detail.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create stories with descriptive sentences and sequences of events about familiar contexts such as cultural traditions or hobbies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct research based on personal inquiry into a topic related to familiar contexts such as national events and issues or professions and occupations.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Present a factual report based on personal inquiry with a visual component that contributes to the effectiveness of the presentation.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Contribute to group discussion by identifying problems and proposing solutions.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Use ASL for aesthetic purposes and for personal enjoyment with emerging skill (e.g., express humour, perform skits or songs, create stories).

outcomes.statement: Explore Deaf culture in Canada by examining historical and contemporary elements of Deaf culture and investigating the cultural and linguistic diversity of Deaf culture.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Select and examine information about Deaf culture from authentic sources.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Participate in activities and experiences to develop understanding of Deaf culture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Inquire into how society’s perceptions of Deaf culture have changed over time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the challenges Deaf people have faced as a result of discriminatory perspectives and non-inclusive services.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess ways others can advocate for people who are Deaf, deaf or heard of hearing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify similarities and differences between students’ other languages and ASL.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Make connections between some elements of Deaf culture and student’s own culture by identifying and examining commonalities and differences, especially in regards to people of similar age who are deaf, deafened or hard of hearing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry regarding diverse groups within Deaf culture using questions such as “How does the language we use reflect our culture?”.

outcomes.statement: Research and share findings about personal and career opportunities available within the Deaf community in Canada.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate and compare information about Deaf institutions and organizations in Canada and the supports they provide the Deaf community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify national impacts and contributions to the arts, sports, and/or work force made by the deaf, deafened and hard of hearing community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research ASL training and certification opportunities available locally, provincially and nationally.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the necessary qualifications and certifications for careers that require fluency in multiple languages such as ASL.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 12 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Apply creative processes for producing arts expressions within a local context.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss and examine how creating in the arts is a process that can be explored in multiple ways (e.g., imagining, planning, researching, generating, experimenting, risking, observing, drafting, reflecting, documenting, practicing, refining, sharing).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how place-based inquiry is dependent on the local context (e.g., locale, people, history, season).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research local place (e.g., local artists, history, geography) as inspiration for arts expression.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine and conduct a place-based artistic inquiry, drawing on ideas, resources and influences from one’s place (e.g., current urban issues, rural or land-based sources of inspiration, newcomers’ worldviews, First Nations and Métis perspectives on local historic events, environmental or social sustainability concerns).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Utilize technology as a tool to organize, express and share ideas.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create place-based arts expressions (e.g., compose music inspired by community, use found objects in visual art, create dance in response to community issue, create drama about local history).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Document and reflect on the creative process (e.g., challenges, discoveries).

outcomes.statement: Design and produce, individually or collaboratively, a multidisciplinary arts expression.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research multidisciplinary arts examples to use as inspiration for own work (e.g., interview artists in person or online, search for project examples).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experiment with various tools, materials, techniques and technologies to combine multiple arts disciplines.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a multidisciplinary project (e.g., individual student or small groups combine art forms, some students combine arts with other disciplines such as science or math).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Document and reflect on ideas, skills, techniques and technologies incorporated in own multidisciplinary project (e.g., individual project or collaborative work).

outcomes.statement: Communicate ideas that have personal meaning, creatively through the arts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on personal experiences as possible sources of inspiration for arts expression.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experiment with various techniques and skills to express personal meaning (e.g., memory, event, experience, concern, interest).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Communicate, through the arts, thoughts and feelings about an idea, event or concept that has personal meaning.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Take risks and discuss the value of mistakes and challenges in contributing to growth.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Collaborate to construct criteria to use when providing feedback throughout the creative process.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply feedback to improve creative work.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the communication of ideas and intent of own work.

outcomes.statement: Investigate use of own and others’ artistic voice.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Investigate inquiry questions such as:
- How is voice represented in each art form?
- How does one develop artistic voice?
- How do we see voice expressed in the work of others?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on own ideas and development of artistic voice (e.g., identifying one’s preferred style, experimenting with ideas of personal relevance, expressing one’s sense of humour).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Express ideas in own style and personal voice.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss potential meanings of ‘artistic merit’.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Establish goals and work towards developing a sense of ‘artistic merit’ in an area of the arts and discover possible engagements within the community.

outcomes.statement: Collaborate with peers and others to build an arts community with a shared purpose.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Decide on a shared purpose for an arts expression/project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop through collaboration with peers and others, where applicable, a plan for the creation of artistic work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create an artistic work with a shared purpose.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Gather feedback on the artistic work during the process and at project completion.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Construct rubrics with peers to determine expectations for collaborative work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on strengths of the work and challenges overcome.

outcomes.statement: Conduct an inquiry into how the arts can challenge or reinforce societal norms of a given time and place.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate questions for inquiry into how the arts reinforce or challenge norms of various time periods.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and discuss examples of controversial arts expressions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the influence of pop culture on societal norms.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine selected First Nations, Métis and international Indigenous artists who challenge societal inequities through their arts (e.g., treaty education outcome SI11 - analyze how the unfulfilled aspects of treaties, with international Indigenous people, have resulted in inequities).

outcomes.statement: Investigate artistic pathways and potential careers within the arts, or other creative fields, of personal interest.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Begin to develop a portfolio of examples that demonstrate skills and interests in the arts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore a creative opportunity one might pursue.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate and identify creative careers that would suit one’s strengths, beliefs and interests.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine working conditions associated with careers in the arts (e.g., travel requirements, working project to project, earning potential, training and professional development opportunities and costs, intense periods of work followed by gaps in employment, maintaining or sharing an artistic space, opportunities for scholarships and grants).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of promotion and advocacy if pursuing a career in the arts (e.g., advertising online, social media).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Refine personal learning plan for continued development and involvement in the arts (e.g., find people in community that share one’s interests).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how the arts support, influence and shape diverse communities (e.g., gender and sexual diversity, people with disabilities, ethnic groups, popular music sub-cultures, social media-based groups).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine local arts expressions and discuss the benefits to communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate inquiry questions concerning the value of the arts for all members of communities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Advocate for the arts in own communities (e.g., create an visual display, exhibition or performance, commercial advertisement, podcast).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Participate in a service learning opportunity involving the arts (e.g., performance at seniors’ home, raising money for foodbank through drama or dance production, selling art work).

outcomes.statement: Explore connections between the arts and ways of knowing (e.g., multicultural, Indigenous, multiple literacies, emotional, intuitive, STEAM disciplines).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Generate inquiry questions to examine the meaning of “ways of knowing” such as:
- What are some cultural ways of knowing?
- What are some subject area or discipline-based ways of knowing?
- What is meant by multiple literacies?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research artists to discover how the work was/is created and its sources of inspiration (e.g., Leonardo’s images, Jane Ash Poitras’ images, Martha Graham’s technique, A Tribe Called Red’s electronic music).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and engage (e.g., in person, online) with artists from various cultural backgrounds to explore connections between the arts and diverse worldviews.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the work of artists who incorporate diverse disciplines within their arts practice (e.g., STEAM - science, technology, engineering, arts, mathematics) and incorporate interdisciplinary ideas into own work.

outcomes.statement: Examine how artists use arts to raise awareness about place and sustainability (e.g., social, economic, environmental).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into ways that artists respond to the natural world without harming the environment (e.g., How do artists source and harvest resources sustainably?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine arts expressions created in response to diverse environments (e.g., constructed, imagined, ecological).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research Indigenous artists whose work incorporates cultural references and/or reflects concern for sustainability.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the use of arts as activism in various places (e.g., locally, nationally, internationally).

outcomes.statement: Apply injury prevention principles to ensure safe work performance in the autobody trade.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1B: Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE), including dust masks, approved respirators, coveralls, chemical resistant gloves, eye and hearing protection and footwear.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify, label, store and handle hazardous materials according to Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the fire plan for the work area, including components such as fire alarms, fire extinguishers, exits and procedures, and make recommendations for improvements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess hazards and apply appropriate safety procedures when working in a confined space.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Disconnect batteries and other power sources prior to undertaking autobody repairs where appropriate.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury or material and equipment damage as a result of unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the proper procedures to follow to report a workplace injury.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply safe and fair work practices, including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess the ergonomic design of the work space and implement appropriate procedures to ensure safety.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Implement a plan for a safe and healthy classroom and shop environment.

outcomes.statement: Use gas metal art welding (GMAW) equipment to complete specified autobody welds.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Welding in Autobody (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of GMAW equipment such as nozzles, contact tips, liners, wire rolls, gauges and flow meters, amperage adjustment and voltage adjustment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the importance of employing correct start-up and shut-down procedures for GMAW equipment including checking and cleaning up the work station.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare various types of wire and shielding gases used for GMAW.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Disassemble, clean and reassemble GMAW welder components.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify metals and perform preparation and assembly tasks prior to welding.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform and analyze a variety of specified welds, including plug weld, spot weld, butt weld and lap weld.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the purpose and proper use and fit of personal protective equipment (PPE) required for welding, including eye protection (lens shades), clothing, hearing protection and footwear while identifying the hazards from which they protect individuals.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Ensure all PPE is cleaned appropriately.

outcomes.statement: Use and maintain autobody air, hydraulic and electric tools and equipment following safe procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Advanced Tooling (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 3 and 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the safe use of air, hydraulic and electric tools such as pneumatic chisel, air ratchet, impact wrench, air polisher, air sand blaster, blow gun, air metal shears, power riveter, floor jack, safety stand and hydraulic rams and attachments.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform correct procedures when using hand, stationary and power tools for specific autobody repairs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Inspect air, hydraulic and electric tools before use and tag for repair as required.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain and store air, hydraulic and electric tools and equipment appropriately.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize and follow safe work practices when using air, hydraulic and electric tools.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research and estimate the cost to purchase air, hydraulic and electric tools to enter the autobody trade.

outcomes.statement: Assess damaged areas to refinish and repaint parts of an automobile.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Automobile Refinishing and Repainting (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-30 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 12

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Estimate technical measurements and determine appropriate procedures and materials to refinish and repaint parts of an automobile.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Prepare a cost estimate of the materials needed to refinish and repaint parts of an automobile.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Practice proper safety techniques when using a sandblaster for metal preparation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply proper sanding techniques using the appropriate type of sand paper to prepare the surface for painting.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the use of reducers and thinners in autobody repair.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practice proper techniques and safety procedures to use a spray gun (e.g., siphon and gravity fed), air compressor, air hose and air regulator to paint part or all of an automobile.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Differentiate between the types of spray booths such as a prep station, downdraft, semi-downdraft and cross-draft used in autobody repair.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and method of application of different types (e.g., epoxy primer, urethane primer surface, polyester primer, urethane sealer and acid etch) of automotive primers.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the purpose and method of application of different (e.g., acrylic lacquer, acrylic enamel, polyurethane and base coat/clear coat) types of automotive paints.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Apply proper techniques to mask an automobile and describe over-masking and under-masking.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Practise proper safety procedures such as wearing coveralls, rubber gloves and safety glasses and using an appropriate respirator to apply automotive primers, sealers and paints.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine the effects of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) on the environment.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Implement a plan to design and organize the workspace to prevent work-related injuries when refinishing and repainting an automobile.

outcomes.statement: Assess panel misalignment issues and carry out repairs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Panel Alignment (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 3 and 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the range of corrective work procedures that may be required to align a panel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine panel misalignment issues (e.g., vertical misalignment, loose latches, hinges) that require corrective action.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Prepare a cost estimate to align a panel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the appropriate corrective action and tools to align a panel (e.g., hood, door, trunk lid, fender, quarter panel).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine proper measurements for panel alignment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate proper use of hand and power tools to align panels.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize and follow safe work practices when using appropriate hand and power tools to align panels.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent workplace injuries when conducting panel alignment.

outcomes.statement: Analyze types and functions of automobile glass and carry out glass repairs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Glass Removal and Installation (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 3 and 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the different types (e.g., laminated and tempered) of glass and their purpose in an automobile.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research legislation related to approved automotive glass materials.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine glass damage (e.g., circular bullseyes, linear cracks, crack chips, dings, pits and star-shaped breaks), location of damage (e.g., inside of windshield, deep damage to both layers of glass, complex multiple cracks, very long cracks, contaminated or edge cracks) and identify appropriate tools, materials and procedures to conduct glass repairs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of using original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and aftermarket automobile glass in repair.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine required procedures to remove and install glass in an automobile.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate appropriate use of hand and power tools to repair glass (e.g., windshield, sidelite and backlite).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise correct safety procedures such as wearing gloves, long sleeved apparel and eye protection when repairing glass.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate issues and potential solutions related to recycling automotive glass.

outcomes.statement: Examine the evolution of automobile air bags and associated sensors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Air Bags (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the location and function of the components of an automobile air bag system.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of air bag systems in automobiles, including increased safety achieved through each improved design.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe “safing” and arming sensors to ensure deployment of an air bag when a collision is severe enough to warrant it.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how certified technicians disarm an air bag system prior to repair and re-arm air bag systems when finished a repair.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Propose an innovative air bag system, including considerations such as automobile type, rate of deployment, placement of air bag system, laws of motion and injury prevention to automobile occupants.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare legislation related to air bags in Saskatchewan with other Canadian jurisdictions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how automobiles are certified to be road safe after a collision.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the advantages and disadvantages of turning on and off automobile air bag sensors.

outcomes.statement: Assess the interior and exterior condition of an automobile and apply detailing procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Automobile Detailing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the interior and exterior condition of an automobile to identify required detailing procedures.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Complete interior (e.g., vacuuming, brushing, steam cleaning, glass cleaning, leather trimming, re-vacuuming, wiping, perfuming) and exterior (e.g., washing, drying, claying, polishing, sealing) detailing of an automobile in addition to:
- inspecting the glass and completing necessary repairs;
- cleaning the chrome with appropriate products; and,
- inspecting the headlight and turn signal glass, light bulbs and completing necessary repairs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Analyze operational complications such as the heating and air conditioning (HVAC) system, stained switches and hazy windows on the interior of the automobile in addition to:
- inspecting the interior and removing after-market attachments that are loose or worn;
- inspecting the carpet and seats for rips, tears and stains (e.g., soil, grease, chocolate, oil, candy, road tar or blood) and completing necessary repairs; and,
- inspecting the door and window weather stripping and completing necessary repairs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the appropriate materials, costs and tools to detail the interior and exterior of the automobile.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the environmental effects of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) used in detailing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine short- and long-term health concerns related to chemical exposure and demonstrate the appropriate safety procedures when using chemicals.

outcomes.statement: Assess damaged areas and carry out repairs to automobile trim.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Automobile Trim Removal and Installation (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 3 and 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify areas of automobile trim needing repair.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Prepare a cost estimate to remove and replace trim.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Identify interior and exterior trim materials and fastening systems (e.g., clips, adhesives, screws) and carry out the process to repair trim including:
- removing door panels and upholstery parts to access fasteners;
- removing vinyl, overlays and decals; and,
- removing weather stripping from all areas of the automobile and installing new materials.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine an automobile and adjust and service trim accessories as needed.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate appropriate use of hand and power tools to remove and install trim.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Practice correct safety procedures such as wearing gloves, long sleeved apparel and eye protection when repairing trim.

outcomes.statement: Analyze plastics in automobile design and carry out plastic repairs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Plastic Repair (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a

- What is my schedule of work hours?

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, with teacher guidance, proper instrumental tone and technique.

courses.name: Biology 20, 30

legacyEvidence.reason: 1992 guide; not in the site's menus; its 30-level part is replaced by the renewed Biology 30 (id 68)
evidence: Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its objectives under 9 headings: “Introduction to Biology”, “Ecological Organization”, “The Diversity of Life”, “Agricultural Botany of Saskatchewan”, “The Chemical Basis of Life”, “Cell Structure and Function”, “Genetics”, “Animal Systems”, “Evolution”.

courses.problem: No outcomes are published on the site for this curriculum; the objectives are taken from its curriculum document (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=67); see `document`.

items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined and changed within biology.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of biology.
To develop students' abilities to access knowledge.
Understand the nature of the study of biology.
Examine the types of questions which biologists investigate.
Exhibit a curiosity about life and the conditions which support life.
Appreciate the nature of scientific investigations and the findings of science.
Recognize the relationship between what is studied in biology and daily life.
Define the term biology.
Use a microscope to examine cells.
Develop proper techniques for handling and care of a microscope.
View prepared slides.
Prepare wet-mount slides.
Sketch what is seen in the field of view.
Estimate sizes of objects observed.
Compare the images produced by light microscopes and electron microscopes.
Discuss examples of how the microscope has altered what we know.
Explain the importance of theory in biology.
Outline the key aspects of a scientific theory. (See the Unit Overview and web.)
Discuss the development of the cell theory.
Recognize the link between the development of cell theory and the technology available to study cells.
Realize the significance of cell theory in establishing the relatedness of all living organisms.
Examine the principles of natural selection as identified by Darwin and Wallace.
Explain how natural selection is the basis of the theory of evolution.
Describe how a theory might change using an example(s).

items.text: To strengthen students' knowledge and understanding of how to compute, measure, estimate and interpret numerical data, when to apply these skills and techniques, and why these processes apply to the study of populations.
To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To promote intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences and objects in the context of the study of the environment.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of ecology.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To support students in coming to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of the study of life.
To develop an understanding that technology both shapes society and is shaped by society.
Explain how the interactions among the soil, climate, and living organisms produce the ecosystems which can be observed.
Identify the components of soil.
Describe the soil types of Saskatchewan.
Determine how soil characteristics influence plant growth.
Describe how climatic variations in Saskatchewan influence plant growth.
Investigate variations in plant growth on slopes.
Identify some soil microorganisms.
Discuss the importance of soil microorganisms.
Appreciate that the soil and the climate are the keys to life in Saskatchewan, and on this planet.
Investigate the interrelationship of agriculture and the environment.
Discuss the following cycles and attempt to illustrate their interrelationship: water, carbon dioxide-oxygen, nitrogen.
Analyze a variety of ecosystems.
Understand the concept of niche and habitat.
Identify the biotic and abiotic components and interactions in the ecosystems observed.
Describe how the human community is dependent on the soil, water, and air.
Formulate some food chains and webs involving the human community.
Describe how the human community in which one lives is dependent on, and influenced by, the climate.
Identify both symbiotic and competitive relationships among organisms within a community.
Investigate a natural community in the neighbourhood of the school.
Compare the similarities and differences between the natural community and the constructed/human community.
Compare communities which have other soil types or other climate types.
Discuss succession in communities.
Identify how human activity, e.g. agriculture and urbanization, has altered succession or changed its rate.
Indicate some determiners of succession.
Describe life in past ecosystems.
Examine the evidence of life in the past.
Debate change and extinction theories.
Investigate the role of humans in creating and sustaining conditions which alter the rate of ecological change.
Explain how populations are counted.
Recall the criteria which define a population.
Identify some populations of plants or animals in the local area.
Describe methods of estimation by sampling.
Estimate some populations using one or more methods.
Analyze population changes.
Identify factors which influence reproduction rates and death rates.
Recognize factors which affect immigration and emigration.
Compare cyclic populations and stable populations.
Discuss the carrying capacity of planet Earth for the human population.
Recognize ecological sequencing.
Identify the sequencing present in the following terms: biosphere, biome, ecosystem, community, and population.
Review several examples of biomes by discussing some of their major kinds of plants.
Draw a climatogram and discuss temperature and moisture as major determiners of a specific ecological area.

factorsEmphasized: D2 scientists and technologists are human
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To use a wide range of possibilities for developing students' knowledge of the major concepts within biology.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To develop compassionate, empathetic and fair-minded students who can make positive contributions to society as individuals and as members of groups.
Describe the principles of classification.
Discuss everyday examples of classification. (Then discuss the value of having a biological classification and some of the unique problems that might manifest themselves.)
Compare several different ways organisms are grouped into kingdoms. (It would be useful to have the students see the historical development of the 5 kingdom structure from a 2 kingdom structure.)
Understand the system of binomial nomenclature. (Discuss the 7 major classification units which include Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, and Species and their associated relationships.)
Use dichotomous keys to help identify organisms. (One could demonstrate that a key locates actual organisms just as binomial nomenclature and the species level identifies actual organisms.)
Recognize the role of monera, protists, and fungi in the ecosystem.
Describe viral structure and activity.
Identify some viral diseases prevalent in plants, animals, and humans in Saskatchewan.
Discuss the various ways bacteria are classified.
Describe some diseases caused by bacteria which affect organisms living in Saskatchewan.
Identify some valuable roles played in the ecosystem by bacteria.
Distinguish between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
Describe how the protist kingdom is classified.
Collect, culture, and observe a variety of protists.
Describe the general characteristics of fungi.
Collect and observe some samples of fungi.
Identify the basic structural features of bacteria.
Describe the diversity of plants.
Compare nonvascular and vascular plants.
Identify, describe, and collect some examples of nonvascular and vascular plants.
Discuss the ways that vascular plants are classified.
Describe grain crops and forage crops grown in Saskatchewan. (Correlate with Unit 20-4.)
Chart the ranges of representative plants of Saskatchewan.
Recognize the diversity of animals.

Describe the characteristics of the major animal phyla. (It is suggested that the teacher consider a mollusk such as a clam or snail, an annelid such as an earthworm, an arthropod such as an insect or spider, and one or more of the chordates, as time allows, which would include a mammal.)
Identify members of each phylum which contains animals native to Saskatchewan.
Describe the habitat and niche of animals native to Saskatchewan.
Contrast innate behaviour in animals with learned behaviour.
Describe social behaviour in animals.

printedNotes.text: Note: Objective 1.8 should be seen as a general organizer and is not intended to be used to rigorously cover great detail on plant tissues.

items.text: To promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences, and objects within the context of the study of ecosystems.
To use a wide range of possibilities for developing students' knowledge of the major concepts within biology.
To develop students' abilities to meet their own learning needs.
To support students in coming to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of the study of life.
Recognize the various biological processes associated with plant systems.
Compare sexual and asexual reproduction in angiosperms.
Describe the processes of pollen production, fertilization and seed formation of plants.
Describe the means by which solutions are transported through plants.
Investigate the environmental and biological influences on growth.
Describe the major plant systems of various cereal, oilseed, pulse, forage, or native crops.
Identify the effects of climate and pest on different stages of crop development.
Review the three major structures of a plant which include the root, stem and leaf along with their locations and functions.

Identify four broad tissue areas found in a plant which include meristematic, protective, vascular and fundamental.
• meristematic: frequent mitotic division for growth which includes cambium.
• protective: epidermis and cuticle.
• vascular: conducts water and minerals (xylem and phloem).
• fundamental tissue: three functions which include food storage, food production and support. (Examples include sclerenchyma, collenchyma and parenchyma. If you use these terms, discuss the Greek/Latin origins and help students make these connections.)
Appreciate the relation of Saskatchewan's biogeographical regions and agricultural activity.
Identify the characteristics of all the biogeographical regions of Saskatchewan.
Compare kinds of grain and forage crops.
Discuss the reasons and issues associated with various land uses and crop diversity.
Identify various species of trees, shrubs, plants and grasses of Saskatchewan.
Compare such plant characteristics as reproduction and growth patterns as they relate to the Saskatchewan environment.
Describe the internal and external influences on plant growth.
Describe the function and effect of cytokinins, auxins, and gibberelins.
Contrast tropisms with responses due to changes in turgor pressure.
Investigate how plants respond to chemicals such as fertilizers and herbicides.
Examine the effect on soil of the application of fertilizers and biofertilizers.
Identify the impact and examples of soil degradation.
Recognize the interconnectedness of agriculture and the environment.
Describe the impact of agriculture on the local environment.
Identify local and global issues associated with agriculture.
Appreciate the complexity of issues such as soil degradation, world hunger and environmental concerns.

notes: Structure as printed: for each core unit, 'Factors of Scientific Literacy Which Should be Emphasized' (codes defined in the guide's Dimensions of Scientific Literacy section; kept as printed in factorsEmphasized), 'Common Essential Learnings Foundational Objectives' (code = CEL abbreviation as printed), and 'Biology Foundational and Learning Objectives' (bold numbered foundational objectives, decimal-numbered learning objectives).
The guide says learning objectives 'can be selected from those listed or can be developed by the teacher and students' (p. 3 printed); they are not all mandatory.
Biology 20: 4 core units (78 h minimum) + optional time; Biology 30: 5 core units + optional time. Optional Plans pages list suggestions only (no objectives) and are not extracted.
The guide states 'Biology 20 is not a prerequisite for Biology 30' (printed p. 82).
Codes like '1' and '1.1' restart in every unit; they are only unique within a unit (and level).

Text extracted with pdfjs-dist (legacy build) from a 1992 WordPerfect-generated PDF; two-column pages split at x=300. Bullet glyphs (WPTypographicSymbols '!') and box-drawing dashes (WPBoxDrawing ')') were mapped to '•' and '—'.

Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of rights and responsibilities in relation to workplace safety.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15B: Workplace Safety – Rights and Responsibilities (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research employer and worker responsibilities with respect to health and safety standards as required by law in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss steps that can be taken to refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios to demonstrate how to properly refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019 and associated Regulations, and how they affect safe workplace practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how workers can participate in and support health and safety activities in the workplace. (e.g., Occupational Health and Safety Committees, professional development, training and following safety procedures).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents, dangerous occurrences, injuries, or illnesses immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among the four Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) hazard categories including physical (e.g., heavy lifting, repetitive motion, slipping/tripping, working at heights, working alone, cuts and burns), chemical (e.g., chemicals, fumes, vapours and gases), biological (e.g., viruses, fungi, bacteria, mold; bodily fluids; sewage; animal/pet waste; and influenza), and psychological (e.g., harassment and bullying, stress, fatigue and shift work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of potential workplace hazards in the five major categories.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities pertaining to workplace hazards and how they can work together to prevent workplace hazards.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of proper orientation, training, appropriate supervision, workplace inspections and following safe work practices, and provide examples of each for a variety of industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify potential safety hazards in a variety of environments including home, school, and workplace.

indicators.label: h
