outcomes.statement: Examine the fullness of God's covenant through Jesus and how it applies to one's life.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify key events from the breaking of the covenant by Adam and Eve to the fulfillment of God's covenant with humanity through Jesus including Luke 22-24 and Acts 1-2.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Explain how the Resurrection reveals core Catholic beliefs such as:
- new life after death
- hope (CCC 1817-1821)
- Jesus as Lord, pointing to the heart of the Christian faith
- the possibility of transformation throughout one's life.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the nature of love including its prominence within the Eucharistic covenant and examples of signs of love in society (e.g., agape/unconditional, eros/romantic, philia and philio/brotherly and sisterly, encyclical Deus Caritas Est – God is Love).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to explore compelling questions about how the Eucharistic covenant affects one's everyday life involving core concepts such as grace, salvation, forgiveness, hope, love and joy.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Represent the Catholic understanding of Eucharist as a source of joy and hope supporting the call to live joyfully within a covenant relationship with Christ.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the following concept: Good works don't bring salvation, but the joy of salvation reveals itself in good works through God's grace.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reassess one's response to Jesus' call to a personal relationship with him through the Eucharistic covenant.

outcomes.statement: Examine the Christian conviction of Jesus as Lord.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how belief in Jesus as Lord affects one's life and community (e.g., joy, hope, forgiveness, generosity).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Evaluate Church doctrine relating to Jesus as Lord, second person of the Trinity, such as:
- Creator of all
- pre-existent Word made flesh
- divinity and humanity of Jesus (i.e., Hypostatic Union).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Evaluate Church doctrine relating to Jesus as Lord of humanity through Mary, the bearer of God (i.e., Theotokos), such as:
- The Immaculate Conception (i.e., Mary preserved from the stain of Original Sin in St. Anne's womb)
- The Incarnation / The Annunciation (i.e., the Word made flesh)
- The Nativity – virgin birth (i.e., Jesus conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the identity of Jesus as Lord through the use of C.S. Lewis' "liar, lunatic, or Lord" apologetic argument.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Support the Christian conviction of Jesus as Lord using scriptural examples such as:
- teachings of Jesus (e.g., parables, Sermon on the Mount)
- Peter's declaration about Jesus at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus' response and subsequent renaming of Peter (i.e., Mt. 16: 13-20)
- The Passion, resurrection and ascension
- the experience of the centurion at the foot of the cross (i.e., Mk. 15:39)
- Jesus being:
- the pre-existing Word (i.e., John1:1-5),
- the way, the truth, and the life (i.e., John 14: 6)
- the son of David, the son of Abraham (i.e., Mt.1:1)
- "I am" through multiple personal identity statements in the gospel of John.

outcomes.statement: Assess how living the Beatitudes of Christ affects individuals and society.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Discuss understanding of the Beatitudes including:
- 'poor in spirit' – recognizing one's spiritual poverty and powerlessness to save oneself
- 'those who mourn' – acknowledging wounded relationships and the need for God's grace
- 'the meek' – keeping one's power or strength under control; curbing selfish desires to be obedient to God's will
- 'those who hunger and thirst for righteousness' – desiring to learn and do the will of God; seeking to live in right relationships
- 'the merciful' – showing forgiveness and/or compassion in a time of need
- 'the pure in heart' – setting one's mind and will to God's call abiding in faith, hope, and love
- 'peacemakers' – reconciling broken relationships
- 'those persecuted for the sake of righteousness' – suffering for following the will of God, living the Beatitudes with courage.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate the concept of joy from happiness and explain how one's joy results from living the Beatitudes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Support the concept that living the Beatitudes is a pursuit of goodness involving more than the avoidance of evil.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how the Beatitudes call individuals to assume personal responsibility within society (e.g., support cultural understanding, environmental and social sustainability, and the marginalized).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Represent the joys and challenges of living out the Beatitudes (e.g., role play, short story, cartoons).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss how individuals and movements, although flawed, can impact society by demonstrating characteristics of one or more of the Beatitudes:
- 'poor in spirit' (eg., Saint Mother Teresa, Saint. Paisios of Mount Athos)
- 'those who mourn' (e.g., Lieutenant-General Roméo Dallaire, marches for missing and murdered Aboriginal women)
- 'the meek' (e.g., Moses, Rosa Parks, Saint Pope John XXIII)
- 'those who hunger and thirst for righteousness' (e.g., Blessed Oscar Romero, Wangari Maathai, Anne Cools, environmental activist groups)
- 'the merciful' (e.g., Irena Sendler, Nelson Mandela, Tommy Douglas, Venerable Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky)
- 'the pure in heart' (e.g., Mary and Joseph as the parents of Jesus, Joseph Chiwatenhwa , Mary Ellen (Bellelle) Guerin)
- 'peacemakers' (e.g., Betty Williams and Mairead Corrigan, Jimmy Carter, Fr. Albert Lacombe, Pîhtokahanapiwiyin/Poundmaker)
- 'those persecuted for the sake of righteousness' (e.g., Agnes MacPhail, Saints Felicity and Perpetua, Louis Riel).

outcomes.statement: Examine how the Paschal Mystery, as the foundation of the Catholic faith, shapes views on suffering, death and resurrection.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the struggles and joy of the Paschal Mystery (i.e., Jesus' suffering, death and resurrection).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how Jesus' suffering, death and resurrection reveals the depth of God's love and power to bring life from death and light from darkness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how arts expressions may challenge, clarify and develop religious and spiritual understanding of the mysteries of suffering, death and resurrection (e.g., hope-filled imagery, icons, expressions of joy, concepts of compassion).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Construct personal views on the nature of suffering by comparing Catholic views of 'redemptive suffering' in light of the joy of the Gospel with:
- traditional First Nations and Métis beliefs
- various worldviews (e.g., Viktor Frankl, Helen Keller, the Buddha).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain or represent personal viewpoints on how one knows that the Creator God understands his or her suffering (e.g., physical, mental, emotional, spiritual domains of the medicine wheel, the suffering of Jesus as the second person of the Trinity).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how the Church calls the faithful to respond in hope to people suffering from grief, end-of-life challenges, and illness (e.g., St. Pope John Paull II's Apostolic Letter On Human Suffering).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how one's personal faith impacts wellness (e.g., physical, mental, emotional, spiritual domains of the medicine wheel).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how Tradition complements Scripture as a form of Revelation in the Catholic church.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss Tradition (i.e., Apostolic or Holy Tradition) and Scripture as the two complementary forms of Revelation (see CCC 80-83).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between Apostolic Tradition and ecclesial traditions within the Catholic Church.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Discuss ecclesial traditions within the Church such as:
- meditations involving stained glass windows such as Blessed are the Pure in Heart and others at St. Augustine's Church in Wilcox, Saskatchewan.
- cultural music including First Nations drumming within Catholic masses
- pilgrim events such as:
- Byzantine celebrations at the Shrine of the Venerable Nun Martyrs Olympia and Laurentia in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan
- events at Saint-Laurent de Grandin established by Fransaskois and Métis peoples
- the annual Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes Pilgrimage at St. Peter's Colony, Saskatchewan.
- sacramentals (e.g., blessings) as distinct from sacraments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the role of Peter within Tradition (e.g., the founding of the Church, Apostolic succession).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish between acts of veneration and worship from a Catholic religious perspective and show how acts of veneration (i.e., devotions) to the Virgin Mary and the saints are part of the Tradition of the Catholic Church.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine liturgy and the Mass within Tradition and their role in Revelation.

outcomes.statement: Examine the Church's mission and its actualization.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review the mission of the Church (CCC773) and recognize how the Church is to be a gift to the world especially in the ways of love, joy, peace and service (e.g., Jn. 15:10-12).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Explain how the evangelical mission of the Church is supported by the five actions identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops including:
- Proclaiming Jesus Christ
- Worship Christ through the sacraments
- Form a communion of people
- Give witness
- Serve.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Describe how evangelization is supported by models of Church proposed by Cardinal Avery Dulles including:
- Sacrament
- Institution
- Servant
- Herald
- Community of disciples.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how the mission of the Church is supported through the celebration of sacraments in various Catholic churches through their rites (e.g., Roman, Byzantine, Chaldean, Coptic).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Contrast the communal nature of the Church with the individualism of modern society.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Examine how joyful involvement in the mission of the Church is assisted by traditions and practices such as:
- use of the liturgical calendar (e.g., feast days, memorial days, liturgical seasons)
- Church pilgrimages or reverence of holy sites
- seeking grace through the sacraments and everyday life
- patronage of the arts throughout Church history
- honouring of Canonized Saints and other Catholic holy men and women
- Church youth groups.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss challenges faced by the Church as she strives to fulfill her mission (e.g., political and social challenges).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how the faith and works relationship impacts the mission of the Church (e.g., an action-oriented mission).

outcomes.statement: Contrast Catholic teachings with secular views regarding human sexual morality and reproductive ethics.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze key themes within Blessed Pope Paul VI's encyclical Humanae Vitae such as:
- humanity belongs to God rather than everything belonging to humanity (e.g., my body, my life, my choices)
- sex as a gift from God
- sex cannot be separated from its purpose (i.e., a unitive act conveying committed love with openness to life).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze key themes within Saint Pope John Paul II's Theology of the Body such as:
- the body expresses the person (e.g., the power and symbolism of body language in our actions including sexual acts)
- sex is an expression of love and a gift from God (e.g., chastity aids in understanding the positive purpose and basic 'goodness' of sex, a reflection of Christ's love relationship with the Church)
- the contradictory natures of love and lust
- discerning the value of self and others including the call to love throughout one's life
- a sacramental worldview (e.g., invisible realities, grace influencing ethics).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the ethical implications of Natural Family Planning as a form of birth control and other birth avoidance techniques (e.g., various forms of artificial contraceptives, sterility-inducing surgical procedures).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Evaluate implications of Catholic, secular and scientific views on issues of sexual behaviour and contraception methods (e.g., chastity, promiscuity, direct vs. indirect sterilization or contraception).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate implications of Catholic, secular and scientific views on moral issues of reproductive ethics (e.g., in-vitro fertilization, designer babies, gender selection practices and eugenics).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Examine the relationship between sexual morality and:
- human dignity
- free will
- power dynamics.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Debate complexities surrounding the issue of clear personal consent including popular culture terminology (e.g., culture of sexual consent, no means no, silence is not consent, or rape culture).

outcomes.statement: Examine how Catholic social teachings influence personal views regarding issues of labour and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Investigate moral issues and consequences for individuals and society relating to:
- labour (e.g., foreign labourers, forced labour, child labour, humane working conditions, employment equity, dishonest accounting practices)
- the environment (e.g., privatization of water, sustainability issues, deforestation, resource extraction, food production practices such as use of animal growth hormones and genetic engineering).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast Catholic, relativistic and Indigenous views of justice concerning labour, the environment and globalization (e.g., legal and moral considerations).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss perspectives on the private, communal or government ownership of water, land and resources from Catholic and various worldviews including those of First Nations and Métis peoples.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess one's opinions and actions concerning various labour and environmental issues (e.g., human trafficking, child labour, climate change).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Investigate how issues of labour and the environment connect to:
- the Creation accounts of Genesis
- the Beatitudes of Christ
- the concept of stewardship.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss contributions of individuals, although flawed, who served as leaders in the field of the environment such as:
- David Schindler and Ronald Reagan for their respective scientific and political leadership surrounding acid rain
- St. Kateri Tekakwitha as patron saint of the environment and ecology
- Pope Francis for his encyclical Laudato Si'.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Discuss contributions of individuals and movements, although flawed, that served as leaders in the field of labour such as:
- Dorothy Day and the Catholic Worker Movement
- Fr. Moses Coady and the Antigonish Movement
- Iqbal Masih as a child labour victim, activist and political martyr
- St. Joseph as patron saint of workers.

outcomes.statement: Assess the value and examine challenges of a life of service in the model of Jesus.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the Catholic understanding of servant leadership including the relationship between service and power (i.e., the ability to create change).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how Jesus is a model of service within Scripture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize how Jesus, by his nature, teachings and actions, is at the root of Catholic social teachings (e.g., the value of solidarity stems from the Incarnation, the preferential option for the poor is reflected in the Beatitudes , the call for social justice is rooted in Jesus' ministry).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between service and the call to 'love as Jesus loved'.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine personal and communal challenges of corporal and spiritual works of mercy within a model of Christ-like service.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Conduct an inquiry into the impact of service on individuals and society considering how service brings:
- joy to an individual
- hope to a community
- peace and justice to a society
- God's grace to humanity.

outcomes.statement: Explain the implications of choosing to live as a "disciple of Christ".
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine implications of the Lord's Prayer for individuals and society.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss challenges and value of living a contemporary Christian life of prayer.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine ways the Church fosters discipleship such as:
- teachings and support for living out the 7 virtues (i.e., the 3 theological virtues of faith, hope and charity and the 4 cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance)
- liturgical seasons as guide to prayer
- Mass/ Divine Liturgy
- liturgy (i.e., the work of the church)
- service
- veneration of saints and Marian devotion
- Scripture study courses
- retreat opportunities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how one's identity as a disciple of Christ within the community of the church is influenced by statements in the Creed including "one, holy, catholic and apostolic" church.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to explore and contribute ideas about the statement: Going to church does not make one a good Christian, but a good Christian will want to go to church.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine one's understanding of and response to a personal call to sainthood using the lives of canonized saints as models of discipleship for contemporary living.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Construct an argument for Mary as a model of discipleship to be valued and emulated through merits such as:
- faithful obedience
- joy
- modelling the Beatitudes (e.g., poor in spirit, meek, pure of heart).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe characteristics of being a disciple of Christ and reflect upon ways of developing these attributes in one's life (e.g., joy in times of tragedy, a spirit of service during times of apathy, gentleness in times of frustration).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Explain how being a disciple of Christ involves courage to live the Gospel in ways such as:
- being 'counter-cultural'
- 'living in the world but not being of the world'
- building a 'culture of encounter'
- being a 'steward of Creation'.

outcomes.statement: Investigate effects of infusion, suppression and rejection of Christian values and teachings on society.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss factors that influence cultural and personal identity (e.g., gospel values, various religious, spiritual, moral and legal views).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how positive and negative portrayals of Christ and Christian teachings affect contemporary society (e.g., portrayals in fictional writing, music, film, academic discourse, architecture, political campaigns).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe effects of the suppression and rejection of Christ and Christian teachings on contemporary individuals, family and society (e.g., the rise of atheism and idolatry, moral relativity or ambiguity, family dysfunction, persecution of Christians, religious extremism, diminished joy in life).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine ways in which Christ and Christian teachings are purposefully and effectively infused in contemporary society (e.g., contemporary worship music, Catholic charitable organizations, Natural Family Planning, Christian corporate philanthropy, Christian prayer at family mealtime, Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, World Youth Day).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify similarities among Church teachings, the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss and represent interpretations of 'the family as the domestic church' (e.g., St. Pope John Paul II's Apostolic Exhortation Familiaris Consortio – The Role of the Family in the Modern World).

outcomes.statement: Examine the benefits and challenges of ecumenical dialogue.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss effects on Christianity of the Great Schism of 1054.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate influences of the Protestant Reformation and Catholic counter-reformation on Christianity and inter-denominational relations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Contrast Catholic and Protestant teachings such as:
- Revelation (e.g., Martin Luther's "Bible alone")
- interpretation of Scripture (e.g., literalists and contextualists)
- the presence of Christ in the Eucharist (e.g., real or symbolic presence)
- the role, training, gender and marital status of the clergy
- the nature of salvation by faith alone vs. the union, by grace, of faith and works
- the theological or scriptural basis for varying number of sacraments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the impact of influential events in modern Church history, including the Second Vatican Council on the Christian call to unity (e.g., Restoration of Unity, 1964).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss examples of Christian churches coming together, seeking to be faithful to Christ's desire that his disciples be one, through:
- common mission or service (e.g., the Anglican rite in communion with Catholics of North America, two or more local Christian denominations working together to feed the hungry, shelter the homeless, provide warm clothing to those need)
- joint witness (e.g., joint communion where appropriate, pro-life rally)
- common prayer (e.g., peace vigils, Week of Prayer for Christian Unity)
- a chance to learn from each other (e.g., The Common Witness Project).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss wounds to Christian unity such as:
- historical divisions (e.g., Church heresies such as Gnosticism, Arianism)
- modern divisions (e.g., the emergence of new sects, churches and cults)
- cultural conflicts including First Nations residential school experiences and others (e.g., misrepresentations of various Christian identities in media and popular culture, pro-life groups pitting church against society).

outcomes.statement: Analyze the personal and societal effects of an imperfect Church institution and imperfect individuals responding to the call for holiness.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Contrast holiness with perfection using John 8:1-11.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collaborate to interpret what it means for the Church to be holy and what it means for people, as individuals, to be holy.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine impacts of sin, acknowledgment of sin, reconciliation and conversion on personal and societal relationships.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Analyze and discuss how a person's faith and religious views may be impacted by religious role models who struggle with issues such as:
- addictions (e.g., drugs, alcohol, gambling, pornography)
- crises of personal faith
- sexual abuse (e.g., as victims or perpetrators).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Analyze effects of the Church's holy missionary work including First Nations residential school experiences and other examples such as:
- World Youth Day
- the establishment and maintenance of holy pilgrimage sites
- the Crusades
- Catholic education throughout the world
- Catholic health care
- Catholic social services.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the relevance of the Beatitudes for those seeking to heed the call to holiness.

outcomes.statement: Describe how one's experience in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat affects one's life and understanding of Catholic identity.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create, in collaboration with one's peers and teacher, a plan for participation in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the planned Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat might affect one's life, faith development and understanding of Catholic identity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact of faith-motivated service and communal endeavors on individuals and communities.

courses.name: Chemistry 20, 30

legacyEvidence.reason: 1992 guide; not in the site's menus; its 30-level part is replaced by the renewed Chemistry 30 (id 69)
evidence: Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its objectives under 21 headings: “Introduction to Chemistry”, “Laboratory Activities”, “Independent Research”, “Atoms and Elements”, “Molecules and Compounds”, “Chemical Reactions”, “Mole Concept and Stoichiometry”, “Optional: Behaviour of Gases”, “Optional: Consumer Chemistry”, “Optional: Organic Chemistry”, “Optional: Teacher Developed Unit”, “Review of Basic Principles”, “Laboratory Activities”, “Independent Research”, “Case Study”, “Solubility and Solutions”, “Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions”, “Reaction Kinetics”, “Equilibrium”, “Acid-Base Equilibria”, “Oxidation and Reduction”.

courses.problem: No outcomes are published on the site for this curriculum; the objectives are taken from its curriculum document (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=70); see `document`.

units.name: Introduction to Chemistry
factorsEmphasized: D2 scientists and technologists are human
D4 science, technology, and the environment
D6 resources for science and technology
D8 limitations of science and technology
D9 social influence of science and technology
D11 science, technology, and other realms
F1 longing to know and understand

items.text: Recognize safe practices and explain the reason for each practice.
Report to the teacher if contact lenses are worn.
Report any allergies to the teacher.
Identify the location of the fire blanket, fire extinguishers, eye wash station, and any other safety equipment.
Know how to use the safety equipment in the laboratory.
Restrain any loose clothing, jewellery, or hair.
Wear eye protection whenever it is prudent or required.
Maintain a clean, uncluttered work area.
Gather and promptly dispose of any broken glass.
Comply with fire drill regulations.
Check procedures before carrying them out.
Follow accepted principles for dispensing, handling, and disposing of chemicals.
Recognize and minimize the hazards of toxic and corrosive chemicals.
Treat all chemicals as if they were hazardous.
Refrain from pipetting by mouth.
Use care when operating a burner.
Neither bring food into the laboratory, nor consume food while in the room.
Wash hands after chemicals have been handled.
Identify and explain how chemistry affects us.
Discuss how advances in chemistry have led to the development of new products.
Outline the societal impact of new chemical products.
Recognize that advances in chemistry are often driven by societal needs.
Explain the relationship between science and technology.
Identify some issues or problems for which a knowledge of chemistry is important in identifying causes and solutions.
Recognize that some problems can not be solved by science.
Use a wide range of language experiences for developing knowledge of the importance of chemistry. (COM)
Show understanding by providing an alternative rephrasing, drawing a diagram or making a model.
Synthesize ideas gleaned from a variety of sources and media.
Identify critical issues in factual and editorial argumentative messages from both print and non-print media.
Create questions as tools to further understanding of concepts.
Develop an understanding of how knowledge is obtained, evaluated, refined and changed within chemistry. (CCT)
Focus attention on personal knowledge, and gaps in that knowledge.
Reflect upon how knowledge is created, refined and applied in chemistry.
Come to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of chemistry. (PSVS)
Understand how application of chemical principles through technology influences the natural environment.
Establish arguments based on human rights, human needs or the needs of the environment with respect to the use of knowledge about chemical principles.
Explore how moral principles influence judgements about the application of chemical principles.
Develop a positive disposition to life-long learning. (IL)
Cooperate with each other in order to enhance understanding through shared information.
Move from choosing among teacher-directed activities toward creating self-directed activities pertinent to chemistry.
Develop a willingness to take risks as independent learners.
Recognize the inevitability of profound change due to technological innovations and changes in society's values and norms.
Be willing to try to influence change by continuing to learn and apply what is learned.

units.name: Laboratory Activities
factorsEmphasized: D2 scientists and technologists are human
D3 impact of science and technology
D6 resources for science and technology
D8 limitations of science and technology
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: Acquire concrete experiences of chemical events which form the basis for abstract understandings.
Gain proficiency in manipulating laboratory equipment.
Strengthen understanding within chemistry through applying knowledge of numbers and their interrelationships. (NUM)
Develop a contemporary view of technology. (TL)
Develop compassionate, empathetic and fair-minded students who can make positive contributions to society as individuals and as members of groups. (PSVS)

units.name: Independent Research
factorsEmphasized: D3 impact of science and technology
D9 social influence of science and technology
F1 longing to know and understand

items.text: Investigate problems in chemistry and in the application of chemistry.
Develop abilities to meet own learning needs. (IL)

Write proposals for individual or group projects, including such things as: a completion date, criteria for assessment, resources to be accessed, preferred method of presentation, suggested audiences for presentation, and meeting dates for review and collaboration.

Take responsibility for their own learning by setting goals, designing plans, developing proposals, suggesting baseline performance levels, organizing allotted time, managing activities, evaluating success, and reviewing the entire process.
Demonstrate an ability to access information from a variety of resources.
Follow guidelines for completing a specific learning task.
Explore issues or topics which address their interests and concerns.
Develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined and changed within chemistry. (CCT)
Participate in scientific inquiry.
Focus attention on knowledge and gaps in personal knowledge related to a specific topic.
Develop compassionate, empathetic and fair-minded students who can make positive contributions to society as individuals and as members of groups. (PSVS)
Learn in a climate that is sensitive, flexible and responsive.
Collaborate with teachers and others to determine and monitor their own learning processes.
Work cooperatively with others.
Accept and respond to constructive criticism responsibly.
Share the results of their research project with other students, teachers, parents, or members of the community.
Share the results of their research by developing displays, exhibits, performances, presentations, demonstrations, lectures, or other appropriate methods.

units.name: Atoms and Elements
factorsEmphasized: F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: Discuss the development of ideas about the structure of matter.
Outline Aristotle's ideas on the nature of matter.
Explain the contributions of the early alchemists.

Summarize the contributions made by Dalton, Lavoisier, Berzelius, Thomson, Rutherford, Milliken, Planck, Bohr, de Broglie, Schrödinger or Heisenberg in developing a model of the structure of the atom.
Understand how theory is used to explain observations.
Identify the relationships among the components of the atom.
Identify protons, neutrons, and electrons as constituents of atoms.
Consider the forces which hold the atom together.
Draw Lewis diagrams to indicate the valence electron structure of atoms.
Recognize the terminology used to describe atoms and their isotopes: atomic number; nucleon (mass) number; atomic mass; atomic mass unit: average atomic mass.
Discuss the concept of the mole.
Distinguish between isotopes of an element.
Recognize that there is a difference between mass and weight.
Calculate atomic mass (atomic weight) values when given the percentage of each isotope of an element.
Examine how elements are described and classified.
Recognize that elements have characteristic properties.
Classify elements according to their properties.
Identify some elements by their properties.
Describe the development of the periodic table by Mendeleev.
Explain the basic principles of organization of the periodic table.
Identify trends and patterns within the periodic table.
Understand the history of the use of symbols for the elements.
Use symbols for the elements correctly.
Use the periodic table to determine the valences of elements.
Compare several forms of the periodic table and recognize that each has its advantages.
Understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize chemistry. (COM)
Incorporate the vocabulary of chemistry into writing and talk about chemistry.
Recognize the periodic table as a source of information.
Apply knowledge of numbers and their interrelationships. (NUM)
Read and interpret information about elements from charts and tables.
Use numerical data to compare and describe elements.

units.name: Molecules and Compounds
factorsEmphasized: D4 science, technology, and the environment

items.text: Use the formulas and names of compounds fluently.
Recognize the component atoms, simple ions, or polyatomic ions in a molecule.
Use both the periodic table and a table of common ions to aid in determining the formulas of binary and other simple compounds.
Use a table of common ions in determining the formulas of compounds containing one or more polyatomic ions.
Write the formula of an inorganic compound, given its name.
Use the oxidation state notation to describe the valence of polyvalent elements, e.g. Fe(III).

Bold statements are foundational objectives; the Common Essential Learnings ones end with the CEL abbreviation in brackets, e.g. '(COM)' (also copied into `cel`). Text extracted with pdfjs-dist (legacy build) from a 1992 WordPerfect-generated PDF; two-column pages split at x=300. Bullet glyphs (WPTypographicSymbols '!') mapped to '•' (and stripped from the start of learning objectives); WPBoxDrawing ')' used as a dash mapped to '—' (in sub/superscripts, where it is a minus sign, to '−'). Subscripts/superscripts (e.g. chemical formulas) are flattened inline, so 'H2O' may appear where the print has H₂O.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

indicators.text: Examine the role of dance in expressing identity, drawing where possible and appropriate on the experience of students and expertise of community members.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the history and role of dance in Indigenous cultures around the world.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the role of dance in preserving and celebrating cultural identity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of dance in resisting colonial assimilation policies in various parts of the world (e.g., treaty education outcome SI11 -analyze how the unfulfilled aspects of treaties, with international indigenous people, have resulted in inequities).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize the role of dance in developing and expressing identity in Indigenous communities around the world.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare various Indigenous dance protocols and their purposes.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine and describe the different complexities related to the roles of men and women in traditional dance around the world.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct research (e.g., digital, live, interview) on a contemporary International Indigenous dance maker and report on such things as: philosophy or focus, subject or themes presented, discipline specific or interdisciplinary work, and the potential influence of traditional practices (e.g., ask inquiry questions such as Do traditional practices and/or Elders influence the work you create? Does your culture influence the subject matter or themes of your work?).

outcomes.statement: Develop personal voice in dance expressed within a global historical context.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how world views changed throughout time and the effects that has had on dance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how specific dances evolved from historical events.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine a retrospective of a choreographers’ (e.g., Alvin Ailey, Merce Cunningham, Isadora Duncan) and/or companies’ work, (e.g., Toronto Dance Theatre, National Ballet School, Netherlands Dance Theatre, Martha Graham Company).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop a dance in response to a global historical issue

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore a variety of historical world events in relation to self-expression through dance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore other artists’ work related to a historical event or issue and examine a similar event or issue through own self-expression.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a global timeline (e.g., photograph, tableau, video and drawing) of historical milestones in dance.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the connection between specific cultural spiritualties and dance.

outcomes.statement: Develop personal voice in dance within the context of contemporary world issues and/or events.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Survey and respond to a range of world dance types and styles, including dances of Indigenous peoples.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine international choreographers who are pioneers in new movements or genres ofdance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Acknowledge and describe how a variety of worldviews influence personal voice through dance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how various dance types and styles emerge and evolve in response to historical and/or current cultural shifts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore and respond to dance practices within a range of cultural and environmental contexts (e.g., legends, myths, ceremonies, influence of nature).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore other artists’ work related to global issues and explore similar issues through own evolving personal voice.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on the development of one’s personal voice in dance.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore a dance-related career path related to own interests.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate and describe various careers associated with dance creation and/or production (e.g., choreographer/dance maker, performer, costume designer, lighting designer, stage manager, director, teacher, music editor, production crew).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate and describe various careers related to health and wellness in dance (e.g., teacher/instructor for Pilates/yoga, fitness trainer, massage therapist, physiotherapist).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate and describe various careers related to entrepreneurship or freelancing in dance (e.g., dance studio owner, photographer, videographer, marketer, event planner, critic, agent, dance wear designer/creator/provider).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Complete a survey to identify careers that would suit one’s strengths, beliefs and interests.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prepare for an interview and/or an audition.

outcomes.statement: view, interact with, and experience the natural and constructed environments of the community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: reads and interprets simple excerpts from stories from the oral tradition; stories should be supported with occasional informative illustrations, photos, or other visual representations; and,

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: reads and interprets a descriptive passage of text or a detailed set of instructions for a process, supported with occasional informative illustrations.

outcomes.statement: produce language that is understandable to others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: produces text on familiar topics, providing detail to support main point, in guided situations;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: communicates thoughts, ideas, feelings for specific purposes and audiences through a variety of verbal and visual media in guided situations;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: retells parts of oral narratives orally and in written form, and combines with various mediums of expression, such as dance, puppetry, art, or drama;

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: communicate meaningfully with accuracy (accuracy primarily the syntactical and semantical conventions of a language).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: produces sounds of language that are difficult for the student learning an additional language, with enough clarity to prevent misunderstandings of common words;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: uses specific vocabulary associated with a range of common topics;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: produces sentences containing a subordinate clause;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: uses a wider range of common verbal affixes with relative accuracy; and,

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: produces a variety of short, simple oral texts in guided and unguided situations.

outcomes.statement: communicate meaningfully with proficiency (proficiency is the ability of an individual to speak or perform in an acquired language).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: produces speech at a normal or slower than normal rate that requires some repetition to be understood by a first language speaker;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: manages simple, routine interactions with ease and asks for clarification when necessary;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: participates in a simple conversation with a Dene speaker using repetition and explanation;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: produces basic phrases, short sentences, and questions using learned vocabulary and simple language structures.

outcomes.statement: communicate meaningfully with coherency (coherency relates to the connectedness of information, thoughts and ideas within discourse).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: conveys an idea in discourse with a logical sequence of events and with simple but effective detail;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: expresses some logical relations in discourse;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: uses simple linking devices, such as "maka-but," "ekosi-so," "kispin-if" and "ohci-therefore," appropriately in spontaneous speech to create a sense of flow and coherency;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: uses a variety of short oral texts on unfamiliar topics in guided situations;

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: uses a variety of conventions to structure texts (e.g., titles, poetry, and riddles/jokes); and,

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: uses a variety of patterns in their own texts.

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow the learner to receive and give information.

indicators.text: discusses plans (e.g., going to the library, going for coffee, meeting for volleyball);

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: uses Dene to persuade or convince (e.g., eka takohteci wipac, kika-ati-sipwehtanaw. You'll arrive soon and then we will get ready to leave. Eka kimiwahki wapahki, kika-nitawipakasimonaw, kakwe-kaskimew or kakwesakocimew) Providing it doesn't rain, we will go and swim;

indicators.text: uses questions to understand new idea;

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe opportunities in the local environment (e.g., home, school, community centre, place of worship, recreational complex) to improve interactive user experiences or address deficiencies that may be resolved through changes in design.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a narrative describing a local environmental design improvement opportunity.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Relate work placement experience to personal and career goals.

indicators.label: a
b

indicators.text: Update personal career documentation (e.g., resume, portfolio) following the work placement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Prepare a letter, note, card or other communication for the work placement employer, expressing appreciation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and/or revise personal and career goals based on the work placement experience.

outcomes.statement: Create 3D CAD models.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Intermediate 3D CAD (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Design 3D CAD models using a variety of CAD tools:
- Explore premade 3D drawings from a variety of views and perspectives.
- Compare surface characteristics of a variety of 3D objects.
- Differentiate between opaque and transparent solids.
- Determine support or raft structures for the model.
- Add lighting and materials to objects in 3D CAD environment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Produce prints of rendered images of 3D CAD models by:
- exporting model to slicing software;
- manipulating model to correct scale for print; and,
- determining material for model print.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop and maintain a portfolio of completed drawings.

outcomes.statement: Produce a presentation floor plan for a residential building.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Presentation Floor Plan (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 35, 36

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss ways multiple floor plans can be generated from a single conceptual design.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Create design sketches based on bubble diagrams and adjacency matrices as developed during conceptual design process that include:
- coloured bubble diagram and preliminary floor plan according to zones (e.g., public, private, service); and,
- legend with colours and zone titles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Produce finished presentation plan including room dimensions, room labels, door sizes, fixture tags (e.g., shower, shelves) and furniture placement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Present the finished product to a client.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Refine presentation floor plan based on client needs and preferences.

outcomes.statement: Produce a presentation elevation for a residential building.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Presentation Elevations (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between presentation elevations and working drawings.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate concepts of scale and proportion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Produce elevation drawings consisting of all four views including the following processes:
- creating annotations to identify all exterior building materials;
- drawing walls and roof, windows and doors, and other visible exterior materials; and,
- adding landscaping details (e.g., side walk, bushes, trees) and shade and shadow to enhance presentation elevation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to share work progress.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Present finished product to an audience.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Refine the elevation drawings based on feedback.

outcomes.statement: Create floor plans for residential buildings.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Floor Plans (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-30 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 36

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss and apply terminology (e.g., exterior walls, interior partitions) associated with floor plans.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Design multiple floor plans to demonstrate understanding of drawing tools and drawing symbols.
- Draw exterior walls and interior partitions/walls.
- Insert doors and windows.
- Insert plumbing fixtures, millwork and TYP (typical, same as nearby comparable features) on construction drawings.
- Locate and place stairwell openings and stairs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Provide detail to floor plan by:
- representing miscellaneous objects (e.g., closets, closet rods, hangers, shelves, balcony handrails, appliances, cabinets); and
- dimensioning using correct architectural symbols (e.g., arrows, slashes).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Label and dimension rooms using correct architectural symbols and following correct standards.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Capture room information (e.g., room area, room function) in a central database for reference and to identify building trends and preferences for future projects.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between a presentation and construction floor plan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore floor plans which take into account universal design and cultural needs.

indicators.text: Investigate various types of foundations (e.g., ICF-insulating concrete form, PWF-preserved wood foundation, cinderblock, concrete).

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c
d

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Investigate and develop elevation plans that demonstrate understanding of required technical vocabulary, drawing tools and symbols.
- Identify grade level on plans.
- Produce front and side elevations for a set of house plans.
- Label materials used to finish house exterior and significant elevations (e.g., top of top plate, top of subfloor).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine required levels for wall and window heights.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore differences among roof types (e.g., flat, gable, shed, mansard, hip).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design roof pitch in accordance with floor plan.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate various types of wall materials with respect to their use, sustainability, cost, individual preferences and energy efficiency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify interior wall components (e.g., top plate, bottom plate, studs).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Label load bearing and non-load bearing interior walls.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify exterior wall components (e.g., top plate, bottom plate, studs, insulation, exterior finish, sheet polyethylene, header, blocking).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Size and locate floor joists according to the National Building Code.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine the boundary of the wall section to be displayed.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Draw a completed wall section to scale.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Insert correct symbols for materials used in construction.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Differentiate between nominal and actual lumber sizes.

indicators.text: Research existing site plans in your community.
