(K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the role of various government regulations (e.g., Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) and the National Ambient Air Quality Objectives (NAAQOs)), and legislation (e.g., Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 and The Clean Air Act in Saskatchewan) in minimizing risks to human health. (S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the sources and production of industrial and photochemical smog and identify measures that can be undertaken to mitigate their effects to human health. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and carry out a process to assess indoor or outdoor air quality, using appropriate technologies to collect and analyze data. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the scientific principles underlying technologies and processes such as air scrubbers, baghouse filters, electrostatic precipitators and catalytic converters that were developed to reduce contaminants in motor vehicle and industrial emissions or to improve indoor air quality. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate whether a personal protective device or substance (e.g., sunscreen, mosquito repellent or protective clothing) is effective in protecting a person from an environmental factor that affects human health. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop a generalization about the relationship between human population density and human health. (S, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the production, reliability and uses of geoscience data to investigate the effects of a changing climate on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the types of questions that scientists attempt to answer with respect to Earth's climate and past, present and potential future climate changes. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how different techniques (e.g., satellite imagery, ice core samples and dendrology) provide scientists with a variety of data regarding climate change. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the Arctic as an indicator region of climate change, including the impact on traditional lifestyles of northern peoples, given the general vulnerability to climate change effects at northern versus equatorial latitudes. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how and why organizations such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Canadian Centre for Climate Modeling and Analysis and Prairie Adaptation Research Collaborative (PARC) work to provide scientific research related to climate change and its potential environmental and societal implications. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the contributions of Indigenous knowledge in policy decisions related to climate change. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the degree to which the scientific community has achieved consensus regarding the reality of anthropogenic climate change. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate potential environmental, economic and societal impacts of climate change in Saskatchewan on human health, population distribution and access to water and other resources. (STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Interpret climate data (e.g., tables, maps, graphs, visualizations and other representations) to determine climate patterns and trends over specific periods. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate how climate models simulate important aspects of past and present climate and climate changes, and provide projections about future effects of climate changes with varying degrees of complexity and reliability. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize how phenomena such as El Niño, La Niña and ocean acidification provide evidence of how the effects of climate change on one earth system (i.e., geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere) can produce effects across other earth systems. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the adaptation and mitigation strategies developed to minimize the potential impacts of climate change on the agriculture, energy, forestry, transportation and/or tourism sectors in Saskatchewan. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Hypothesize how life on earth might respond to a changing global climate given different scenarios change such as sea level rise, extreme weather events, water shortages, increased spread of disease, flooding and acidification of the oceans. (K, STSE, S, A)

outcomes.statement: Investigate technologies and processes used for mitigating and managing resource use, waste generation and pollution associated with a growing human population.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify factors that have contributed to historical and contemporary trends in human population growth and that may influence future growth. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the environmental impact of human population changes over the last century on a specific region or area with respect to resource use, waste generation and pollution. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research First Nations and Métis beliefs and practices that demonstrate a sustainable perspective on using resources wisely and minimizing waste. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the strengths and limitations of models (e.g., I=PAT) that scientists use to quantify the impact of population, consumption, technology and stewardship on the environment. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the impact of factors such as advances in food security and access to medicine that support a growing human population. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze benefits and challenges associated with the use and production of fertilizer for food crops necessary to sustain a growing human population. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe technologies and processes that have been developed to minimize the impacts of mining, forestry and/or agricultural operations on air, water and soil quality and quantity. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the waste generated throughout the life cycle of a product. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design and carry out a waste audit, and propose a plan of action for waste reduction and/or diversion based on the findings. (S, A, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate advances in technologies and processes (e.g., sewage treatment plants, incineration, composting, engineered landfills and curbside recycling) used for storing, handling and disposing of human and/or livestock waste. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Debate the benefits and consequences of public policies (e.g., municipal, provincial or federal) regarding the handling, storage, transportation, treatment and disposal of hazardous waste. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the function and condition of freshwater aquatic systems such as rivers, streams, lakes, wetlands and watersheds.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how to measure the condition of an aquatic ecosystem using chemical factors, physical factors and biological indicators including indicator species, keystone species and invasive species. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how the presence or absence of traditional medicines can serve as indicators of water body health. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Measure abiotic factors (e.g., turbidity, temperature, dissolved oxygen and particulates) of an ecosystem using a variety of techniques and technologies (e.g., probe ware, pH paper, Secchi disk, Imhoff settling cone and chemical water quality test kit) effectively and safely. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the diversity of life in a specific aquatic ecosystem through water sampling, classifying aquatic biota, assessing biodiversity and calculating a water quality index and/or algal productivity. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the interdependencies between abiotic (e.g., pH, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, temperature, total dissolved solids, phosphorous, nitrogen, stream flow and biochemical oxygen demand [BOD]) and biotic factors in a functioning aquatic ecosystem. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate bacterial content in surface water and compare the presence of coliform bacteria to surface water quality standards following appropriate safety procedures. (A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess how an integrated watershed management approach can address issues (e.g., water supply, drainage, storm water runoff, habitat protection and water rights) that affect water quality and the health of all living things within a watershed. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the benefits of the ecological goods and services provided by riparian zones and wetlands (e.g., marshes, swamps, bogs and fens) in protecting water resources. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize different characteristics of lakes from naturally oligotrophic to eutrophic as well as possible causes (e.g., clearing of land, excessive fertilizer runoff and treatment plants) and consequences of cultural eutrophication. (K)

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of maintaining healthy water for humans and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze emerging health challenges such as the spread of disease, mercury in fish, blue-green algae and E. coli in drinking water that result from changes to the condition of aquatic systems. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the rationale for developing and enforcing water quality standards such as the Saskatchewan Surface Water Quality Objectives and the Canadian Water Quality Index and legislation such as the Canada Water Act and the International River Improvements Act. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how individuals, organizations (e.g., watershed associations), First Nations and government agencies (e.g. Saskatchewan Water Security Agency) work to ensure clean and abundant water through producing water regulations and allocation policies. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess how irrigation projects affect food production, water availability, soil salinization and groundwater. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the operation and effectiveness of technologies and processes developed to protect drinking water sources locally and globally. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the impacts of point source and non-point source pollution on humans and aquatic systems. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the sources, effects, and management and mitigation strategies of contaminants such as pathogens, organic matter, heavy metals, sediment, heat, petrochemicals and inorganic chemicals such as pesticides in aquatic and/or marine ecosystems. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate how human activities (e.g., overfishing, photo- degradation of plastic waste, shipping, coastal development and offshore extraction of oil and minerals) impact marine ecosystems (e.g., coral reef degradation, introduction of invasive species and reduced fish populations). (STSE, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the role of muskeg and moss in water filtration and food preservation for First Nations and Métis and other communities. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research advances in technologies such as desalinization plants, water treatment plants and home water filtrations systems, which are designed to maintain and improve water quality. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design a system of source water protection for a community`s drinking water recognizing the precautionary principle (STSE, A, S)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of soils as an integral component of terrestrial ecosystems.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how First Nations and Métis people value soil as an integral component of Mother Earth, including traditional ways of looking after soil. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize how the breakdown of parent material through various processes (e.g., weathering, erosion, deposition and decomposition of organisms) results in soil with varying properties (e.g., colour, texture, structure and pH). (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Understand the interconnectedness between soil characteristics, ecozones and natural vegetation in Saskatchewan. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with different soil mixtures, using black earth, compost, sand, top soil, manure, peat moss, vermiculite, loam and/or sand, to determine their suitability for growing different plant species. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain common methods scientists use to sample and monitor soil quality over time. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Collect and analyze soil data (e.g., pH, nitrate, phosphate, potassium, porosity and moisture) using technologies such as sensors and soil test kits safely and effectively. (A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research causes and consequences of soil degradation (e.g., wind and water erosion, salinity and desertification) and mitigation strategies (e.g., conservation tillage, contour farming, grassed waterways and shelterbelts) used to reduce the loss of topsoil. (A, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recognize the role and diversity of organisms (e.g., nitrogen fixing bacteria, fungi, mycorrhizae, insects, plants and protists) found within soil environments. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of soil in biogeochemical cycling, including carbon storage and nitrogen fixation, nitrification and denitrification. (STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine how phenomena such as erosion, desertification and soil pollution, whether natural or human-caused, affect soil productivity and food production. (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate how various small- and large-scale composting systems such as composting toilets, trench composting, vermicomposting, windrow composting, anaerobic digestion and mechanical biological treatment work to maintain and improve soil quality. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Collaborate with a group of peers to propose a landscaping investigation or action plan concerning an aspect of an urban ecosystem (e.g., rooftop gardens, green walls and green spaces) while ensuring conditions affecting local soil are represented. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine the role plants play in an ecosystem, including the ways in which humans use plants.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the many roles of plants including their roles as providers of ecological goods and services as well as natural capital. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the significance (e.g., medicinal, spiritual, nutritional and shelter) of plants, including tobacco, in First Nations and Métis cultures. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how plant morphology and physiology determines the role of plants in an ecosystem (e.g., anchoring soil, filtering air and water, providing shelter for other organisms and providing organic matter to the ecosystem). (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interpret the relationship between photosynthesis, respiration and net primary productivity. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify factors that influence plant pollination and reproduction, including the role of integrated pest management. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the relationship between plants and climate change, including plants' roles in reducing greenhouse gases, as well as potential impacts of climate change on plant growth and distribution. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine advances in crop science that have influenced the types and yields of agricultural and/or horticultural crops grown in various areas of Saskatchewan. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the economic, environmental and societal impacts of various agriculture practices (e.g., industrial, traditional, subsistence, sustainable agriculture, organic farming, urban agriculture, local food and community supported agriculture). (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyse forestry practices (e.g., selective cutting, clear cutting, shelterwood system and integrated resource management) in terms of productivity, profitability and environmental stewardship. (STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess the impact of agriculture or forestry on a natural ecosystem. (S)

outcomes.statement: Recognize the need for intact habitat to support animal populations and biodiversity.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Justify the need for habitat protection and restoration in terms of biodiversity (e.g., genetic diversity, species diversity and habitat diversity) and resilience within ecosystems both locally and globally. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe examples of First Nations and Métis people's contributions in recognizing the effects of natural and human- caused changes to habitat on historical migration patterns of animals in Saskatchewan. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how habitat management and protection decisions are influenced by the extent to which Indigenous land rights (e.g., custodians of the land versus individual land ownership) are reflected through the spirit and intent of various treaties. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the roles of individuals, governmental and non- governmental organizations such as the Saskatchewan Prairie Conservation Action Plan, Ducks Unlimited and the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC), and legislation such as the Species at Risk Act (SARA) in protecting and maintaining habitats and biodiversity. (A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Relate an organism's specific adaptations and behaviour to its niche in an ecosystem. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Correlate the range and habitat of various animals with Saskatchewan's ecozones and ecoregions and identify changes to an animal's range and habitat due to human activities such as agriculture, mining, oil and gas development, forestry, urbanization and recreation. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the implications of the competitive exclusion principle with respect to animals and plants in an ecosystem, including the introduction of invasive species and the potential for shifting ecozones due to climate change. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate the importance of a keystone species in a specific terrestrial ecosystem. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess current or potential impacts of a changing climate on a specific representative animal and its habitat. (S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Provide examples of projects undertaken to restore damaged or destroyed habitats. (STSE)

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 7 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Explore the purposes of money.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Why Money Matters (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Explore common responses to questions such as:
- Why do people and communities need money?
- How much money does one really need?
- What are common financial decisions people and communities face?
- How do personal and community financial decisions affect self and others?
- Why is it important to manage personal and community finances?
- What influences one’s perception of, and value of, money?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss reasons why money is valued (e.g., safety and security, ability to have choices, comfort and control, ability to give back and to share, adventure and freedom).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the concept of opportunity cost (i.e., every money decision involves a trade-off).

outcomes.statement: Apply decision-making strategies to various personal and community financial scenarios.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: The Decision-Making Process (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how factors such as needs, wants, habits, values, risks, economic influences and current financial situation affect decisions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and role-play various scenarios using decision-making strategies such as agonizing, procrastination, spontaneity, compliance and security.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the effectiveness of various decision-making strategies applied to various personal and community financial scenarios.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how different decision-making strategies may be used for various personal or community financial situations.

outcomes.statement: Develop personal goals using a variety of goal-setting models or approaches.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Goal-Setting (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between needs and wants.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on personal needs and wants (e.g., private journal).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the significance of setting goals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the characteristics of various decision-making and goal-setting models (e.g., SMART and PACED) and approaches (collaborative; consultation with mentor, Elders or community leaders).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop personal short-, medium- and long-term goals that include goals for building personal competence and confidence in managing one’s money/finances.

outcomes.statement: Investigate methods for handling and storing personal and financial information securely.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Information Security (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify various documents such as receipts, bank statements, job applications, resumes and passports which contain sensitive information that others could use fraudulently.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize when personal information (e.g., social insurance number, account numbers, passwords, passport information and personal address/location) should remain confidential.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify how documents that contain sensitive information may be stored and protected using various tools and techniques such as a safety deposit box, a fire proof safe, a secured electronic folder and shredding.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the need for keeping debit and credit card information such as the card number, card verification value/card verification code (CVV/CVC), and personal identification number secure.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the level of security associated with common payment methods such as cash, cheque, electronic transfer, credit card, bank draft, manager’s trust cheque and prepaid credit card.

outcomes.statement: Apply the concept of net worth to variousscenarios.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Net Worth (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between assets and liabilities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between appreciating and depreciating assets.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine the value of an asset at a specific time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of assets and liabilities that determine personal or community net worth.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how negative equity affects investing and net worth.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design scenarios that demonstrate the importance of net worth to an individual’s or community’s financial plan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate personal or community net worth for various scenarios.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Calculate net worth and determine its importance within an overall financial plan for a variety of scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Examine the principles of budgeting.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Budgeting - Budgeting Fundamentals (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the role and importance of budgeting in financial planning for personal and other uses (e.g., organization, club and small-scale event).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of the types of income (e.g., employment, gifts, awards and scholarships) and expenses (e.g., fixed and variable) typically included in a personal budget.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of tracking income and expenses over a period of time prior to developing a personal budget.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify reasons why people fail to follow budgets.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss pitfalls of living beyond one’s means.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Provide examples of the types of income and expenses that might be included in a non-personal budget (e.g., organization, club and small-scale event).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of opportunity cost in determining how to spend money.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a simple budget for self or for another use (e.g., organization, club and small-scale event).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Summarize how budgets will evolve and change as one moves through various life stages.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine various cultural, community or religious perspectives on budgeting.

outcomes.statement: Develop and analyze monthly and annual spending plans based on income and expense tracking.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6B: Budgeting - Designing and Analyzing Spending Plans (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the similarities and differences between a budget and a personal spending plan as financial planning tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine a variety of tools (e.g., computer or mobile applications) designed for tracking expenditures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss potential dangers (e.g., violating third party access clause in banking agreement) associated with using tracking applications to monitor activity on financial accounts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and implement a system for tracking monthly and annual incomeand expenses using appropriate technology for various scenarios.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify income and expenses as monthly or annual and fixed or variable.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify common categories (e.g., housing, utilities, entertainment, travel and food) found in personal spending plans.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss reasons for having an emergency fund

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create a list of tips for setting up, contributing to and using an emergency fund.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research budgeting advice such as the ‘50/30/20 Rule’ commonly provided by financial experts.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze monthly and annual expenses for various scenarios to determine patterns and trends in personal spending.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop and refine monthly and annual spending plans for various scenarios that reflect tracked income and expenses.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Reflect on the relationship between a spending plan and personal financial habits.

outcomes.statement: Examine basic services typically provided by financial institutions for accessing and managing personal finances.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Financial Institutions - Exploration (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify various types of financial institutions (e.g., virtual banks, bricks-and-mortar banks, credit unions, alternative lenders, international banks, insurance companies, mortgage companies and securities dealers and advisors).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify First Nations financial institutions (e.g., First Nations Bank of Canada and Indigenous credit unions) and others (e.g., Habib Canadian Bank and Bank of China--Canada) responsive to various cultures in Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research common financial services or products such as chequing and savings accounts, debit and credit cards, telephone banking, mobile banking, online banking and automated teller machine (ATM) banking.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify fees commonly associated with various financial services.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss reasons why consumers are often skeptical of financial institutions’ practices and fees.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore ways to minimize financial service fees.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the process and requirements, including personal identification required, for applying for an account at a financial institution.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify commonly used terms (e.g., service charges, interest rates, deposits, withdrawals and overdrafts) within the financial services industry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate how financial institutions make money, including the rate differential between lending and deposit rates.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the prevalence of payday lenders and cheque cashing centres in Saskatchewan, the services they provide and the fees typically associated with those services.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of accessing the services of payday lenders and cheque cashing centres.

outcomes.statement: Explore documents and processes used to conduct and monitor common financial transactions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Conducting and Monitoring Financial Transactions (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss common financial transactions (e.g., deposits, withdrawals, direct deposits, e-transfers, issuing/cashing/depositing cheques, pre-authorized payments and direct deposits).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common financial transactions and service charges reported on an account statement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how an e-transfer works for both the sender and the recipient.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research stop payment options for an e-transfer.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of monitoring one’s financial transactions and account statements for accuracy.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways to monitor financial transactions manually and using technologies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research terms and conditions commonly associated with an account, such as the process and time restriction for reporting inaccuracies on a bank statement or the rules for clearing fraudulent items.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research emerging payment trends.

outcomes.statement: Explore the attributes and uses of cheques.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Cheques (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what a cheque is and why cheques are used.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution and current use of cheques and predict the future of this payment form including the impact of technologies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify information found on a cheque including the account number, transit numbers and financial institution number.

indicators.label: d

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Explore the importance of safe food handling, preparation and storage.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2B: Safe Food Handling (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the importance of personal hygiene and using personal protective equipment (e.g., gloves) for food safety.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss causes of food borne illnesses.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate common symptoms (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, bloating) of food poisoning.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the importance of proper food storage (e.g., dried, frozen, refrigerated, food-safe containers) in safe food handling.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of safe thawing practices using various methods (i.e., cool running water, microwave, refrigerator).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research best practices (e.g., proper food storage, wearing and changing gloves, using separate equipment) involved in mitigating the risk of cross-contamination for individuals with severe food allergies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore aspects of food contamination such as how it occurs and how to identify spoiled food.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine safe food temperature zones for various foods (e.g., poultry, egg dishes, pork, beef).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the two types of contamination (i.e., direct and indirect/cross contamination).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the conditions (e.g., temperature, time, acidity [pH], moisture, a food source, poor personal hygiene and poor sanitation) necessary for a food borne illness to survive.

indicators.label: k
l
indicators.text:
Research and compare the three categories of contamination:
- biological (e.g., bacteria or viruses);
- physical (e.g., objects that enter any stage of food preparation); and,
- chemical (e.g., cleaning products and naturally occurring).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to safely dispose of used oils.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine safe and responsible recycling and disposal of kitchen waste.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to prepare recipes using proper food safe practices (e.g., frequent hand washing, avoiding food cross-contamination, washing produce, cooking to proper food temperatures).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Plan, prepare and serve a meal at home.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Establish teamwork guidelines for preparing, serving and eating food in the classroom setting.

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

items.text: The intent of this course in geography is to acquaint and explain to the student the basic distributions of physical and cultural phenomena over the earth's surface. Through analysis of these distributions, and some of the societal processes, an understanding of the environment, society and economy of the different regions of the world should be achieved. Further, the study of geography should lead to an appreciation of the fact that the world is one, that no region exists in isolation, that, today, all parts of the world are interdependent. To ensure the attainment of the above, the geography program should foster in the student the development of the following understandings, skills, and attitudes:

items.label: a
items.text: There is no split between "physical geography" and 'regional geography". Geography is a chorological science (i.e., deals with distribution) which needs and uses the facts of many sciences to arrive at an understanding of differences betweeu regions.

items.label: b
items.text: Geography is unified by its method and viewpoint and not by its subject matter. Much of its subject matter may be contained in other disciplines -- in history, in physics, in geology, in economics, etc. -- but its viewpoint is distinctive; it is the regional viewpoint.

items.label: c
items.text: The regional viewpoint infers the recognition of differences and of similarities between areas across the earth's surface. Regions are distinguished on the basis of definite criteria, both physical and cultural.

items.label: d
items.text: Classification of phenomena (physical or cultural) into categories of greater or lesser degree of generalization should lead to the understanding of areal variation in their occurrence and hence to an appreciation of regional distribution.

items.label: e
items.text: In recognizing relationships occurring between different classes of phenomena, e.g., areas of dense population coinciding with great natural resources, one must be careful to differentiate between cause and effect re-lationships and those relationships which are accidental.

items.label: f
items.text: The major device for demonstrating regional differences and distributions is the map. In addition the geographer uses a variety of descriptive devices including statistical diagrams of many kinds.

items.label: a
items.text: To read with comprehension in the field of geography.

items.label: b
items.text: To analyze, interpret and cvaluate data provided in many forms (statistical, map, or other).

items.label: c
items.text: To discover geographical relationships and to recognize regional differences.

items.label: d
items.text: To present, orally and in writing, in organized fashion, the results of geographical research.

items.label: e
items.text: To use, and construct where possible, the various tools of geography including globes, maps, charts, and graphs.

items.label: f
items.text: To make casc studies, local or other, and thus develop understanding of relationships between environment and human activities.

items.label: g
items.text: To undertake geographical studies, including elementary field work, of the local area to achieve first hand understanding of the fundamental approach of the geographer.

items.label: a
items.text: Recognition that the state of knowledge is not finite, that new methods of research and new concepts are continually evolving, that understanding of the world in which we live is very incomplete.

items.label: b
items.text: Willingness to undertake research with an open mind and to arrive at generalizations based on unbiased appraisal.

items.label: c
items.text: Willingness to recognize that cultural differences across the world are the result of geographical, historical and societal factors rather than a result of "racial" dissimilarities.

items.label: d
items.text: A willingness to recognize that regions of similar physical environment may be occupied by very dissimilar economics and societies and that these dissimilarities are a result of numerous factors including stage of cultural and technical development, together with differences in the objectives of the peoples concerned.

items.label: e
items.text: A willingness to understand that no region exists in isolation, that all parts of the world are inter-related and interdependent.

items.text: THE GRADE XI GEOGRAPHY COURSE

The intention of this course is to provide an under-standing of the geography of North America. The overall approach should attempt to provide understanding of the broad regional differences, physical and cultural, which occur within the continental area. Recognizing that political boundaries sometimes interfere with the full appreciation of geographic relationships the course has been designed to provide a framework of units, some of which may have international distribution while others may occur within a single nation. Nonetheless, it would be wrong to assume that major political boundaries, i.e., the international boundaries, are not geographic boundaries of considerable consequence: they interfere with free movement of men, materials, and even, sometimes, ideas -- and they were so created.

North America has been divided into a number of regions (units) which are not necessarily coterminous with the chapter headings of the text. These regions are broadly based, as far as possible, on groups of common characteristics. Obviously no line separates them but, rather, between them are broad zones of transition. Yet these regions do have validity and are useful as a toolin the analysis of all features which relate to the physical and cultural background of North America.
Basic to description, analysis, and synthesis in terms of the regional separates (units) is the use of maps pertinent to the separation and understanding of the regions.

units.name: Unit I & II
units.siteUnitName: Discovery and Exploration + Cultural Patterns and Economic Geography

items.text: Notth America is typified by north-south trending relief elements while the major political boundary, i.e., between Canada and U.S.A., trends east-west, thereby separating physically similar areas.

As a general characterization, North America can be separated into three main divisions: a northerly area too cold for agriculture; a western area generally too mountainous or/and too dry for agriculture, and an eastern humid area generally suited to agriculture.

These same divisions are applicable to North America as the home of the aboriginal population (map page 9) - the north representing the caribou, and other hunting areas; the western cordilleran area exhibiting specialized economics, not all based on agriculture; the eastern area showing adaptations to hunting in the drier interior and maize growing in the more humid sections.

These broad separates indicated here tend also to provide a gross picture of the distribution of population in North America, recognizing that some coastal and irrigated areas in the far west have developed large nodes of population.

But certain areas have been highly significant. The east, the area of initial settlement, faced Europe, receiving immigrants from the latter and developing trade with it. lajor routeways especially the Hudson-Mohawk, the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes, and the lississippi, provided ingress to the continental interior and funnelled the products of the latter eastward. Early industrial development occurred in the east and with the use of coal from the Appalachians and iron ores of the northeast and Lake Superior regions, the industrial supremacy of this area was ensured. Today the "heart" of North America includes much of the-north-eastern.and-mid-western United States together with the adjacent Great Lakes - St. Lawrence Lowland area of Canada. City development has been great and, today, many of these cities have grown to incorporate or make contact with satellites or other cities: indeed along the east coast from southern New England to Baltimore there is almost continuous urban development, making this the outstanding conurbation in the world -- a megalopolis.

The United States has demonstrated man's abilities to develop continental resources and has achieved the highest standards of living in the world. Canada, with lesser population and with its rather narrow zone of high potential for development, shows many parallels in growth. But in Central America, for many reasons, development has been slower. Both Canada and Central America show considerable emphasis on the export of raw materials and dependence on.foreign, especially American, development capital.

items.text: The development of the lowlands was stimulated by their accessibility to the peoples and markets of Western Europe.
The region possessed a climate which proved fairly well suited to intensive agricultural development within the lowlands.
Huch of the early industrial capacity was a direct outcome of the agricultural production of the region.
The natural waterways in this region have provided a major impetus to the development of this, the industrial heart of North America.
Heavy concentration of population has transformed many features of the landscape.

units.name: Unit V: Region: The Prairies and the Great Plains Region of Canada and the United States.
units.siteUnitName: The Prairies and Great Plains of Canada and the United States

items.text: Variation in climate and topography related closely to differences in farming and rancing activities, some areas specializing, as for example, in Spring wheat. 2。1 Dry climate has necessitated the development of special farming techniques and seed varities. Large farming units and principles of "Big Business" are characteristic of most forms of land-use.

Economic stability has been promoted through crop diversification, irrigation, improved methods of cultivation, government aid, etc.; development of mineral resources (coal, petroleum, natural gas, potash, etc.) and the introduction of industry have also assisted in providing greater economic diversity.

The Plains are sparsely settled. Changes in the economy and in transportation and other facilities have led to rural depopulation and to urbanization. Hajor cities, e.g., Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Kansas City, Denver, etc., tend to lie on the margins.
The 49th parallel separates politically but does not create essential differences in land-use.
The Western Cordillera is a good example of "Unity in diversity". The variety of landforms, climate and human response gives the whole region a distinctive geographic personality.

The Western Cordillera exhibits the greatest contrasts in human and economic geography found in any part of the North American continent; these contrasts are apparent in agriculture, fisheries, forest industries, minerals, power, and industry.
There is a close relationship between the irrigated lands of the cordilleran region and the distribution of agriculture and population.
The Western Cordillera is an area potentially rich in resources but man has had to overcome natural handicaps in their development.
Tropical climate and its effects on vegetation and land-use.
Geographical location and land forms and their influence on agriculture and settlement.
History of settlement and population characteristics.
Poverty of the masses, riches of the few.
Developpent of resources.
Contrasts between Liddle America and the United States and Canada in products, exports and economic development.
Economic interdependence with northern neighbors.

units.name: Unit VIII: The Canadian Shield and the Northland

items.text: There is a close relationship between peneplenation, uplift, stream rejuvenation, glaciation and permafrost, on the one hand, and the problems of land and water transportation and communication, poor drainage, the scarcity of arable soil, hydro-electric power potential and the accessibility of mineral deposits, on the other.

The physical characteristics - terrain, permafrost, climate of the Canadian Shield and Northland create major obstacles to transportation and communication. These in turn retard the utilization of resources and the extension of settlement.
The nature of rock structure and the effects of glaciation are related to the comparative surface accessibility of mineral deposits.

The Canadian North possesses great potential wealth in furs, forest products, minerals, hydro-electric power, and even agricultural lands (Clay belt). Present and future development of these resources is contingent on over-coming the handicaps of a short growing season, permafrost, muskeg, great distances, difficult climate, difficulties of road and railway construction, the expense of air transport and isolated settlement patterns.
The Eskimo has survived in the northern desert (tundra) by developing skills that enable him to exploit the meagre offerings of his environment, particularly those of the sea。
The location and vast extent of the Northland has given the region a new significance strategically.

This is an area characterized by recent massive economic and political changes.The original pattern·of English settlement, based on the plantation, led to the importation of slave labor and its social consequences. The breakdown of plantation agriculture led to new patterns of land-use and the relocation of some older activities, e.g., cotton to drier areas. This has been a difficult area marked by cleavage in economic and cultural opportunity. Industrial activity is increasing, e.g., Gulf Coast, T.V.A., (as example of change); and forms and types of agriculture are undergoing rapid transformation. The South is no longer the "cotton belt" or the "deep south" but a competitive region within the American complex.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between provincial and federal health and safety rules and guidelines as applied to hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential hazards in salons, appropriate safety equipment (e.g., personal protective equipment (PPE)) and appropriate safety precautions (e.g., public sanitation, trip hazards).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss general safety practices when using common salon equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Brainstorm general safety guidelines for a salon such as managing wires on the floor, extension cords, walkways and handling chemicals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on the impact that salon cleanliness (e.g., dust, organization) has on safety and business feasibility.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how technician’s choices and behaviours impact safety (e.g., wearing sandals or clothing that exposes skin can cause damage to self or clients).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of ergonomics for the health and well-being of technicians.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the effects that wellness components such as posture, exercise, rest, stress management, hygiene and nutrition have on the success of a hairstylist or esthetician.

outcomes.statement: Justify the importance of proper sanitation, disinfection and sterilization.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3B: Sanitation, Disinfection and Sterilization (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the terms sanitation, disinfection and sterilization.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the three levels of infection control (i.e., sanitation, disinfection and sterilization).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe contamination and decontamination.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate the purpose and application of antiseptic versus a disinfectant.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify given scenarios as sanitizing, disinfecting, or sterilizing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Classify single-use implements versus multi-use tools.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the different levels of disinfection (i.e., high, intermediate and low level) and describe situations when each level is appropriate.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare different techniques for sanitizing, disinfecting and sterilizing instruments and surfaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate techniques for sanitizing and disinfecting instruments and surfaces.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate different processes for disinfecting, sanitizing and sterilizing non-porous items (e.g., glass, metal, electric files, linen).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Recognize the difference between a chemosterilant and a high level disinfectant.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare labels on chemicals for proper use and disposal.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Critique sanitation practices when performing a service (e.g., manicures, pedicure, facial, makeup application, cut and style).

outcomes.statement: Initiate and develop ideas for artistic expression, within the context of hair, that incorporate the elements of art and principles of design.

indicators.text: Justify why examples of hair creations are appealing based on elements of art and principles of design.

outcomes.statement: Examine how beauty can be an expression of a person’s worldview, culture and self-identity.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9B: Inclusive Beauty (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of worldview, (e.g., attitude and principles) culture (e.g., ethnic background and subculture) and self-identity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how techniques and trends in hairstyling and esthetics reflect worldviews, culture and self-identity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine hairstyles, skin care, nail techniques and make-up examples within the local community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the impact that worldview and culture have on an individual’s definition of beauty.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and discuss historical and current societal attempts to control (e.g., government regulations/intervention, school dress code) self- expression (e.g., significance of the braid) of beauty.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore ideals of beauty (e.g., size of earlobes, length of hair, piercings, length of nails and gender expression) across cultures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the question, how does an individual’s expression of human beauty reflect their worldview, culture or self-identity?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on personal aesthetic choices (e.g., makeup, hair, nails) and their potential to communicate worldview, culture or self-identity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how a traditional Western definition of beauty (e.g., hair texture, light-coloured eyes and skin, hetero normativity) excludes and marginalizes expression of identity and culture.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how cultures that have been historically excluded and marginalized are challenging the stereotypical Western ideal of beauty.

indicators.label: h

indicators.text: Compare ingredient lists of various professional nail products.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the potential impact nail and foot care products could have on the health of clients.

outcomes.statement: Examine maintenance and use of hairstyling equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16B: Hair Styling Equipment and Maintenance (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify single-use and multi-use manual tools, styling tools, cutting tools, electric tools, chemical service tools and equipment used in hairstyling.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how manual tools, electric tools and equipment are used in hairstyling.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate application of hairstyling manual tools, electric tools and equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize how proper ergonomic practices are necessary to maintain the health of stylists.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of sanitation and safety for each tool and piece of equipment used in hairstyling.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe and perform sanitization, sterilization or disinfection of tools and equipment (e.g., spraying disinfectant, wiping and soaking; handling/storing cleaning towels, capes, aprons and smocks).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe and perform an inspection process (e.g., check for product build- up and determine when a tool must be removed from service) to maintain manual tools, electric tools and equipment (e.g., remove debris from filters in hairdryers, clippers and clothes dryer and discard refuse and product waste according to regulations).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss and apply safety practises when using all tools and equipment (e.g., adjust hydraulic chairs and other equipment according to stylist’s ergonomic support, use personal protective equipment (PPE), locate first aid and eye wash stations, discard sharps according to regulations and recognize all hazards).

outcomes.statement: Analyze characteristics of hair and scalp.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hair and scalp disorders such as psoriasis, alopecia, dandruff and dry or oily scalp by performing a visual inspection with hands or comb.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss and practice different types of hair and/or scalp treatments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify infections (e.g., vegetable, animal, staphylococci) on the scalp.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of hair repair products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss types of treatments for scalp conditions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Execute a scalp treatment including preparation, draping, safety and sanitation procedures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the theory of massage including purpose of scalp massage, massage movements and the benefits of massage.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the questions: What impact does hair texture and hair characteristics have on the analysis of client hair care needs? Why is it important to use industry language (e.g., hair texture and characteristics) when discussing hair?

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct a client consultation for a hair repair treatment.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Perform a scalp massage.

indicators.label: k

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how culture, religion and self-identity are expressed through different hairstyles and adornments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how different hairstyles can be created with different hair textures (e.g., fine, medium, coarse, kinky and curl pattern) and hair characteristics (e.g., density, porosity, elasticity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how different hairstyles enhance facial shapes and features.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate long hair roller set and up do comb-out techniques.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate roller set variations (e.g., indentation and combination pin curl/finger wave/roller set).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Prepare hair for an up do using balanced, controlled and clean sections.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create up-do hair styles for a variety of hair textures (e.g., fine, medium, coarse, kinky and curl pattern) and hair characteristics (e.g., elasticity, porosity, density).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create a foundation support by backcombing and smoothing using tools and styling aids.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Construct hair direction and design towards a focal point.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Practice inserting bobby pins/hair pins discretely.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Implement the elements of art and principles of design to generate a hairstyle from a visual support (e.g., picture, video, technology and social media).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the questions: How has language related to hair been used to racialize beauty? What impact does language have on hairstylist professionalism? How do hairstylists remain open to conversations that honour the perspectives of colleagues and clients?

indicators.label: a

indicators.text: Explore chemical reactions of hair products (e.g., bleach, colour and toner) and their effects on hair.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of and difficulties in defining terms such as Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care within a global context. (K, A, S, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine how personal, cultural and societal beliefs affect ethical decisions regarding health care.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about ethical dilemmas within health care. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Understand the core ethical questions to be considered when making health care decisions:
- What can be done for the patient? (intervention technologies)
- Does the patient understand the options? (informed consent)
- What does the patient want? (autonomy)
- What are the benefits? (beneficence)
- Will it harm the patient? (non-maleficence)
- Are the patient's requests fair and able to be satisfied? (justice)
- Are the costs involved fair to society? (economic consequences) (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze a health care issue with respect to the core ethical questions. (K,A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Contrast how procedures to prevent illness, such as immunizations, vitamin supplements, physical activity, nutrition and prayer, might be viewed from the perspective of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care. (K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine ethical considerations related to various practices and treatments (e.g., chemotherapy, radiation, acupuncture, sweat lodge, blood transfusions, herbal remedies and hirudotherapy) that might be considered in Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss individual, community and cultural beliefs regarding issues related to life and death such as home birthing, blood transfusions, contraception, abortions, organ donation, autopsies, euthanasia, cremation, burials and medical aid in dying. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine ethical considerations and perspectives related to issues such as the use of cadavers in professional studies, dissection and raising animals for the purpose of dissection, and public exhibits of plastinated organs and bodies, all of which could provide increased scientific understanding of human anatomy. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Understand a patient's rights in Saskatchewan and in Canada concerning health care decisions such as developing an advance care directive, refusal of treatment, informed consent and the role of a proxy or substitute decision-maker. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize the importance of considering linguistic and cultural needs when providing health care services. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess how various ethical considerations (e.g., personal beliefs, informed consent, the roles of institutional review boards and regulatory agencies) may influence an individual's decision to participate in a clinical study of a new biomedical intervention (e.g., vaccine, drug, treatment, device or process). (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Debate a decision related to ethics in health care from the viewpoint of individuals who hold different belief systems. (K, A, S, STSE)
