indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among the ways in which medical practitioners and the public use terms such as disease, illness, ailment, disorder, infection, medical condition, syndrome and abnormal condition. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate how the immune system uses a layered defense to respond to pathogens, including the difference between the innate and adaptive immune system.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the symptoms, possible causes, stages and scope (e.g., cells, tissues, organs and/or systems) of a pathology that affects one or more body systems. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., illness narrative, journal, timeline, story, video or diorama) of the progression of a specific pathology from the perspective of a real or hypothetical individual, including impacts on their lifestyle. (K, A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline the history of a disease or illness and its causes, including societal and cultural perspectives. (K, A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare prepared slides or digital images of healthy and diseased tissues to identify how pathologies affect cells. (K, A, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare how bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Streptococcus, and Escherichia coli) and viruses (e.g., common cold, influenza and herpes) differ in how they are transmitted, their impact on the human body and how each is treated. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the role of homeostasis in various phenomena such as regulation, heart rate, breathing, urination, sweating, digestion, body temperature, blood composition and stress.

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of macronutrients (i.e., carbohydrates, proteins and fats) and micronutrients (e.g., vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals) in maintaining human health.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify which macronutrients and micronutrients are commonly found in each food group (i.e., vegetables and fruit, grain products, milk and alternatives, meat and alternatives and oils and fats). (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how the body breaks down and uses simple (e.g., monosaccharide and disaccharide) and complex (i.e., polysaccharide) carbohydrates and dietary fiber. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the role of fats (e.g., saturated, unsaturated and trans fats) in processes such as long term energy storage, supporting vitamin absorption, creating cell membranes, synthesizing hormones, cushioning and protecting organs and helping us feel full. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the roles of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) in managing cholesterol levels.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the role of proteins in the production of antibodies, hemoglobin and insulin, structural support and building and maintaining muscle. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how enzymes (e.g., amylase, pepsin, lipase and protease) found in the mouth, stomach, pancreas and small intestine aid in the chemical digestion of food. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize issues (e.g., hypo/hyperglycemia, high/low cholesterol and denaturation of proteins) that may arise when macromolecules disrupt homeostasis. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Establish the relationships between dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis reactions in relation to the macronutrients (e.g., glucose + fructose = sucrose). (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how micronutrients (e.g., vitamins A, B, C, D, E and K, and iron, calcium and phosphorous) are necessary for health. (K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the food source and health claims associated with various phytochemicals (e.g., carotenoids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, phytoestrogens and organosulphur compounds). (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the connection between undernutrition or overnutrition and development of diseases such as anemia, scurvy, Type 2 diabetes and heart disease. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Investigate the contributions of various people (e.g., Justus von Liebig, Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, Claude Bernard and Emil Fischer) in advancing scientific understanding of nutrition. (STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain the role of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) as a molecule indispensable for the functioning of cells and life. (K)

outcomes.statement: Analyze dietary choices based on personal and cultural beliefs and scientific understanding of nutrition.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about the role of nutrition in supporting healthy eating practices. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how various factors (e.g., activity level, muscle mass, gender, age, weight and height) affect personal energy requirements. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate personal energy requirements and record personal caloric and macronutrient intake for a specified period. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare results of personal macronutrient intake to recommended daily intake (RDI) values. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how analysis of excrement (e.g., Bristol stool chart) and urine (e.g., urine analysis by color, clarity, odor, pH, nitrites, protein, glucose, tinkle test and Pee-O-Meter) serve as indicators of healthy functioning. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how the dietary recommendations in Canada's Food Guide compare with recommendations in food guides from other countries. (S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the value of information from food labels (e.g., ingredient list, nutrition facts table, nutrient content claims and health claims) to guide personal food choices. (A, S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design a healthful diet based on personal lifestyle choices. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the use of tools (e.g., body mass index [BMI], skinfold caliper, BOD POD and hydrostatic weighing) that provide information about body composition. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of processed foods, nutrition supplements, growth hormones, genetically modified foods and food additives (e.g., caffeine, aspartame, food coloring and monosodium glutamate [MSG]) on human health. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Evaluate physiological and psychological effects of nutritional disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia and obesity and their connection to body image and nutrition deficiencies. (K, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Assess whether eating practices such as carbohydrate loading, fad diets, vegetarianism, veganism, fast food, energy drinks, 100-mile diet and fasting provide sufficient nutrition to support healthy functioning. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine how various eating practices (e.g., pre-contact First Nations and Métis, kosher, halal and fasting practices during observances such as Lent and Ramadan) are based upon cultural and religious beliefs. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Explore the tools and procedures used to diagnose and monitor medical conditions.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess the significance of monitoring vital signs in health care, including obtaining accurate medical history and patient perception of pain. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify examples of procedures (e.g., visual inspection) and tools (e.g., stethoscope, octoscope and sphygmomanometer) commonly used for non-invasive diagnostic observations in health care. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Measure and record vital signs (e.g., pulse, respiration, temperature, blood pressure and degree of pain) of self and/or others. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the procedures, safety concerns and relevance of common laboratory tests (e.g., blood testing, blood glucose, culture swabs, urinalysis, stool, biopsy and microscopy) used in medical diagnosis. (K,S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the operation, risks, benefits and imaging modalities (e.g., sound, light, radiation and nuclear medicine) of medical imaging tools, including X-ray radiography, magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], computed tomography [CT], ultrasound and positron emission tomography [PET]). (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe technological advances in medical imaging tools (e.g., X-ray, ultrasound, computerized tomography and magnetic resonance imaging). (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss factors (e.g., severity of illness, dose received, cost and availability) that influence the choice to use a diagnostic tool or procedure. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the responsibility, including preparation and expectations, of the patient in diagnostic and imaging procedures. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify differences in tools and procedures used in diagnosing illness from the perspectives of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of diagnosis in improving the care of patients, protecting the health of clients and improving the economics of health care. (K, STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of interpreting diagnostic findings to support treatment options for specific pathologies.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify tools and procedures that may be used to assist health care providers in monitoring the progression of a specific pathology. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Suggest explanations based on interpretation of data from diagnostic assessment tools (e.g., identifying a broken bone in an X-ray, ultrasound of a pregnancy to determine number of fetuses and identifying high blood pressure based on given values). (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Interpret diagnostic results and choose an appropriate course of action based on participation in a role-play, simulation and/or case study. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why medical practitioners often use multiple tools and procedures to establish a medical diagnosis. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss possible implications (e.g., incorrect diagnosis, improper treatment and psychological effect on patient) associated with incorrect interpretation of diagnostic findings for the patient and others. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe some treatment options (e.g., dialysis, radiation therapy, surgery and organ transplantation) which have been designed to address specific health care issues. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe various treatment options that might be considered at various stages of a specific pathology from the perspective of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and/or alternative approaches to health care. (K)

units.name: Unit One: Death of the Old Order

items.text: Know that the process of adjusting to change will vary from one society to another.

Know that the process of adjusting to change will involve a number of stages:
- Denial/rejection of the change occurs when the change is unthinkable.
- Acknowledgment of change occurs when the new idea is given some credence and recognition.
- Acceptance of change occurs when more of an individual's behaviour centres on the new approach than the old; and,
- Defence of change-occurs-when the old idea is-seen as-wrong and-the-new-idea is viewed-as common sense.
Know that change can be either evolutionary or revolutionary.
Know that an interplay exists among social, economic, political and cultural domains within a society and that changes within one of the domains will impact the other forces.
Know that new visions of humans and society emerged during the early decades of the twentieth century which were to profoundly impact how nations viewed/interacted with other nations/peoples.

Know that the early decades of the twentieth century witnessed a confluence of forces that produced events and conditions, such as a world war, which seriously challenged the traditional institutions and political status quo in many nations.
Know that the impetus for change within a society can originate from events beyond the political.
boundaries of that society/nation.

Learn and practise the following analytical skills:
- defining the main parts;
- describing cause and effect relationships; and,
- describing how the parts of the whole are related to each other.
Learn and practise using the criteria of paradigms as a basis for making evaluations.
Learn and practise defining a problem, stating a hypothesis about the problem, and finding data which will confirm or disprove the hypothesis.

Values Issues The student will discuss:
- Whether a nation's decision-making processes should be influenced by external conditions such as involvement in a major war.
Whether the authoritarian. or democratic style of decision making and leadership is superior.
What should be the criteria in determining whether individual rights or societal/collective rights should be a paramount importance to the society.
What the proper balance between individual rights and collective rights should be in a society.
Whether conditions ever exist which demand that order and security take precedence over individual rights.
Know that an issue is a situation, problem or question in which there is uncertainty and/or opposing viewpoints.
Know that controversy occurs when there is uncertainty or opposing views about how and what to do to revolve an issue.

Know that dialectical thinking is:
- the process of searching outin a case the conflicts, contrasts, contradictions, and the differences in the content and; and,
- finding the idea that unites them while keeping and using the tension between them.

Know that the effective use of problem solving, dialectical reasoning, decision making, and conflict resolution abilities requires an individual to be able to ask and answer fundamental questions such as:
- What is this all about?
- What would be the best way of solving this?
- How can I generate a list of different things I can do?
- Would this way be better than that way?
- Is this approach getting me what I want?
- Do I like the results I'm getting?
- Am I really doing the right problem or is the problem something else?

Know that metacognition is the ability to think about one's own thinking processes and decide which of the many different strategies available would be useful for solving a problem or dealing with an issue.
Know that major political events, such as wars, are seldom the result of a particular event but are the culmination or outcome of many interrelated issues and actions.
Know that paradigms are long-lasting patterns of ideas, beliefs and values that act as criteria for decision making.
Review using information from their personal background as a source of data to develop conceptualizations.
Practise describing cause-effect relationships.
Review using criteria as a basis for making evaluations.
Should all persons affected by a possible decision have equal influence in formulating that decision?
Should the degree of influence exercised by an individual in the decision-making process reflect the position of that individual within the society?
… Should decisions made by agreement of those concerned carry more moral authority than decisions made by one individual for the group?
Know that protecting the sovereignty of the nation involved the preparation of contingency plans for hostile aggression, including military activity.
Know that individuals need to feel that they have significant input in the decision-making -processes-guiding.the.events-impacting-on their lives.
A society has to balance the freedom of individuals to choose how they want to express their individuality and potential with the rights of others to order and security.
Know that a society has to balance the freedom of the individual with the rights of the group.
Know that authoritarianism is a system of government in which decision-making is controlled by traditional leaders of government and coercion is utilized to:enforce compliance.
The system is based on the power of bureaucracies, the police, and loyal armies.
Know that an egalitarian model of decision-making allows those parties impacted by a possible decision to be meaningfully involved in arriving at that decision.
Know that power is the ability to make and carry out decisions.
Learn to use analogies as a means of furthering one’s understanding of concepts.
Review using criteria as a basis for making evaluations.
Practise identifying cause-effect relationships.
Practise drawing inferences from historic and contemporary events and situations.
Should a national -government be required to consult the public when making significant decisions such as a declaration of war?
Does good leadership mean placing controls on people so that they are disciplined and orderly?
Does good leadership mean empowering people to take charge of their lives so that they can create a better society?
In a democratic society, how can freedom and rights be balanced against accountability and responsibility?
Know that an interplay exits among social, economic, political and cultural domains within a society and that changes within one of the domains will impact the other domains.
Changes in the economic structure of a nation will promote changes in the politics and political priorities of that nation.
Economic needs will influence the foreign policies-and-activities-of a-nation.
Know that change can be either -evolutionary or revolutionary.
Know that individuals and societies need a period of adjustment in order to adapt to change.

The process of adjusting to change generally follows a process:
- Denial/rejection of the change occurs when the change is unthinkable. Any acceptance of change at this stage is coincidental.
- Acknowledgment of change occurs when the new idea is given some credence and recognition.
- Acceptance of change occurs when more of one's behaviour centres on the new approach than the old.
- Defence of change occurs when the old idea is seen as wrong and the new idea is basically viewed as common sense.
Know that a world perceived as hostile required the availability of sufficient military resources to protect a nation's sovereignty.
Often alliances with other nations were necessary to achieve that objective.
Know that modern nation states view the protection of sovereignty as being critical to national survival.
The threat to sovereignty may emanate from disruptive internal forces.
External threats may emanate from the policies and actions of other nations.
Practise stating a proposition based on an appropriate principle that will guide behaviour in this situation.
What are the factors which will-predispose-the – adoption of a particular decision-making style?
Will the support and commitment of the membership to a decision be influenced by the method in which that decision was made?

Know that nationalism involves:
- loyalty and commitment to the values and traditions of a nation or people seeking nationhood;
- assertion of a peoples' right to:
- have or extend territorial sovereignty command respect, fear or obedience of other peoples; and,
- occupy ancestral land.
- Knowthat for many groups, nationalism was based much more on their ethnic background than on membership in a large nation state which may be controlled by people of a different ethnic origin.
Know that a group's ethnicity is determined by its collective history, geographical location, language, social organization, and belief systems.
Know that this empire was a fragile political home to a number of nationalities, each of which desired political power and varying degrees of independence.
The Germans of Austria,who held the political power, constituted only one-third of the Empire's population.
The German dominance was being challenged by Hungarians, Czechs, and other ethnic groups.

Know that those groups in society, that had traditionally held the power to control and direct the society, felt that their power was being threatened by the middle and lower classes and became defensive about maintaining their control.
Know that nationalism can be used to stifle dissent and to force a consensus among various groups within society that otherwise would not occur.
Practise making up a classification system that can be used to summarize and order data for presentation, discussion, and analysis.
Learn to examine the logic of arguments using concept maps.
Learn to look for the bias and assumptions in logical arguments and to evaluate their validity.
Is there a style of decision making that can decrease the likelihood of decisions that are or appear to be unjust towards individuals or groups?
Do tradition and traditional beliefs hinder achieving equal justice for all individuals?
How can the rights of the minority be protected within a society?
What method should a minority utilize to ensure that their rights are respected within a society?
use violence as often as necessary in order to make the majority and authorities aware of the problem; or,
use non-violent tactics that will not alienate the majority but may result in lessening their support of the minority cause?
Know that nationalism mixed with racism has the potential to create serious barriers and dissension among peoples.

Know that racism is the idea that there a causal link between the physical traits individuals inherit and their traits of personality, intellect, or culture which make individuals of one race superior to individuals of another race.

Know that some groups of people, who believed that they were being denied access to the decision-making processes, demanded radical and sweeping changes to broaden access to the decision-making processes of all institutions within society.
Know that as societies become more specialized, they became more dependent on resources and markets outside of their borders.
Know that the capacity of industrialization to increase the material well-being of people made it too attractive for any society to resist.
Know that the high value placed on science had much to do with its capacity to make possible the production of goods and services.
Know that scientific developments convinced people that progress was possible and that an optimistic view of the future was a reasonable assumption.
Learn to use the critical attributes of concepts as the basis for classifying data for analysis.
Practise constructing and evaluating generalizations.
Learn to select and apply values as criteria for evaluating generalizations.
Practise using the critical attributes of concepts and values as criteria to evaluate historical situations.
Is the Golden Rule a legitimate place to begin a search for fundamental values about human dignity?
Are such-concepts-as race and ethnicity useful devices to categorize people and guide one's behaviour towards others?
are racial and ethnic diversity quite minimal when compared to the biological similarities among people; or,
can the behaviour of people be in part attributed to their racial ethnic background?
Do all people belonging to a particular race or ethnic group have the same perceptions of the world?
On what basis should one resolve the contradiction between what one wishes to believe and what the facts or values suggest should be believed?
Know that for many, science was a more reliable method of gaining accurate knowledge about reality that the traditional ways of religion, custom, and trial and error.

In the nineteenth century, intellectuals began to apply the methodology of science to the study of society in an attempt to find whether there were a set of universal laws governing society in a manner similar to those governing the physical.environment.
Know that it was generally accepted that all natural processes were governed by a set of natural laws, such as the law of gravity, which are unchanging and dependable.

Know that the Newtonian paradigm believed that all parts of nature are interconnected in a linear cause and effect relationship and that it would eventually be possible to predict all aspects of the behaviour of nature.
Know that, for many, the process of evolution was seen to be a natural process which looked as if it were similar to other physical laws governing the physical universe.
Know that, for many, if the natural behaviour of organisms were accepted to be competitive then survival of the fittest might be considered an universal law.
Know that if survival of the fittest could be seen as a natural law governing nature then it was accepted that it may also govern the social order of humans.
Learn to use the criteria of paradigms as a basis for making evaluations.
Review distinguishing facts from opinions and conclusions.
Learn to identify the stated and unstated assumptions in a communication.
Learn to identify the underlying logic being used in a communication.
Do paradigms serve as instruments to help define the world and events, or do they restrict a person's perception of the world and events?
Can human behaviour be adequately interpreted by applying a particular paradigm?
What are the consequences of adopting a particular paradigm?
How should people treat the idea of certainty when they understand the limitations paradigms place on human understanding?
If it is possible that beliefs which at some point were accepted as truth can now be shown to have serious shortcomings, how should individuals go about deciding what can be relied on as truth?
Know that most industrialized nations relied on markets outside of their borders to supply them with raw materials and to provide markets to sell their surplus productivity.
Know that economic growth depends on an economy's ability to produce a surplus (profit) .. which-can-be-saved-for-investment in enterprises which, in turn; willproduce a surplus.

Know that many European nations had exhausted the resources and opportunities to create new wealth within their homelands, and that the establishment of colonies offered an opportunity to gain new resources and new opportunities to create wealth.
Know that within various colonizing nations there were populations which actively supported the establishment of colonies.

items.text: Know that all nations must determine how to use their available human and material resources and that determination will involve choices among perceived/real demands on those resources.

Know that governments have a number of policy options when establishing relationships with Indigenous peoples.
Accommodation - The national government can meaningfully involve Indigenous people in formulating policies that impact the lives of Indigenous people.
Assimilation -The national government can institute policies aimed at having Indigenous people abandon their distinctiveness and acquire the culture and priorities of the majority society.

Genocide - The national government can resort to an extreme policy in which the Indigenous people are either deliberately killed or left unprotected from official and unofficial interests. The ultimate goal is to eliminate the Indigenous people.

Know that ecological engineering is the process of finding and bringing together organisms from nature, putting them into a new, contained environment where they will flourish and work for society.

Humans have to replace their arrogance with a spiritual dimension that allows them to relate to the natural world.
Humans will have to change their present relationship with the environment.

Necessary changes must include:

Know that social ecology holds the view that ecology includes both natural and human relations.

Should the interests and well-being of future generations take precedence over the interests and well-being of the present generation?
Know that the Gaia hypotheses suggest that the earth and all its systems makes up a single cybernetic system in which life produces and regulates its own environment.
Know that in most:societies there are competing interests that have to be reconciled.
Know that as resources become more scarce, it becomes more difficult to make decisions that satisfy conflicting interests without resorting to arbitrary measures of some kind.
Know that the future is not precisely predictable. All that can be said is that some basic principles will likely continue to be important in the conduct of human affairs.
Know that the process of change will continue for the foreseeable future.
Know that people in the future, just as in the past, will have to continue to adapt to new circumstances as they develop.

Should the marketplace be the sole determinator of how the earth's resources are used?
Who should be involved in determining the allocation and utilization of the earth's resources?
What criteria should be used to determine the utilization and allocation of the earth's resources?
What factors are essential to ensure the well-being of an individual and of a society?

Know that decision making can be:
- active in the sense of attempting to control and direct events; or,
- passive in allowing events to control and direct the decision.
Know that throughout much of human history, people could live in isolation from other regions of the world.
This is no longer true because the policies and practices of one nation can seriously affect the economy, environment, society, and politics of another nation.
Practise constructing grids as a way of organizing information for analysis.
Practise making hypotheses based on responsible assumptions and inferences.
Should the goals and priorities of the individual take priority over the goals and priorities of the society?

outcomes.statement: Apply effective project management strategies to the development of personal or professional projects.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Project Management (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for diversity (e.g., language, culture, ability, mobility, gender and sexual diversity) of the intended audience or audiences of one’s project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Develop a written production plan for an information processing project, that includes:
- a project proposal which outlines:
- the project idea;
- the purpose or goal;
- the target audience; and,
- the optimal format of the finished product.
- a planning tool such as a storyboard which demonstrates:
- the project timeline;
- necessary resources; and,
- the desired final outcome.
- a plan for assessment of the project and the plan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply the production plan to the development of a project, revising as necessary.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate a logical problem solving approach when difficulties arise in carrying out a project.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Proofread and critique a project, and edit the project according to feedback from other interested parties (e.g., clients, supervisors, focus groups).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Distribute or present a finished project to the intended audience.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on the effectiveness and the execution of the production plan to determine what should be changed or improved.

outcomes.statement: Apply principles of digital citizenship to digital communication.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Digital Communication B (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe principles of digital citizenship with respect to digital communication.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify possible motivations for sharing and communicating online.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe etiquette, rules and options when using digital communication technologies including social media platforms, e-mail, texting and instant messaging.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Justify the importance of respecting diversity (e.g., language, culture, ability, mobility, gender and sexual diversity) in digital communication.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the opportunities and challenges of developing and managing relationships using digital communications.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the effectiveness and impact of developing and managing online relationships (e.g., online friendships, following others, gaming conversations, online chats).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Manage online communication to align with personal values and goals, recognizing the permanence of a digital legacy.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how and why online communication can become viral.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe potential positive and negative effects of viral online communication.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize that reaction to posts or comments, such as “likes”, arguments and an increase in the number of views, can cause emotional effects (e.g., gratification, distress, frustration) for the sender and/or recipient.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Evaluate the potential effects of online communication in relation to issues such as bullying, sexting, homophobia and discrimination.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Propose strategies to combat the spread of harmful and anonymous postings.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Identify options for dealing with inappropriate online communication or behaviour.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Build a digital portfolio showcasing one’s use of digital communication.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and apply principles of digital law as it applies to current Canadian context.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6B: Digital Law B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that laws are necessary to protect the rights of all citizens.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine Canadian copyright laws and identify ways in which they apply to citizens in a digital environment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain why laws do not always reflect current digital technologies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the role of personal responsibility with respect to intellectual property rights and plagiarism.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the ethical and legal implications of activities such as digital stalking, sharing illicit content, hacking, piracy and plagiarism.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify different types of licensing (e.g., closed source, copyright protected, open source, public domain) for original work.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate options for licensing one’s own original work.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe consequences for unacceptable or unlawful online behaviour in school and community environments.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate acceptable practices while undertaking activities such as searching, remixing and sharing in a digital environment.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore careers in the field of digital law.

outcomes.statement: Consistently apply proper ergonomics and touch keyboarding techniques and skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7B: Keyboarding B (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify repetitive strain injury symptoms and the risk factors for injuries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine potential long-term consequences of not applying proper ergonomics while keyboarding.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design a workstation and organize work flow to support physical and mental well-being.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate healthy ergonomic practices (e.g., keyboard and monitor position, sitting position) while using various devices such as laptop computers, cellular phones and tablets.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate touch keyboarding skills (alphabetic, numeric, punctuation, and basic service keys).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Type with a speed and accuracy of over 40 correct words per minute.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use function keys to perform actions (e.g., undo, redo, close, save, print).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use modifier keys to insert special characters (e.g., dollar sign, checkmark or flower), mathematical symbols (e.g., percentage, division or approximately equal symbols) and various alphabetic (e.g. French, Nëhiyawëwin or Ukrainian) symbols.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use modifier key shortcuts to perform actions (e.g., print screen, redo, italicize, bold).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Use appropriate modifier keys to insert special characters, mathematical symbols and letters with accents.

outcomes.statement: Compose and publish business documents using a word processing application, following conventional formatting standards.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8B: Word Processing B (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review common professional documents (e.g., business letters, meeting agendas, meeting minutes, event itineraries) and note common standards utilized.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a variety of professional documents (e.g., business letters, agendas, minutes, itineraries) with and without templates.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify default settings in a document.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select and apply user preferences such as language, font type and size and line spacing in a document.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compose a formal document with elements according to a specific style guide (e.g., American Psychological Association [APA], Modern Language Association [MLA], Chicago).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how features such as hyperlinks, tables and graphs can increase the effectiveness of messaging in documents.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Insert features (e.g., hyperlinks, tables, charts, pictures, graphs, graphics) into a document.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct a table to organize and format information in a document.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Apply headings styles throughout a document to generate an automatic table of contents.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Use mail merge to insert content from a database, spreadsheet or table into documents.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Prepare documents for online publication using portable document format (PDF) software.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Use elements such as equations, symbols, date and time, watermark, borders and shading in the composition of documents.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Create engaging documents (e.g., business brochures, newsletters, magazines, posters, flyers) that demonstrate effective formatting and clear messaging.

outcomes.statement: Investigate solutions for known and potential computer related problems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9C: Computer Technology C (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a list of common computer related problems, questions or required procedures encountered by end users in the school and community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify troubleshooting supports including hardware manuals, product warranties and LED error codes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the advantages and disadvantages of free security technology and security technology available for purchase such as firewalls and anti-virus software.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore factors (e.g., need versus desire for new technology) that influence the purchase of computer technology tools.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain appropriate care of a technological device, including associated hardware.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how and why the storage capacity of a device should be monitored and maintained (e.g., disk cleanup, internal storage management).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a list of steps to follow in the event of problems with computer technology (e.g., hardware, software, a technology network).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a tool (e.g., Frequently Asked Questions [FAQ] page on a website, manual, flowchart, poster) to be used for troubleshooting computer related problems.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the function of computers and their components, and examine their suitability for various users’ needs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Hardware Design (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the functions of internal components of a computer (e.g., CPU, RAM, ROM, cache, hard drive, motherboard, power supply).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between a hard disk drive (HDD) and a solid state drive (SSD).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define and describe computer hardware (e.g., USB, Ethernet, HDMI), speed measurements (e.g., megahertz, gigahertz), and size measurements (e.g., megabytes, gigabytes, terabytes).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify basic hardware differences (e.g. dimensions, supported interfaces, power wattage requirements) from data sheets or specification listings for hardware components.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the functions of common computer peripheral devices (e.g., printer, monitor, scanner, keyboard, mouse, speakers, USB flash drive).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess users’ computing needs and recommend appropriate hardware components for different scenarios (e.g., a home video enthusiast, a distance education user, a student with a disability).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate accessibility tools to assist users of various operating systems in accommodating physical attributes such as individual sight, hearing or motor skill challenges.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the features and functions of computer networks.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Networking (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 9A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the purpose and characteristics of computer networks.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the functions of computer networks, including the role of a wireless router.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between wired (ethernet) networks and wireless (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth) networks.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe similarities and differences between personal home computer networks and business computer networks.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Inventory the projected uses of a home computer network.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain various methods (e.g., shared file access, shared printer access, Internet access) for sharing network resources.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify common networking applications (e.g., email, instant messaging, synchronous real time communication) and protocols (e.g., domain name system [DNS], file transfer protocol [FTP], hypertext transfer protocol [HTTP], hypertext transfer protocol secure [HTTPS], network interface controller [NIC]).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify layers of digital security, including networks, operating systems, applications and data, and the responsibility of users of each to enhance digital privacy and security.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess security limitations to current computing networks.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the implications of constant availability of computing networks on the lives of people.

outcomes.statement: Explore computersimulated reality technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality and mixed reality.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13A: Computer-simulated Reality Technologies A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 4B, 5B and 9B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Differentiate between computer simulated technologies, including:
- virtual reality (VR): immerses users in a fully artificial digital environment;
- augmented reality (AR): overlays virtual objects on the real-world environment; and,
- mixed reality (MR): does not just overlay, but anchors virtual elements to the real world.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe examples of applications of VR (e.g., gaming chat rooms, flight simulation), AR (e.g., filters applied to digital photos, games such as Pokémon Go) and MR (e.g., virtual surgery).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify hardware or devices (e.g., headsets, wearables, computer with high-end processor) needed to interact with VR, AR and MR.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how features of VR, AR and MR, including audio, frame rate, field of view, degrees of freedom and latency, relate to user experience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate the use of a VR, AR or MR technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe interactions between humans and computer-simulated reality technology.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research safety precautions related to the use of VR, AR and MR, including precautions regarding online purchases.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss limitations of current VR, AR and MR technologies and predict possible directions of future technologies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore careers in the fields of VR, AR and MR.

outcomes.statement: Explore the societal impact of computersimulated reality technologies such as virtual reality, augmented reality and mixed reality.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13B: Computer-simulated Reality Technologies B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 6B and 13A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore applications of computer-simulated reality technologies in various fields (e.g., medicine, education, manufacturing).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss ethical issues associated with computer-simulated reality technologies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe possible effects of interactions between humans and computersimulated reality technologies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore societal implications of the increasing prevalence of computersimulated reality technologies in our daily lives and routines.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how using emerging computer-simulated reality technologies can benefit society or individuals.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the impact of computer-simulated reality technologies on societal needs and desires such as communication, entertainment, health care, research and exploration.

outcomes.statement: Prepare and analyze charts that display data from a spreadsheet.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15D: Spreadsheets D (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 15C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the characteristics of pie, line and bar charts that can be created using spreadsheet data.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify other types of charts that can be created using spreadsheet data.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how charts display data differently than rows and columns in a spreadsheet and how chart presentation can influence one’s perception and interpretation of data.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create pie, line and bar charts to display data.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Move, size and delete charts created from spreadsheet data.

indicators.label: f

e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

outcomes.statement: Improvise in a jazz style on an instrument showing developing understanding of applicable jazz theory.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: To increase understanding of jazz style, analyze musical events within a solo or composition (e.g., shout chorus, form, dynamics, pitches, changes, articulation).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Play and/or transcribe recorded music of recognized performers through methods such as:
- play blues heads and simple and more complex jazz tunes by ear
- sing roots of the chord progression of the solo
- call and response with the teacher (or other students)
- sing and/or play along with solo
- sing the solo being studied without listening to the recording at the same time
- notate the solo including elements such as form, chord changes, pitches, rhythms articulations, and dynamics
- start with short sections, such as a few bars or a single lick, and gradually increase the length and complexity of the selection.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Create simple, short three or four note jazz licks and develop these licks by methods such as:
- transposing
- transforming
- adding single notes
- decorating
- connecting licks with segments of scales.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Show improvement and growth in the presentation and construction of improvised solos in a performance setting.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express oneself in the jazz idiom, using new ideas, new concepts, and a variety of styles.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Demonstrate, through writing, describing, and/or playing, the understanding of jazz theory including:
- II-V-I chord progressions
- modes of major and minor scales
- blues form
- 32-bar song form (AABA).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Improvise to show an understanding of the function of guide tones within a musical form or chord progression.

outcomes.statement: Integrate the understanding of jazz theory into personal musical performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare, rehearse, and perform music in a jazz style in solo, small group, or large ensemble settings.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement, and tone that help create a jazz style, and apply this knowledge while music making.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize and define musical forms emphasizing AABA (32-bar song form) in music that is listened to and/or performed.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design (with help from the teacher), implement, and evaluate a personal plan to improve the individual performance process, and to enhance knowledge and understanding of jazz (e.g., as part of the process of improvement, include recording and listening back to the performances, practices, and/or rehearsals).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore conventions regarding jazz articulation, and use those conventions in performance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Know, describe, and use proficiently in performance the standard notation conventions such as note durations up to 16th notes, Codas, D.S.s, and dynamic markings.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize and describe standards of notation in jazz music that are different from traditional "classical" notation (e.g., falls, doits, turns, and hats, as well as notation conventions such as how off-beat quarter notes should be written).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use jazz vocabulary to relate jazz theory to personal musical learning (see Jazz Glossary).

outcomes.statement: Show growth in individual instrumental techniques and knowledge of the elements of music, and apply these to create or show a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate and record technical development, with assistance from the teacher, and develop strategies to improve.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate technical inquiry questions and take action on the findings of the inquiry (e.g.,"What can I do to get better?" or "How could I change this performance, paper, or arrangement?")

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Play with a tone appropriate to the style and personal development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Work towards internalization of the concept of expressive playing and demonstrate this knowledge through playing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Play a two octave chromatic scale.* Play major, dorian, mixolydian, and blues scales in A, D, G, C, F, B♭, E♭, A♭, and D♭ concert, two octaves when possible.*

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Sight read music at one level below the general level of the music being performed by the ensemble.
*For students playing drum set, teachers may substitute other technique directly related to set playing, although the drummers should know the scales on mallets and perform the set techniques in addition to the mallet technique.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond as a jazz performer when playing jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of personal tone such as pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, and time.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the rest of the ensemble (e.g., their tone, pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, time, balance, and blend).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond to the ensemble's response to the student's responding to them (e.g. when the lead player starts to play out or articulate a certain way, does the band follow and does the lead player recognize it?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the conductor/leader, including his/her gestures, cues, tempo, expressions, and body language.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to the acoustic properties of the performing space, including the sound, tone, loudness, and reverb of the room, and adjust playing accordingly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: React to the audience, to their presence (or not), body language, expressions, and their reaction to the music (e.g. applause, cheering, being asked to play quieter).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Know the history, culture, style, form, and tempo of the music being performed and respond to the music (written or not written) by reading the music and/or performing the notes and/or changes appropriately.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recall previous experiences and knowledge (in music and in life) and integrate these into solo and group jazz performances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know any special emotional context that may apply to the music, generate the appropriate emotional feeling or energy, and/or change the personal emotional state of the performer to synchronize it with the emotional context of the music being performed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Know,predict, and/or anticipate what is next or might be next in the music and prepare for that while performing in the moment of the music.

outcomes.statement: Listen to jazz as a jazz performer when not personally playing the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to jazz music and analyze form, tone, style, era, dynamics, articulation, time signature, characteristic rhythms, time, balance, blend, key and/or pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the development of the jazz music (head, arrangement, or improvisation) as a whole or in smaller sections.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on the structure of the chord progression and the potential development of the chord progression.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the characteristic sounds, licks, tone and other elements of well-known players and/or groups.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Individually or as a class, identify performers and/or groups on recordings just by listening to the characteristic sounds or ideas presented in the music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on just one instrument from the beginning to the end of the musical selection (e.g., Did the player play the same way all the way through? How was it different or the same? What did he/she play that the student also might be able to play?)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on the melody, bass line, fills (including drums and percussion), background lines, chord progression, roots, and sing along with the recording.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the history, cultural heritage, and effect of current events as these apply to the musical selection.

outcomes.statement: Develop ability to analyze jazz music independently in real time while making or listening to the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually and in groups, develop, experiment with, and purposefully use strategies to solve different challenges related to music making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common chord progressions or forms including but not limited to blues, AABA form, and II-V-Is, in music performed and/or listened to (including progressions that break from the norm).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the time signature on first hearing a piece of music, including complex time signatures such as 5/4, 6/4, triple metres like 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8, in addition to simpler time signatures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: On first hearing a piece of music, use previously developed strategies to learn the time signature of the music, and where appropriate clap on 2 and 4.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Know the pattern of strong and weak beats that are identified with the time signatures.

outcomes.statement: Individually develop and apply criteria to use in critical evaluation of performances of jazz music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to the music of the great jazz performers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate criteria of excellence through listening to the music of the great performers (e.g., What is it that makes the music great? What do the great performers do that the student or student's ensemble do not?).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Individually for each student and in groups for the ensemble, design and implement a plan for improvement based on the criteria generated from listening to the great performers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: When listening to a musical selection, describe and classify the music using appropriate jazz language (e.g., style, period, composer, culture, and performer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Refine the skills in listening actively, continue to develop listening skills, and recognize that listening actively contributes to the authenticity of performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the value of original thought, technical proficiency, place, era, and other concepts in the music of the great jazz performers.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate the knowledge and the implementation of the skills, techniques, and attitudes necessary for successful ensemble performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Know the basic functions and challenges of the parts within the student's section in the ensemble by demonstrating the ability to perform those specific tasks that are particular to the instrument that the student plays in the ensemble (e.g., comping for guitar and piano, walking lines for the bass, solo chairs in the horns, and position in a section).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Individually attend to melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy, and articulation in the preparation and performance of jazz, with direction from the teacher as necessary.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Continue to work on playing in tune with good balance and tone and know the intonation tendencies of the student's instrument.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Establish a "professional" attitude towards conduct, focus, and communication skills in rehearsal, preparation of materials, and presentation of products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Show respect for the personal work of self and others through appropriate critique.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Critically examine and assess the student's individual work and personal contributions to group projects/performances, with direction from the teacher as necessary.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Be accepting of appropriate critiques from others and work towards implementing the solutions to that critique.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate personal knowledge of the value of individual practice and know how to practice, conduct an ongoing evaluation of the student's personal practice skills, and implement a plan to improve.

outcomes.statement: Explore personal ability to distinguish aurally the different eras, genres, styles, and feels of jazz by listening to and/or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually develop (through listening) a list or understanding of the basic characteristics of different jazz styles, genres, periods, and place, and implement that knowledge into practice and performance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Individually and/or in groups work towards being able to categorize jazz music into styles, genres, periods, and/or place on first hearing the music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore aspects of jazz such as history, performers, styles, and eras through a variety of media.

outcomes.statement: Examine jazz music and its performers and educators and their influence in the world.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the challenges that jazz artists with black, First Nations, and mixed race heritage had (from the beginning to the middle of the 20th century) in their daily life, and reflect on whether the situation has changed today.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify influential players of the student's instrument, investigate why these performers are so influential, listen to their music, and pay special attention to performers from Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and describe how jazz artists may raise or have raised awareness about local, national and international issues (e.g., songs such as Billy Holiday's "Strange Fruit" and John Coltrane's "Alabama" or issues involving artists such as Benny Goodman and segregation, John Stetch and cultural heritage, and Randy Weston and cultural heritage).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research career avenues in jazz and music in general.

outcomes.statement: Explore the relationship between jazz and "classical" music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of jazz in "classical" music (e.g., Stravinsky, Bernstein, Copland, Ravel, Gershwin, Milhaud) and the influence of classical music on jazz composers (e.g., Ellington, Brubeck, Corea, Beiderbecke).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how Canadian and international copyright laws may affect the lives of consumers of jazz.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 3 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the history of journalism and its role in society.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the role of journalism in democracy.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the economic, social, historical and political influences on journalism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the relationship between ownership of media and the production and consumption of news.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the changing roles, processes and structures within journalism.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the experiences and responsibilities of a contemporary journalist.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between amateur and professional journalists and examine the impact of each on the profession of journalism.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role and impact of student journalists within the school and community.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the risks, challenges and opportunities associated with professional journalism.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess the impact of journalism on public opinion and that of public opinion on journalism.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how changes in technology have impacted and continue to impact research, editing and producing forms of journalism.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of digital media on print, broadcast and photojournalism texts.

outcomes.statement: Examine journalistic ethics, rights and responsibilities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between rights and responsibilities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research codes of ethics, principles and standards (e.g., Canadian Association of Journalists Ethics Guidelines, The Canadian Press Stylebook and Canadian Broadcasting Standards Council Codes) that guide Canadian journalists and the journalism industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine legal implications of journalistic rights and responsibilities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore international journalistic codes of ethics and their role in protecting the integrity of journalistic expression.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss legal and ethical issues (e.g., authorship, copyright, ownership and cultural appropriation) associated with publishing journalistic texts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine school-related policies for sharing information and publishing journalistic texts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop and implement a class code of ethics for Journalism Studies 20.

outcomes.statement: Examine print, broadcast and photojournalism texts for accuracy, style and journalistic conventions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss how language, text structures and distinctive conventions communicate information in a variety of journalistic texts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the quality, reliability and authenticity of various journalistic texts, including print, broadcast and photojournalism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine perspectives, beliefs or biases evident in a variety of journalistic texts and their potential impact on the consumer.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the representation of groups and individuals (e.g., whose voice is heard, whose voice is missing) in journalistic texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the elements (e.g., timeliness, proximity, prominence, conflict, progress and emotions) of a newsworthy story.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine different journalistic styles to explore how similar ideas, information or issues are communicated in a variety of texts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss consumer responsibilities (e.g., think critically, ask questions and verify information) when engaging with journalistic texts.

outcomes.statement: Employ journalistic interview skills to gather and communicate information.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Select, use and evaluate critically a variety of before, during and after strategies to construct and communicate meaning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Plan for the interview (e.g., identify the purpose, determine the format and prepare questions).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use oral language that is respectful and inclusive to build relationships and a sense of community (e.g., cultural and linguistic background).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Employ appropriate eye contact (cognizant of cultural variations and norms), speaking rate, volume, enunciation, inflection and gestures to communicate ideas effectively.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Demonstrate effective, active listening behaviours:
- Listen with a purpose to understand and learn.
- Adapt listening and focus to the purpose and situation (e.g., in person, telephone and virtual conference).
- Identify the ways the speaker communicates (e.g., word choice, tempo and tone).
- Recognize the overall key ideas and issues.
- Interact appropriately for clarification.
- Recognize the speaker’s attitude and bias.
- Recall and summarize the main ideas and conclusions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Employ a variety of notetaking tools (e.g., charts, lists and digital recordings), with the source’s agreement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Apply elements of effective interview skills:
- Engage with the source’s ideas, arguments and work.
- Be flexible and prepared to change the direction of an interview.
- Demonstrate a courteous, professional and neutral demeanour.
- Use a variety of techniques (e.g., pause, redirect, ask probing or open-ended questions) to elicit responses.
- Maintain an independence of judgement.
- Allow the subject to do the talking.
- Confirm the source’s agreement to the interview format and process.
- Ask for the source’s permission to call back if the need arises.

indicators.label: i

outcomes.statement: Employ journalistic research skills to gather and communicate information.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the elements (e.g., timeliness, proximity, prominence, conflict, progress and emotions) of a newsworthy story.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Record details (e.g., habits, customs, human institutions, cultural groups, events and natural world) of everyday life as documentable and symbolic subject matter that contributes to social understanding.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Locate, assess and summarize information from a variety of sources.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct extensive research to verify facts and elaborate with details.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Document sources and integrate quotations by adhering to journalistic conventions and reference tools (e.g., The Canadian Press Stylebook and New Canadian Media Ethnic Media & Diversity Style Guide).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop and use time management strategies to produce quality materials within publication timelines.

outcomes.statement: Create and publish a variety of print journalism texts that explore identity, social responsibility and social action.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Create a range of print journalism texts (e.g., news story, editorial, sports story, feature story and review) to explore personal viewpoints and others’ perspectives on issues related to:
- identity (e.g., experiences, traditions and worldviews);
- social responsibility (e.g., environmental sustainability, human rights and treaty rights); and,
- social action (e.g., advocacy, stewardship and volunteerism).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore what makes a story newsworthy (e.g., proximity, prominence, timeliness, oddity, consequence, conflict, human interest, extremes/superlatives, scandal and impact).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Select, use and evaluate critically a variety of before, during and after strategies during pre-production, production and post-production of print journalism texts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when writing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine audience and purpose and select appropriate format.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Employ the elements of a news story:
- Use the news writing style appropriate to the story.
- Write effective headlines.
- Use precise, simple words.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compose print texts that present an objective perspective and accurate details.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Select, use and evaluate critically a variety of before, during and after strategies during pre-production, production and post-production of broadcast journalism texts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when writing and speaking.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine audience and purpose and select appropriate format (e.g., television, radio, podcast or website).

indicators.label: f

Employ the elements of a news story:

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the skills and dispositions of effective broadcasters.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Present original broadcast texts that demonstrate an objective perspective and accurate details.

indicators.text: Select, use and evaluate critically a variety of before, during and after strategies during pre-production, production and post-production of photojournalism texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when representing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine audience and purpose and select appropriate format (e.g., television, radio, podcast and website).

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the skills and behaviours of effective photojournalists.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create photojournalism texts that present an objective perspective and accurate details.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply photo-editing techniques to communicate a message and to evoke a response.

outcomes.statement: Explore and share findings on a topic, issue or question related to concepts addressed in Journalism Studies 20.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate ideas for topics, issues or questions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine the topic, issue or question for exploration.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Formulate and revise questions to focus the exploration.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop and implement a plan to access, gather, and evaluate ideas and information from a variety of sources (e.g., human, print and digital).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Utilize the creative process (e.g., planning, drafting and revising) in preparation for sharing findings.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document and track the creative process to communicate progress and understanding of the topic, issue or question.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Share the findings of the exploration in a format suitable for the identified audience and purpose.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process (i.e., exploration and sharing).

outcomes.statement: Establish goals and plans for language learning and use relevant to Journalism Studies 20.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Select and use assessment tools (e.g., rubrics, checklists and success criteria) to determine language learning goals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a plan for achieving language learning goals based on self-assessment of achievements, needs and interests.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Monitor and reflect on progress in achieving language learning goals based on self-assessment and feedback.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider alternative strategies to attain language goals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Select a range of products to document own growth and explain the reasons for choices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on attainment of personal goals for effective language learning, including new understandings, skills and strategies.
