outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe procedures to lift and support vehicles.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Vehicle Lifting and Support (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow appropriate safe practices related to lifting and supporting vehicles, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify appropriate lifting and support equipment needed for the task.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify lift and balance points for different types of vehicles.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Position vehicles safely and correctly before lifting.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Lift and lower vehicles in a safe manner using floor jacks and jack stands.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Raise large drivetrain assemblies using hoists and transmission jacks.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Lift and lower vehicles on a hoist in a safe manner using proper procedures.

outcomes.statement: Locate automotive service information utilizing appropriate sources.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Automotive Service Information (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the type of information available from common automotive service information sources (e.g., manuals, computers, scan tools, diagnostic charts, technical bulletins and apps).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine correct service information such as torque specifications, wiring diagrams and disassembly/assembly procedures from appropriate sources.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate care in handling manuals, computers and scan tools.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze vehicle identification numbers (VIN) and compliance labels.

outcomes.statement: Perform appropriate automotive maintenance procedures safely and correctly.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9D: Automotive Maintenance (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices when performing automotive maintenance procedures, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Locate and follow manufacturer’s lubrication and maintenance schedules.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and choose lubricant types and filters for different vehicles and service conditions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform automotive drivetrain (e.g., engine, transmission, transfer case, differential) lubricant and filter changes.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Perform manufacturer recommended system maintenance such as checking spark plugs, fuel filters and positive crankcase ventilation valves.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform chassis and body lubrication according to manufacturers’ specifications.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Perform complete multi-point vehicle inspections (e.g., belts, hoses, leaks, constant velocity [CV] boots).

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive wheel bearings and hubs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Automotive Wheel Bearings (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., avoid dry spinning bearings with air and follow correct procedures when working with bearing presses) when working with automotive wheel bearings, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common automotive bearing types.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Handle, clean and repack wheel bearings following appropriate procedures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Inspect and evaluate wheel bearings and hub condition.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Remove and install wheel bearings, cups and seals using appropriate tools and equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Remove and install wheel bearing hub assemblies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Adjust wheel bearing pre-load appropriately.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Follow correct torqueing procedures for all wheel bearing fasteners and discuss how improper torqueing can be a safety issue.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive hydraulic systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Automotive Hydraulics (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., avoid having pressurized hydraulic fluids pierce the skin or enter the bloodstream and avoid contact with brake fluid on painted surfaces) when working with automotive hydraulic systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper procedures for disposal of used hydraulic fluids and explain potential environmental concerns associated with disposal of hydraulic fluids.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the properties of different hydraulic fluids (e.g., brake fluid and power steering fluid).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how Pascal’s law applies to force, pressure and area in hydraulic systems.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Diagnose common hydraulic system failures such as air and fluid leaks.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Diagnose and repair hydraulic failures in automotive hydraulic systems (e.g., brake, clutch and power steering).

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive brake systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13A: Automotive Brake Systems (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 12

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of asbestos dust from brake components, avoid dust inhalation and avoid contact with brake fluid on painted surfaces) when working with automotive brake systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List the properties, maintenance and testing procedures of different types of automotive brake fluids.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the construction, application, and inspection of brake components (e.g., brake hoses, lines, wheel cylinders, calipers, drums, rotors and hardware).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how principles of friction apply to disc and drum brake systems.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss factors that influence automotive brake performance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the purpose, construction and operation of electric, hydraulic and vacuum power brake assist systems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify common brake problems and related diagnostic procedures.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Perform common automotive brake system scheduled maintenance such as resurfacing brake drums and disc rotors.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Remove, install and/or adjust brake system components and bleed air from hydraulic brake systems using appropriate methods and tools.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Follow correct torqueing procedures for all brake systems fasteners and discuss how improper torqueing can be a safety issue.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair anti-lock brake systems (ABS).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13B: Antilock Brake Systems (ABS) (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 13A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of residual pressures and ensure all electrical wiring is located away from moving parts) when working with antilock brake systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the different types of ABS and their use in braking, stability control and traction control.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the function and operation of ABS and their components.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Diagnose and perform ABS repairs according to manufacturers' recommended procedures, including bleeding the system as necessary.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Follow correct torqueing procedures for all ABS fasteners and discuss how improper torqueing can be a safety issue.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive suspension systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: Automotive Suspension Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of the dangers of welding or heating steering linkage components and be aware of spring tension) when working with automotive suspension systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how different types of springs (e.g., leaf, coil, torsion bar and air) are used in automotive suspension systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the operation of suspension components (e.g., shocks, struts, sway bars and ball joints) and their effects on vehicle stability.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Inspect and evaluate suspension component condition for damage, corrosion, wear and excessive play.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Diagnose and perform repair procedures (e.g., remove and replace parts in pairs, disassemble and reassemble a strut and spring assembly and replace ball joints) on automotive suspension systems using appropriate equipment (e.g., ball joint press and strut spring compressor).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Make preliminary wheel alignment adjustments after suspension components (e.g., struts and control arms) have been replaced.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Follow correct torqueing procedures for all suspensions systems fasteners and discuss how improper torqueing can be a safety issue.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive steering systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Automotive Steering Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of the dangers of welding or heating steering linkage components) when working with automotive steering systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the operation and components of linkage and rack-and-pinion steering systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the parameters (e.g., caster, camber and toe) that affect wheel alignment and how misalignment of each can affect vehicle handling and tire wear.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how steering component wear or damage can affect handling, steering control and alignment geometry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Inspect and assess steering components for damage, corrosion, wear and excessive play.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Diagnose and perform common steering system repairs using appropriate equipment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Make preliminary wheel alignment adjustments after replacing steering components (e.g., pitman or idler arm and tie rods).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Follow correct torqueing procedures for all steering systems fasteners and discuss how improper torqueing can be a safety issue.

outcomes.statement: Measure and adjust wheel alignments.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14C: Wheel Alignments (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 14B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., ensure proper connection of wheel alignment equipment and be aware of pinch points) when performing wheel alignments including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Connect wheel alignment equipment appropriately to obtain alignment data.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Read and interpret wheel alignment data to determine which adjustments are necessary.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Make final wheel alignment adjustments according to manufacturer’s specifications, measured with an alignment machine.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive cooling systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Automotive Cooling Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., check coolant pressure and temperature) when working with automotive cooling systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper procedures for disposal of used coolants and explain potential environmental concerns associated with antifreeze disposal.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how cooling systems remove and dissipate heat from engines, including the role of antifreeze.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the function of the components of a liquid cooling system.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the operation of liquid and air cooling systems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform common cooling system tests (e.g., visual inspection, pressure tests, leak detection and coolant tests) and maintenance procedures (e.g., checking fluid levels and flushing the cooling system).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Diagnose and perform common automotive cooling system repairs such as removing and replacing belts, radiator, water pump and thermostat.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Fill automotive coolant systems according to specifications and purge air from systems where required.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair automotive exhaust systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Automotive Exhaust Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of hot surfaces and dangers of using pipe bending equipment) when working with automotive exhaust systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Dispose of automotive exhaust system components such as catalytic converters properly.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the function and operation of automotive exhaust systems and their components.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply appropriate care and attention when working with fragile exhaust components such as O2 sensors, catalytic converters and ceramics.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Inspect and evaluate exhaust systems for leaks, mounting issues, corrosion, blockage and noise.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Diagnose and repair common automotive exhaust system faults.

outcomes.statement: Explain multi-cylinder engine construction and operation.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19A: Multi-cylinder Engine Theory (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 18

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the construction and function of major engine sub-assemblies (e.g., cooling, exhaust, lubrication systems) in multi-cylinder engines.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between common automotive engine configurations (e.g., inline, V-type and opposed).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between common automotive valve train configurations (e.g., cam in block, single overhead camshaft and dual overhead camshaft) in multi-cylinder engines.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how the events of combustion change with different fuel sources (e.g., diesel, varying octane gasoline and compressed natural gas [CNG]).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the air flow of naturally aspirated and forced air (e.g., supercharged and turbocharged) engines.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the purpose and operation of internal engine components (e.g., camshaft, crankshaft and pistons) and variations (e.g., cam lift, piston shape and ring design) of each component.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Define and determine engine measurements such as displacement, compression ratio and clearance.

outcomes.statement: Perform basic engine diagnosis, testing and repair.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19B: Engine Testing, Diagnosis and Repair (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of high voltage shock hazards, pinch points, hot surfaces, sharp surfaces, moving parts and fire hazards) when performing basic engine diagnosis, testing and repair, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Follow established systematic diagnosis procedures, including visual inspections and diagnostic tests, to identify specific engine problems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Adjust, repair and/or replace engine components to solve problems and optimize performance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how engine modifications can affect engine performance.

outcomes.statement: Diagnose, service and repair manual transmissions and transaxles.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g. lift and support components properly and be aware of component weight and pinch points) when working with manual transmissions, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify common symptoms and faults associated with manual transmissions.

indicators.label: g

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the history of mass media and its role in society.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between media, media texts and mass media.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the historic and evolving purposes and principles behind mass media.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine the evolution of mass media as a means of communicating issues related to:
- identity (e.g., experiences, traditions, worldviews);
- social responsibility (e.g., environmental sustainability, human rights and treaty rights); and,
- social action (e.g., advocacy, stewardship and volunteerism).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss the impact of technology on the production and consumption of, and interaction with, media texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the economic, social, political and environmental influences on and of mass media.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Consider how historical, cultural, political and social contexts influence the presentation of ideas, themes and issues in media.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the power and influence of mass media and popular culture on personal identity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the impact and influence of mass media and popular culture on society.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the opportunities and challenges associated with the production and consumption of, and interaction with, mass media.

outcomes.statement: Examine the use of language conventions, text forms and style in media texts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the language cues and conventions used in a variety of media texts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore mentor texts to analyze the use of language cues and conventions, considering the personal, cultural, political and historical contexts in which they were created.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the distinctive characteristics of media genres and text forms.

indicators.text: Discuss strategies and techniques that producers of media texts employ to develop their ideas and present them in fresh and interesting ways.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine different media styles to explore how similar ideas, information or issues are communicated in a variety of media texts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss how language, text forms and style create meaning and influence the interpretation of messages in media texts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the quality, inclusivity and authenticity of the message in various media texts.

outcomes.statement: Critically interpret a variety of media texts for message and meaning.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the purposes and audiences of a variety of media texts (e.g., news articles, poems, films, television shows, songs, advertisements, games, emails, packaging, clothing and blogs).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Examine traditional and contemporary media texts that present different viewpoints and perspectives on issues related to:
- identity (e.g., experiences, traditions and worldview);
- social responsibility (e.g., environmental sustainability, relationships and treaty rights); and,
- social action (e.g., advocacy, stewardship and volunteerism).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain ways that individuals, society and culture shape and are shaped by the language, text forms and content of media texts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interpret the interrelationship between the message, the audience and the medium.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze media texts for explicit and implicit messages, concepts, viewpoints, themes and tone.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss consumer responsibilities (e.g., think critically, ask questions and verify information) when engaging with media texts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consider how historical, cultural, political and social contexts influence the presentation and interpretation of ideas, information and issues in texts.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze and compare different media texts to explore how similar ideas, information or issues are communicated.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine representation (e.g., language, culture, ability, mobility, sexual diversity and gender) in media texts, including the perspectives, beliefs and biases that are evident in the texts.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Interpret and discuss the use of language and techniques in a variety of media texts, considering the personal, cultural, political and historical contexts in which they were created.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss legal and ethical issues (e.g., authorship, copyright, ownership, public domain and cultural appropriation) associated with media texts.

indicators.text: Examine the need for societal standards (e.g., legal, ethical and community norms and values) and cultural awareness in media.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss consumer rights and responsibilities (e.g., to compliment, to complain or to advocate), related to advertisements and marketing of mass media.

items.text: Explore historical and contemporary elements of the natural environment and kinship.
Recognize personal roles and responsibilities in family and community according to the Michif/Métis core values).
Discuss the traditional and contemporary roles of women in maintaining kinship ties and caring for each other.

Discuss places in Canada where Michif French is and was historically spoken (e.g., St. Laurent, St. Eustache and Saint Ambroise in Manitoba, the St. Louis Batoche, St. Laurent, the Duck Lake region in Saskatchewan, and the Lac la Biche, St. Paul, St. Albert and Bonnyville areas in Alberta).
Investigate opportunities in Saskatchewan to participate in Michif French language revitalization.

Discuss the transmission and endangerment of the Michif French language (e.g., Why was Michif French not always taught at home? Why were people reluctant to speak Michif French? Why and when did this stigma shift?).
Compare Michif languages (Northern, Heritage & Michif French) in terms of their origin, similarities, and differences.
Consider effective ways that local Indigenous language revitalization approaches have been implemented.
Discuss Indigenous language revitalization projects in other parts of the world and how successful strategies can be applied to Michif Language revitalization efforts in Saskatchewan.

Identify institutes and organizations that support efforts (e.g., resources, lesson plans, recordings) to revitalize Michif languages (e.g., Gabriel Dumont Institute, Louis Riel Institute, Métis Nation - Saskatchewan, Rupertsland Institute).
Discuss with representatives of Michif/Métis organizations about their efforts to revitalize Michif languages.
Explore Michif language programs that exist (e.g., Michif Kindergarten, online classes, in-person classes, language nests, post-secondary classes, community-led Michif classes).
Apply, with some support, a variety of before, during, and after comprehension strategies to construct meaning in Michif French written texts and oral communications.
Learn through la manyair dis promnii (e.g. with Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, family, peers) both inside and outside of the classroom.

Explain interpretation of written texts and oral communications, after listening or reading, using strategies such as:
• discussing key words in written texts and oral communications;
• making connections between new information, prior knowledge and personal experience; and,
• reacting with emotion (e.g., empathy, surprise, appreciation or dislike).
Develop personal language learning tools (e.g., personal Michif French Dictionary, self-created pronunciation audio files) on topics such as: hunting, trapping, harvesting, kinship, Michif languages.

Consult resources (e.g., Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, peers, family, Michif French dictionaries and mobile apps, anchor charts and websites) and visual aids (e.g., pictures, graphs and drawings) to help construct meaning of written texts and oral communications.
Use tools (e.g., charts, vocabulary lists, personal dictionaries, audio files) to help construct meaning of written texts and oral communications.
Apply, with some support, a variety of strategies to produce Michif French written texts and oral communications.
Learn through la manyair dis promnii (e.g., with Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, family, peers).
Practise the Michif French language for communication on topics such as the natural environment, kinship and Michif languages.
Use tools such as graphic organizers and outlines to make a plan for speaking or writing.

Consult resources (e.g., Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, peers, family, Michif French dictionaries and mobile apps, anchor charts and websites) and visual aids (e.g., pictures, graphs and drawings) to support the production of oral and written messages.

Practise taking risks (e.g., trying unfamiliar approaches, experimenting with various forms of expression, utilize social-emotional learning techniques such as positive self-talk and humour to build confidence) to reduce linguistic insecurity.
Use prior knowledge for personal expression in Michif French.
Experiment with physical (e.g., gestures and facial expressions) and auditory (e.g., laughter, tone, volume) cues to convey meaning.
Retell (in Michif French) a Michif French oral communication with Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, peers, or family members.
Establish goals to further one’s learning journey of Michif French language and culture.
Consider strengths and needs in the development of goals for improving personal Michif French language learning and use.
Use a self-assessment tool created by self, peers and/or teacher, to target areas for improvement.
Develop goals and plans for improving speaking, listening, reading and writing in Michif French.
Explore Michif /Métis ways to cope with challenges (e.g., visiting, spirituality, meeting with Lii pleu vyeu).
Seek opportunities to communicate in Michif French (e.g., at community events and celebrations).

Reflect on identity through the Michif / Métis worldview and language by considering questions such as:
• How does la manyair dis promnii help to improve my understanding of the Michif French language and worldview?
• How does my use of Michif French shape the way I understand the natural environment?
• How does my use of Michif French shape the way I understand kinship?
• How does my use of Michif French shape the way I understand the revitalization of Michif French?
Apply, with some support, when listening and reading, Michif French language concepts including context-specific vocabulary, sentence structure and linguistic conventions.

Employ context-specific and common vocabulary (e.g., lii zanimo - animals, lii plaant - plants, la faamii - family, Lii pleu vyeu (Elders), la laang - language) while recognizing the differences in pluralizations.
Discuss the use of plural personal pronouns (e.g., nou, nouzootes, vou, vouzootes, onn, i).
Recall appropriate prepositions in context (e.g., annaryayr - behind, annavaan – in front of, dissu– on top of, ennhou - above, akoootii – beside, didaan – inside).
Apply basic knowledge of definite (e.g., le, la, laay, lii) and indefinite (e.g., aen, de, day, dii) articles.
Recognize context-specific adjectives (e.g., vyaand sesh - dry meat, bell rasaad – nice beads, groo pwashon - big fish, taant shawkii - angry aunty, laay zwayzoo shaantay – singing birds).

Paraphrase simple sentences in context (e.g., Je tapray shassii - I am hunting, Je ramaas lii grenn - I am picking berries, Je tapray promni sou ma faamii - I am visiting my family, Onnay contaan - We are happy, Onnay fyayr daytr Michif - We are proud to be Michif).
Apply, with some support, when speaking and writing, Michif French language concepts including context-specific vocabulary, sentence structure and linguistic conventions.

Use context-specific and common vocabulary (e.g., lii zanimo - animals, lii plaant - plants, la faamii - family, Lii pleu vyeu - Elders, la laang - language) while recognizing the differences in pluralizations.
Classify the use of plural personal pronouns (e.g., nou, vou, onn, i).
Practise appropriate prepositions in context (e.g., annaryayr - behind, annavaan – in front of, dissu – on top of, ennhou - above, akoootii – beside, didaan – inside).
Apply basic knowledge of definite (e.g., le, la, laay, lii) and indefinite articles (e.g., aen, de, day, dii).
Explore context-specific adjectives (e.g., vyaand sesh - dry meat, bonn rasaad - nice beads, groo pwashon - big fish, taant shawkay angry aunty , laay zwayzoo shaantay – singing birds).

Summarize simple sentences in context (e.g., Je tapray shassii I am hunting, Je ramaas lii grenn - I am picking berries, Je tapray aen promni sou ma faamii – I am visiting my family, On nay contaan – We are happy, On nay fyayr daytr Michif - We are proud to be Michif).
Construct meaning, with some support, of a variety of short oral non-fiction and fiction Michif French communications on familiar topics.

Listen to or view a variety of short oral Michif French messages (e.g., how to videos, storytelling videos, in-person visiting, songs) that address elements of:
• the natural environment;
• kinship; and,
• Michif language revitalization.
Demonstrate comprehension of oral messages in a variety of ways (e.g., informal conversation, class discussion, visual arts, graphs, and concept maps).
Identify the intended purpose and audience of oral communication.

Respond appropriately to simple questions during daily conversations regarding familiar topics (e.g., gathering and harvesting, kinship and community gatherings, food and drink) in two or three short phrases.
Extract main points from short oral Michif French messages or interactions with visual aids (e.g., illustrations, diagrams and concrete examples).
Make connections between the message in oral communication and personal life experiences.
Construct meaning, with some support, of a variety of short written non-fiction and fiction Michif French texts on familiar topics.

Read a variety of short written Michif French texts (e.g., children’s books, recipes, dictionaries, conversational sentences, student created texts) that elements of:
• the natural environment;
• kinship; and,
• Michif language revitalization.
Identify the intended purpose and audience of written texts.
Interpret directions on how to arrive at local historical spaces.
Describe the main character(s), conflict and theme in short stories and dramatic texts.
Follow basic imperative written instructions.
Navigate Michif French language websites and mobile apps to construct meaning in Michif French texts.
Explain the vocabulary words in context in written texts on familiar topics.
Paraphrase the message presented in short written texts on familiar topics (e.g., kinship, harvesting medicines, trapping, fishing, animals).
Make connections between the message in written texts and personal life experiences.
Produce, with some support, a variety of short oral non-fiction and fiction Michif French communications on familiar topics.

Produce a variety of short oral Michif French communications or messages related to elements of:
• the natural environment;
• kinship; and,
• Michif language revitalization.
Respond appropriately to other speakers when participating in guided conversations.
Participate in conversations to share information on predictable and familiar topics such as the environment, family, celebrations and language.
Share opinions on familiar topics (e.g., stewardship, genealogy, language use) and invite others to share theirs.
Provide instructions for performing a task (e.g., fishing, fire making, harvesting plants, finding local historical spaces) and model the procedure.
Communicate time in the past, present and future (e.g., in the summer, last week, next month, at midnight).

Present oral productions (e.g., short autobiographies, how-to instructions related to big ideas, dialogues about language revitalization) using a variety of visuals (e.g., illustrations, videos, maps, pictures) to support expression.
Produce, with some support, a variety of short written non-fiction and fiction Michif French texts on familiar topics.

Produce a variety of short written Michif French texts related to elements of:
• the natural environment;
• kinship; and,
• Michif language revitalization.

Convey personal information and emotions with simple sentences. (e.g., Onn nambraas not faamii toot no sœur ay no frer. - We embrace our family, all of our sisters and brothers; Own zhoue avec di loo - We play with water; La faamii paarl la laang aansaamb. - Family speaks the language together)
Express opinions and perspectives on various topics (e.g., land-based experiences, family, celebrations, language revitalization) in a simple personal letter.
Recount personal experiences (e.g., land-based experiences, family events, genealogy) using a variety of narrative text types (e.g., short stories, scrapbooks, skits, poetry).
Share factual information in a simple formal text (e.g., newspaper article, family history and first-person account).
Experiment with Michif French language and vocabulary through a variety of texts (e.g., poems, short stories, songs, skits and videos).
Apply appropriate language and vocabulary when producing texts (e.g., menus, surveys, posters, social media posts, news articles).

notes: Structure as printed: one section per level ('Michif French 10/20/30 Outcomes and Indicators'), each grouped under the four goal headings Culture (CU), Strategies (ST), Language Knowledge (LK) and Applications (AP). Units here are those goal headings within a level. Outcome codes: goal + course level + number (legend p. 17 printed). Indicators are lettered a., b., …; bullet sub-lists inside an indicator are kept on their own lines ('• …').
The text mixes English with Michif French words (e.g. 'Lii pleu vyeu', 'la manyair dis prominii'); they are copied as printed, including their spelling and diacritics.

outcomes.statement: Apply, with guidance, techniques (i.e., instrumental, vocal or creative technologies) and knowledge of the elements of music to solo and/or ensemble performances.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate instrumental or vocal technique and knowledge of the elements of music in a peer setting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain, orally or in writing and using language appropriate to the genre, how the elements of music are used in the music being performed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generate a plan for musical growth using technical inquiry findings (e.g., in what ways could I/we record progress? How could I improve my musical performance using specific tools, technologies and techniques?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the skills and techniques required for successful ensemble performances

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of the role of individuals and sections within one’s ensemble by performing the specific tasks particular to one’s instrument.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Track technical development and develop strategies to improve.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Begin making expressive, interpretive and creative choices to communicate and interact with ensemble members and/or audience.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate musicality (e.g., emotional expressiveness) in solo and/or ensemble performance.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increased ability to interpret notation to communicate musical ideas (e.g., graphic/invented, tablature, standard and culture-specific forms).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Read and interpret written musical communication of increased complexity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use self and peer assessment to revise, refine and share music through notation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the legal and ethical implications of music production and distribution.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent musical ideas using standard notation (i.e., Western music notation, tablature).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Represent musical ideas using non-standard notation (e.g., abstract symbols and text, time-based pictographs, rap and hip hop flow diagrams with lyrics under beat numbers, braille, colour coded) and/or culture specific forms and models (e.g., unwritten, memorized with fixed and/or variable elements).

outcomes.statement: Compose to express musical ideas developing the use of the elements of music and the principles of composition, respecting cultural contexts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore ways of communicating musical ideas so they can be reproduced by others.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Express musical ideas through composition individually and/or in ensemble settings.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to apply the elements of music (i.e., melody, harmony, rhythm, dynamics, form, tone, texture) and principles of composition (e.g., repetition and variation, tension and resolution, balance and unity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate, through rehearsal, an ability to reflect on, refine and revise solo and ensemble compositions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply increased aural skills to making musical decisions for sound compositions.

outcomes.statement: Improvise on an instrument or with voice or other creative technology, implementing increased levels of music theory, cultural or performance practice.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Improvise around a given structure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use feedback to inform decision making, evaluation and action in improvisation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine improvisation within a diverse range of cultural and social contexts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the work of musicians engaged in improvisation and begin to apply learning to own musical work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate growth in the presentation and construction of improvised solos in a live setting.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express ideas.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate increased knowledge of selected musical concepts (e.g., elements of music, composition principles) through improvisation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate increased aural skills.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Imitate or transcribe more complex musical ideas (e.g., listen and play).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Apply language appropriate to the musical style to talk about improvisation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Seek opportunities to improvise in daily music experiences (e.g., during song writing, digital music composition, DJ and hip hop performance, jam solos).

outcomes.statement: Identify and describe characteristics of powwow and other social music of Saskatchewan First Nations peoples.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage with First Nations Elders, Knowledge Keepers and/or musicians to identify characteristics of music associated with various powwow dances (e.g., fancy dance, men’s and women’s traditional, jingle dress).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the ways of knowing and learning (e.g., songs passed down/gifted, songs composed) that are applied to learning First Nations traditional and contemporary music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how the work of contemporary musicians is influenced by First Nations traditional music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations music and musicians from Saskatchewan and international locations influence and respond to social, political and cultural issues (e.g., treaty education outcome SI11 - analyze how the unfulfilled aspects of treaties, with international Indigenous people, have resulted in inequities).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize different purposes for First Nations ceremonial and social music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe various powwow protocols and their purposes, including protocols specific to the music.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the purpose of the different roles of men and women in traditional drumming and singing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify differences in music and protocols among First Nations.

outcomes.statement: Identify and describe characteristics of the music of Saskatchewan Métis peoples.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage with Métis musicians to examine characteristics of Métis music.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe qualities of traditional and contemporary Métis music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize how specific selections of contemporary Métis musicians are influenced by tradition.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the music of selected Saskatchewan Métis musicians.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how Métis music and musicians in Saskatchewan influence arts and cultural communities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine regional and/or stylistic differences in Métis music including among individuals and groups.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond critically to own musical expressions and, with guidance, implement a plan for musical growth.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine own musical expressions, using peer feedback and self-assessment, in order to improve.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to musical elements such as tone, pitch, dynamics, intonation, phrasing, style, rhythm and time, within own musical expressions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generate a plan for musical growth using technical inquiry findings (e.g., In what ways could I/we record progress? How could I improve my musical performance using specific tools, technologies and techniques?).

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond to musical expressions of others, understanding how personal preference impacts critical analysis.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Express initial reactions, while listening to music, and conduct further analysis based on evidence in the work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine and classify music representing various genres, styles, time periods, places, social groups, world cultures, composers and performers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond critically (e.g., written, oral, arts expression) to music from various genres, styles, times, places, social groups and cultures, using terminology specific to the music genre.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyse the characteristics of excellent performance through listening to and watching other performers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyse and interpret music, examine the importance of musical text using evidence from the piece and/or performance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Make personal connections to the music, understanding how personal preference impacts critical analysis, and provide reasons for individual preferences.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore ways in which technology, acoustics, equipment (e.g., instruments, accessories, amplification systems, acoustical designs, technologies) and personal wellness impacts quality of sound.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply techniques to improve sound quality through care and maintenance of instruments and/or voices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into ways technology (e.g., microphones, software, pedals) and materials (e.g., drum heads, mutes, baffles, curtains) can manipulate sound.

outcomes.statement: Aurally distinguish and describe characteristics of the different eras, genres and styles through researching, listening to and/or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify musical, cultural, aural, textual clues that indicate the music’s place in time.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of personal experience and cultural and historical contexts on the creation of selected music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how music from the past is recreated today, or how music of today can be reinterpreted in styles from the past.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the evolution of instruments, voice and creative technologies and their use in various cultures and time periods.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain audience and performer norms and protocols within the genre.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Respond as an audience member and perform in a manner appropriate to the genre (e.g., First Nations powwow, symphony, world music, jazz, African or Latin percussion group, rock band) respecting cultural and performance norms and protocols (e.g., deportment, attire, respect for local tradition, await invitation to join jam session, bowing, encore, standing during Grand Music 10, 20, 3039Entry and Honour songs and anthems, etiquette concerning use of cameras and recording devices).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Anticipate and prepare for how audiences might react to the music performed in relation to, for example, venue, genre, demographics or type of event.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the origins of performance and audience etiquette (e.g., clapping following jazz solos, silence between symphonic movements) in different genres of music.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine ways in which audience responses in different musical genres affect the musician’s performance and the audience’s experience.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate and perform music from around the world (e.g., Afro Caribbean, South American, Middle Eastern), describe characteristics of each genre and style, and discuss the infusion or influence of non-western music in contemporary western popular music.

outcomes.statement: Examine the impact and role of music in own life and investigate music careers and pathways for continuing engagement in music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate relationships between music and personal wellness including mental health (e.g., music therapy, social connection) and identify and discuss associated research.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine ways that different genres/styles of music influence one’s wellbeing (e.g., rock music elevating moods, ballads encouraging reflection or relaxation).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how music is infused in daily life (e.g., to influence consumers via advertising, shopping environments, cultural music festivals) including media (e.g., film, video games, television, social media, apps).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore music from own cultural heritage and examine opportunities and benefits for continuing lifelong engagement in music (e.g., community choirs, bands, musical theatre).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Generate questions and conduct an inquiry into potential career avenues in specific disciplines and music in general (e.g., audio engineer, DJ, orchestral musician, composer/songwriter, producer, music therapist) and investigate opportunities for continuing study at the post-secondary level (e.g., scholarships, entrance requirements, auditions).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine legalities in music such as copyrighting, trademarking and contracts (e.g., performance contract fees, licensing and financial compensation for digital distribution of recordings, First Nations traditional laws).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine ethics (e.g., copying pirated music files, sampling, compensation from streaming services, stereotyped representations in lyrics and music videos) and legalities (e.g., Music 10, 20, 3040copyrighting, trademarking, First Nations traditional laws, contracts) related to creating and producing music.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research supports for musicians such as unions, professional associations, agents, Elders and Knowledge Keepers, provincial and federal grants (e.g., funding for creation, touring and recording).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss entrepreneurship and personal qualities required for pursuing a career in music.

outcomes.statement: Examine the work and impact of influential local, Canadian and international musicians.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify, listen to and discuss the work of musicians who have made an impact on music.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate why notable musicians and their work are/were influential (e.g., current, historical, community, representing gender and sexual diversity).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how music and musicians influence and respond to social, political and cultural issues(e.g., world music, music concerned with human rights, environmental sustainability).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research influential musical educators and their programs and methods (e.g., Kodaly, John-Baptiste Arcand, Orff, Buffy Sainte-Marie, Jose Antonio Abreu).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how change (e.g., personal, social, technology) influences musical works.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and analyse how music is used in everyday lives (e.g., video games, films, social media, apps).

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d

items.text: Students will be made aware of the 12 Principles Common to First Nations Philosophies and related resources. Students will be provided with the opportunity to relate Indigenous philosophy with their own and other philosophies and codes of ethics or behaviour.
Students will develop an understanding of the role that a people's philosophy has in shaping their lives and relationships.
Students will develop an appreciation for an Indigenous worldview and identify it as practised by Indigenous peoples.
Students will develop their comprehension, interpretation and creative thinking skills in representing an Indigenous worldview using a variety of media.

items.group: C.E.L. emphasis is placed upon the following foundational objectives:
items.text: To support students in coming to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of Native Studies. (PSVS)

items.group: C.E.L. emphasis is placed upon the following foundational objectives:
items.text: To promote both intuitive imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, and experiences in a meaningful way. (CCT)

items.group: C.E.L. emphasis is placed upon the following foundational objectives:
items.text: To promote an understanding of discrimination, bias, racism, sexism and all forms of inequality, and a desire to contribute to their elimination. (PSVS)
Students will discuss or write about their perspectives regarding key aspects of philosophy and worldview using their own language. (C)
Students will explore how cultural heritage shapes understanding, and how moral principles influence behaviour. (PSVS)
Students will make connections to prior learning through a previewing exercise. (C)
Students will work cooperatively and contribute positively in group learning activities. (PSVS)
Students will summarize important understandings from the videotape in a variety of ways. (C, CCT)
Students will identify, discuss, and represent philosophical concepts in a variety of ways. (C, CCT)
Students will discuss factors that put the natural environment at risk. (PSVS)
Students will refine their understanding of prejudice, discrimination and racism. (PSVS)
Students will use a variety of sources to cover the breadth and depth of a topic. (C)
Students will understand human rights and their relationship to human needs. (PSVS)

Students will explore how cultural heritage shapes understanding and how moral values influence behaviours. (PSVS) Have students read the Ethics Common to First Nations. Where else have the students heard or seen these maxims stated or applied? Relate the Ethics to your school's code of behaviour or that stated in the Education Act under the sections detailing the responsibilities of principals, teachers, and students. Have students relate the 12 Principles Common to First Nations Philosophies to the Ethics common to First Nations which are the subsequent behaviours and attitudes. Relate the Ethics to the 10 Commandments of the Hebrews in the Bible's Old Testament, the Codification of Roman Laws by Julius Caesar, the Canada Act and Charter of Rights and Freedoms, 1982. Relate the Ethics Common to First Nations to the Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, or the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights, 1976. Have students determine the human needs that give rise to legislated human rights and First Nations' ethics. Most of these documents appear in the Social Justice Unit of the Student Resource Guide and are suitable subjects for further investigation and discussion, as they define what is acceptable behaviour before the Creator, and in society. It is appropriate to utilize materials from the Social Justice Unit, or any other unit if they are relevant to the issue or concept being discussed. A holistic perspective is necessary to fully understand and appreciate the implications of facts and concepts arising from the case studies.

Students will explore how moral principles and cultural philosophy influence peoples' behaviours and practises. (PSVS) Invite an Elder or Aboriginal spiritual teacher into the classroom to speak about aspects of Indian philosophy and spirituality. Refer to the Inviting Elders to the School.

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous peoples' political rights are based upon the traditional exercise of such rights;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Political rights of Indigenous peoples have historically been repressed by mainstream societies;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: The repression of Indigenous peoples' political rights has caused social turmoil and conflict and resulted in the n~ar extinction and subjugation of many Indigenous cultures and societies;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous peoples continue to struggle for empowerm~nt through the recognition of their unique political rights;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Political concerns involve control over internal affairs and relationships with mainstream societies;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Political concerns vary among Indigenous peoples;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Varied methods and strategies exist and must evolve to resolve political issues;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: The pursuit of self-determination and self-government by Indigenous peoples is a global phenomenon;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Individual and organized effort is necessary to protect the rights of Indigenous peoples and assist them in realizing self-government;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Commonalities exist among Indigenous peoples and their struggles for political, social, economic, spiritual and cultural survival and development.

Students will relate these concepts to the historical Euro-Canadian treatment of Aboriginal peoples. (CCT) Have students, in small groups, read and discuss the following Proclamation of 1992 which is based upon many of the attitudes and historical situations created and developed by traders, settlers, and governments (Canada) in their attempts to colonize the "New World". .

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous peoples' concept of development is defined by their common respect for the land. That concept is both individual and communal;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous peoples' concept of development reflects the principles of wholeness and change. Indigenous peoples view their society and the world holistically;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: The right to self-determination and self-government is essential to Indigenous peoples' concepts of personal and communal development. Dependence upon others decreases self-determination and domination by others leads to social injustice;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Development, that has been forced upon Indigenous peoples, denies their human and Aboriginal rights;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous peoples and their traditional territories are threatened by the effects of foreign concepts of development which are insensitive to Indigenous beliefs and practices;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Development projects designed, funded and supported by non-Indigenous corporations, agencies and banks have created widespread situations of poverty, debt, urbanization, ethnocide and genocide;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous peoples and social scientists, globally, are demanding more culturally-sensitive programs for personal, social and economic development;

items.stem: Students will understand and appreciate that:
items.text: Indigenous principles of development, conservation and change are increasingly relevant to non-Indigenous science and technology, and schemes for sustainable development, pollution control and waste management.

Increase their understanding of the history, nature and effects of prejudice, discrimination, racism, ethnocide and genocide;

Increase their awareness of organizations, inquiries, and task forces which strive to identify injustice, and strategies which seek to promote, implement or enforce social justice;

indicators.text: Design and participate in an exit interview with the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Prepare and present a report on the work study experience including aspects such as:

- Dress code
- Job description
- Employer expectations
- employer evaluation process
- Absence and late policies
- Problem solving
- Communication.
