outcomes.statement: Service Learning – Explore how participation in activity-based service learning benefits self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how participating in service learning develops positive citizenship and community involvement, including relationship building to support reconciliation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate a variety of fitness-related opportunities (e.g., coaching/officiating minor sports, helping seniors who are housebound, senior centre fitness class, Special Olympics and walking school bus) that can benefit the well-being of self and/or community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal interests and skills to determine the most appropriate role (e.g., coach, instructor, manager, official, volunteer) in a specific activity-based service learning opportunity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore requirements (e.g., safe contact standards in football, concussion protocol and criminal record check) for individuals seeking a role in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Participate in activity-based service learning such as local, provincial and national cultural (e.g., pow wow, children's festival and multicultural celebrations) and sporting (e.g., rodeo, track and field and national championships) events.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document participation in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on perceived benefits for self and community from participation in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore careers in your community related to physical activity, health and wellness.

outcomes.title: Service Learning

outcomes.statement: Health- and Skill-Related Fitness – Explore components of health- and skill-related fitness through physical activity.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- How might participation in physical activity affect my lifestyle?
- What factors might influence how I pursue personal fitness goals?
- How might my physical activity interests change based on my fitness goals?
- What organizations and events exist to support my fitness?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how to measure components of health- (e.g., cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular strength and endurance) and skill-related (e.g., agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed) fitness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how to use fitness appraisal tools (e.g., fitness apps, sit and reach board and stop watch) to collect data on specific components of health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how to apply principles of training such as FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type), overload, progression, reversibility and specificity to improve health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess, through participation, how different training styles and approaches (e.g., cross fit, pilates, plyometrics, weight training and yoga) improve components of health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the drawbacks of overemphasizing specific components of fitness when engaging in physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify personal aerobic thresholds, such as maximum and target heart rates, while participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Collect and analyze health -and skill-related data, using fitness appraisal tools and available equipment (e.g., free weights, medicine balls, stability balls and wobble boards), to identify personal strengths and weaknesses.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop a personal fitness plan with a focus on improving components of health- and skill-related fitness.

outcomes.title: Health- and Skill-Related Fitness

outcomes.statement: Body Management – Explore and participate in body management activities as pathways towards personal well-being.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in body management activities (e.g., aquatics, dance, gymnastics, karate, pilates, weight training and yoga) to enhance personal well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how fundamental movement skills transfer between different body management activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits that can result from participating in body management activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Propose solutions to potential challenges (e.g., cultural, financial, safety, motivation and time) that might restrict an individual's participation in body management activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of a body management activity from another culture by teaching it to peers or other members of the community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis body management activities (e.g., jigging, hoop dance, pow wow and hand games).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Evaluate the influence of current societal trends (e.g., CrossFit and yoga) on individuals' participation in body management activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the benefits of technology (e.g., apps, fitness watches and heart rate monitors) when engaging in body management activities.

outcomes.title: Body Management

outcomes.statement: Complex Skills – Demonstrate improvement in performance of complex skills.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate complex skills within various activities and/or games in multiple environments (e.g., air, land, snow/ice and water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate First Nations and Métis perspectives on holistically developing complex skills (e.g., throwing a ball using either hand).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the components of a specific complex skill.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine, through feedback, which components of a complex skill to target in order to improve performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply principles of practice (e.g., part-whole and whole-part-whole) to improve performance of complex skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how improved performance in a complex skill can influence proficiency in other complex skills.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Document progress (e.g., blog, journal, photos and video) of improved performance of one or more complex skills.

outcomes.title: Complex Skills

outcomes.statement: Physical Activity within Multiple Environments – Investigate how physical activity within multiple environments contributes to the well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the benefits for well-being of self and others that can result from participating in physical activities within multiple environments (e.g., air, land, snow/ice and water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify opportunities to participate in outdoor physical activities within your community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Participate in fitness, leisure and/or competitive activities in multiple environments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and/or participate in an outdoor experience (e.g., biking, canoeing, geocaching, hiking, ice-fishing, skiing and trapping) that promotes personal well-being.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the environment when participating in physical activities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when interacting with the environment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use technology (e.g., backpack, compass, fitness and activity apps, global positioning satellite, hiking boots, maps and satellite phone) appropriately and responsibly when participating in physical activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Propose potential solutions for challenges (e.g., cultural, financial and geographical location) that might limit individual's participation in physical activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Document and reflect on how participation in physical activities within multiple environments contributes to the well-being of self and others.

outcomes.title: Physical Activity within Multiple Environments

outcomes.statement: Games, Tactics and Strategies – Compare how effective tactics and strategies enhance performance and enjoyment in physically active games.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize how prior knowledge of tactics and strategies can transfer to different games.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify tactics and strategies used in traditional First Nation and Métis games (e.g., double ball, knuckle hop, lacrosse, leg wrestling and snow snake).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate effective tactics and strategies in target, invasion/territorial, net/wall, striking/fielding, low organization and inventive games to enhance performance and enjoyment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between individual and team tactics and strategies used in individual/partner and group/team games.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of effective tactical and strategic decisions used in a variety of game situations while participating in individual/partner and group/team games.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal use of effective tactics and strategies incorporated in game situations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Modify tactics and strategies to enhance participation in games for all students.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss and apply different models (e.g., teaching games for understanding, sport-model and Long-Term Athlete Development) for teaching games, tactics and strategies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Present a game from another culture, including its tactics and strategies, to peers or members of the community.

outcomes.title: Games, Tactics and Strategies

outcomes.statement: First Nations and Métis – Examine First Nations and Métis worldviews regarding learning through physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing inform people's interactions with self, others and the environment through physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how First Nations and Métis people use story-telling to convey knowledge about learning through physical activity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how the benefits of physical activity (e.g., endurance, flexibility and social skills) serve a purpose to meet the demands of activities such as hunting, observation skills or learning social values.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate local, traditional First Nations and Métis ways of relating to and using the environment when participating in activities (e.g., orienteering and navigation, setting fishing nets and traps, and snowshoeing).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Participate in traditional First Nations and Métis games (e.g., snowsnake, double ball, lacrosse, leg wrestling and knuckle hop), dance (e.g., jigging, hoop and pow wow) and activities (e.g., snowshoeing and archery).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how skills developed in traditional games, dance and activities could be transferable to other contexts.

outcomes.title: First Nations and Métis

outcomes.statement: Nutrition – Examine how healthy nutritional choices support a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare personal nutritional practices to the recommendations in Canada's Food Guide.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how an individual's nutritional choices may be influenced by factors such as cultural eating practices, finances, advertising and marketing and/or geographical location.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze personal daily caloric intake to determine if it meets energy requirements (e.g., basal metabolic rate calculation) of a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the limitations of calorie counting as a method of determining how much food to eat to support a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the role of macro and micronutrients and hydration in supporting a physically active lifestyle, before, during and after activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how nutrition-related illnesses (e.g., cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes) may be impacted by participation in physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how nutritional trends (e.g., ketogenic, gluten free and high protein diets) compare with the recommendations in Canada's Food Guide.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify how a specific nutritional trend can influence personal nutrition practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create or evaluate a nutrition plan that supports a physically active lifestyle considering food availability, cost, likes and dislikes.

outcomes.title: Nutrition

outcomes.statement: Skeletal and Muscular Systems – Investigate the effect of physical activity on the skeletal and muscular systems of the human body.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the major bones, joints and muscles that are affected by participation in a specific physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the three types (i.e., concentric, eccentric and isometric) of muscle contractions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the three types of muscle contractions on muscle development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and perform isolated and compound movements that target major muscles.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and perform different exercises that increase the efficiency of slow and fast twitch muscle fibres.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how various types of exercise incorporate specific joint actions (e.g., abduction, adduction, circumduction, eversion, inversion, pronation and supination).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research common injuries (e.g., fracture, sprain and tear) to bones, joints and muscles that result from physical activity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the cause and treatment of injuries (e.g., stress fracture, tendonitis and muscle strain) that result from over-use of a bone, joint and/or muscle during physical activity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of a sedentary lifestyle on skeletal and/or muscular systems in the short and long-term.

outcomes.title: Skeletal and Muscular Systems

outcomes.statement: Personal Mental Health – Investigate the benefits of physical activity on mental health.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the short- and long-term effects of physical activity on factors that can affect mental health such as anxiety, body image, depression, self-esteem and stress.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the interrelationship between physical activity, hormone levels (e.g., dopamine, cortisol, endorphin and serotonin) and physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss First Nations and Métis understandings of the interrelationships between physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate physical activity as a strategy to enhance personal positive mental health.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Document personal perceptions of how physical activity affects mental health over an extended period of time.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in individual (e.g., jogging, meditation and yoga) and group (e.g., cooperative games, fitness classes and team sports) activities may provide mental health benefits.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Communicate (e.g., brochure, display, oral, presentation software, video and website) research findings on community resources (e.g., Kids Help Phone and Sask Health) designed to support individuals and raise mental health awareness.

outcomes.title: Personal Mental Health

outcomes.statement: Student-Directed Study – Create and implement a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physical Education 20.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates understanding of a Physical Education 20 topic of interest to the student.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed study through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation or research paper.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study.

outcomes.title: Student-Directed Study

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore connection between topics in Physical Science 20 and occupations of personal interest. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify which physical science related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally and/or nationally. (STSE, S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common to people involved in physical-science related jobs. (S, A)

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Interview or connect with others to discuss physical science related occupations. (K, S, A)

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Physical Science 20 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Physical Science 20. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a physical science topic of interest to the student. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying a concept related to Physical Science 20. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate an issued related to physical science, including developing materials to support the arguments for and against a position. (A, K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Analyze, qualitatively and quantitatively, the effect of heat on matter during temperature changes and changes of state using kinetic molecular theory.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between heat and temperature using the kinetic molecular theory of matter. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the importance of heat and fire for First Nations and Métis peoples, and how they use their understanding of heat transfer to solve practical problems related to cooking and shelter. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how the concept of a closed system and the law of conservation of energy underlie the study of heat and heat transfer. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Measure the specific heat capacity of various metals using a calorimeter. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the latent heat of fusion and/or latent heat of vaporization of various substances using a calorimeter. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Measure some physical properties of water, such as density at various temperatures, specific heat capacity and latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare, in quantitative terms, the heat capacities of some common materials, including water, and explain how heat capacity can influence choices of materials used in the development of technologies related to clothing, food and shelter. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct a heating or cooling curve for water, or other substances, using personally collected data and appropriate graphing techniques or software. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use appropriate technologies such as temperature probes and calorimeters safely when collecting data. (S, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Calculate the quantity of heat ($Q = mcT$), specific heat capacity, latent heat of fusion ($Q = mH_f$) and latent heat of vaporization ($Q = mH_v$) during changes of state, using the correct number of significant figures. (S, K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Calculate and experimentally verify the amount of heat exchanged and final temperature reached when mixing two known quantities of known substances, and suggest sources of experimental error and improvements to experimental design. (S, K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine traditional and contemporary applications of heat transfer such as heating a drum skin, using heat to make copper tools, energy control in buildings, heat pumps and insulated and moisture wicking clothing. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore, qualitatively and/or quantitatively, the expansion and contraction of matter during heat transfer or temperature change. (S, K)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Investigate effects of the thermal expansion and contraction of matter in technological applications such as road, bridge and building design, plumbing, power line construction and industrial engineering. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Discuss how the anomalous properties (e.g., density, phase and thermodynamic properties) of water, as compared with other liquids, affect the environment and Earth’s climate. (STSE, K)

outcomes.statement: Determine the quantities of heat involved in chemical reactions through experimentation and calculation.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between endothermic and exothermic chemical reactions, including those that occur in solutions. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the historical development of thermodynamics, including significant discoveries and inventions, and the contributions of engineers and scientists such as Carnot, Maxwell, Boltzmann, Lord Kelvin and Gibbs. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Measure, using a thermometer or temperature probe, and record the temperature change in an exothermic and/or endothermic chemical reaction. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Calculate the theoretical quantity of heat absorbed or released in specific exothermic and/or endothermic reactions, including combustion reactions, using various quantities of reactants given the heat of reaction. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain why the actual heat of reaction differs from the theoretical heat of reaction, with reference to sources of error and percent error calculations. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of analyzing the quantities of heat involved in chemical reactions. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the molar heat of reaction associated with dissolving ionic compounds in a solution. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the quantity of heat involved in the use of various commercially available cold and/or heat packs. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design, create and evaluate the effectiveness of a cold pack and/or heat pack given the goal of having no excess reactants remaining at reaction completion. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the fuel consumed and heat energy output of various combustion reactions involving common fuels (e.g., methane, propane, octane and ethanol). (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Predict products of the five basic types of chemical reactions and evaluate the impact of these reactions on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Observe and analyze synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single-replacement and double-replacement (including acid base neutralization) reactions. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Represent synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single- replacement and double-replacement (including acid base neutralization) reactions using atomic models, other manipulatives, skeleton equations, balanced chemical equations and International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the importance of skeleton equations, balanced equations and IUPAC nomenclature in communicating understanding of chemical reactions. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Predict products of synthesis and decomposition reactions given the reactants. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the feasibility of single-replacement reactions based on the activity series of metals and/or non-metals. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Predict products of double-replacement reactions, including acid-base neutralization reactions, and precipitate formation using solubility rules. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Distinguish between the products of complete and incomplete combustion reactions and potential consequences of the latter for living things and the environment. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design, and carry out if practical, an investigation to demonstrate the difference between a complete and incomplete combustion reaction. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Select and apply proper techniques for handling and disposing of lab materials, as outlined in Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015) standards, and interpret Safety Data Sheets (SDSs). (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze and compare the fuel consumed and carbon output of various combustion reactions (e.g., methane, propane, octane and ethanol). (STSE, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how the outcomes of various chemical reactions may benefit or harm living organisms and affect the environment. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Research how industrial, mining and/or agricultural processes involve chemical reactions. (STSE, S, K, A)

outcomes.statement: Construct an understanding of the mole as a unit for measuring the amount of substance.

indicators.text: Pose questions about how to measure quantities of substances that are not readily countable. (S)

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why chemists use the mole to represent the amount of a substance. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline how individuals such as Avogadro, Berzelius, Davy, Proust and Dalton have contributed to modern understanding of the composition of compounds. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Celebrate mole day on 10/23 or 6/02 by bringing a multiple of a mole of substance to school, consuming a mole of a substance and creating and/or sharing cartoons, articles, pictures or songs relevant to the mole. (A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the molar mass of various molecular and ionic compounds. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Perform molar conversions, including mass to mole, number of particles to mole, volume to mole, concentration of a solution to mole and their inverse operations, using the correct number of significant figures. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Prepare solutions of known concentration using molarity and dilution calculations. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the use of solutions in industrial, mining and agricultural processes. (STSE, S, K)

outcomes.statement: Use stoichiometry to determine the relative amounts of substances consumed and produced in chemical reactions.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about how to determine the amount of material required to produce a finished product. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine the relative numbers of moles of each substance in a variety of chemical reactions using balanced chemical equations. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Relate the use of the mole to the coefficients in a balanced chemical equation, and compare this to mass and volume as measurable quantities. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform stoichiometric calculations to predict the outcomes (e.g., concentration, mass, volume, number of particles and energy transferred) of chemical reactions, using the correct units and correct number of significant figures. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and carry out experiments to support stoichiometric hypotheses using appropriate instruments to collect data accurately and precisely. (S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Communicate results of experiments using narrative and formal lab reports. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the limiting and excess reagents in a variety of chemical reactions through stoichiometric calculations and experimentation. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the theoretical and actual yield for a variety of chemical reactions by calculating the percent yield. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how actual yield differs from theoretical yield using the concept of sources of error. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Predict how to maximize the yield of a particular chemical process. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the economic impact of the yield of chemical reactions with respect to maximizing product and profit and minimizing waste production. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Research how the reactants used and products formed through chemical reactions in industrial, mining and/or agricultural processes can affect human health and/or the health of the environment. (STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the properties and characteristics of one-, two- and three- dimensional waves in at least three different media (e.g., springs, ropes, air and water).
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about the nature and prevalence of waves in the world around us (e.g., What are waves? Where do we find waves in the world around us? Do all waves exhibit the same properties and behaviours? Why are waves important to study?). (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine First Nations and Metis perspectives on waves, including waves as carriers of energy. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize that scientists understand waves as the transmission of energy originating from a vibrating source that determines the frequency and amplitude of the wave. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Communicate information about the properties and characteristics of waves using appropriate terminology, including medium, pulse, vibration, cycle, periodic motion, frequency, period, amplitude, phase and wavelength. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Rephrase questions about waves (e.g., What controls the frequency of a wave? What controls the speed of a wave? What happens when two or more waves meet?) into experimentally testable formats. (S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of transverse and longitudinal waves including crests (positive pulse), troughs (negative pulse), compressions, rarefactions and the relationship between direction of vibration and energy transfer. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the transmission of waves, including rectilinear propagation and the nature of the medium and its relationship to the speed of the wave. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Trace the historical developments of technologies used to measure the speed of light and/or sound. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve problems related to speed, period, frequency and wavelength using the universal wave equation ($v = λf$), the period-frequency relationship ($T = 1/f$) and the correct number of significant figures. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Illustrate constructive and destructive interference in one-, two- and three- dimensional waves, including the principle of superposition and standing waves, using point-source and straight-source waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Observe and describe diffraction of waves through single and double slits and diffraction gratings. (S, K)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide examples of applications of the properties and characteristics of waves or electromagnetic radiation in various technologies (e.g., ultrasound, sonar, Doppler Effect, sonic booms, satellite dishes, microwaves, mobile phones, wireless routers, Bluetooth, radio waves, X-rays, radar and remote controls). (STSE, K)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore wave-related phenomena such as natural vibrations, forced vibrations, resonance and harmonics in the context of musical instruments and human hearing. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine data or experimental results that provide evidence for the scientific theory of wave-particle duality of light. (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Examine, using physical materials, ray diagrams and mathematical equations, how waves reflect from a variety of barriers.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the behavior of waves as they strike parallel, oblique, and curved barriers. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of specular (regular) and diffuse reflection of waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate the application of the law of reflection when a wave strikes a straight barrier and when a wave encounters the boundary between two different media. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of wave and particle reflection in everyday situations such as echoes, reverberation, room acoustics, radar, sonar, parabolic microphones, ultrasound, water waves, satellite dishes, billiard balls and ball-based sports. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate image formation in plane, concave and convex mirrors, including constructing ray diagrams. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the properties, including type (real or virtual), attitude/orientation (upright or inverted), magnification (smaller, larger or same size) and position (relative to the mirror surface or vertex), of images formed in plane, concave and convex mirrors. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply the laws of reflection, the magnification equation ($M = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o$) and the curved mirror equation ($1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$) to solve problems related to the reflection of waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the implications of wave-based technologies in furthering scientific understanding of phenomena such as Earth’s internal structure, the topography of the ocean floor and the rock cycle. (STSE, K)

outcomes.statement: Analyze, using physical materials, ray diagrams and mathematical equations, how waves refract at boundaries between different media.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose scientific questions about how waves behave when they travel from one medium to another. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the behavior of waves, including partial reflection and refraction, the critical angle and total internal reflection, at a boundary between different media. (S, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Relate refraction, and the refractive index of a medium, to the change in the speed and direction of waves at a boundary between different media. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate image formation in converging and diverging lenses, including constructing ray diagrams. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the properties, including type (real or virtual), attitude/orientation (upright or inverted), magnification (smaller, larger, or same size) and position (relative to the optical center) of images formed in converging and diverging lenses. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply Snell's Law ($n_1\sinθ_1= n_2\sinθ_2$), the magnification equation ($M = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o$) and the lens equation ($1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$) to solve problems related to the refraction of waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore applications related to fiber optics, lenses and human vision including polarization, the lens makers equation and total internal reflection. (STSE, S, K)

courses.name: Physics 20, 30

legacyEvidence.reason: 1992 guide; not in the site's menus; its 30-level part is replaced by the renewed Physics 30 (id 72)
evidence: Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its objectives under 14 headings: “Core Unit I: The Physics of Everyday Things”, “Core Unit II: Waves”, “Core Unit III: Light”, “Core Unit IV: Heat”, “Optional Unit V: Sound”, “Optional Unit VI: Optics”, “Core Unit I: Kinematics and Dynamics”, “Core Unit II: Mechanical Energy”, “Core Unit III: Electricity”, “Core Unit IV: Nuclear Physics”, “Optional Unit V: Applications of Kinematics”, “Optional Unit VI: Fluid Mechanics”, “Optional Unit VII: Electromagnetism”, “Optional Unit VIII: Atomic Physics”.

courses.problem: No outcomes are published on the site for this curriculum; the objectives are taken from its curriculum document (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=71); see `document`.

Define the following terms: wave, disturbance, medium, pulse, vibration, cycle, periodic motion, simple harmonic motion, transverse vibration, longitudinal vibration, crest, trough, compression, rarefaction, frequency, period, amplitude, phase, wavelength.
Give examples of periodic motion.
Apply the correct units for period and frequency in problem solving and applications.
Solve problems involving period, frequency, and wave motion.
Explain that the universal wave equation applies to all types of waves.

Define the following terms: interference, constructive interference, destructive interference.

Predict the resulting wave pattern when two waves travelling in opposite directions meet at a given point.
Illustrate constructive and destructive interference using diagrams, models, or computers.

Explain that waves travel at a constant speed in a uniform medium.

Explain the relationship between frequency and wavelength for waves in a fixed medium undergoing a change in frequency.
State the laws of reflection.

Demonstrate an understanding of wave transmission, reflection, and refraction by relating these phenomena to practical and common experiences.
Interpret the relationship between speed and wavelength for waves undergoing refraction.

Explain standing wave interference patterns by relating them to an understanding of constructive and destructive interference.

Explain that only certain resonant frequencies will produce standing wave interference patterns.
Explain that waves exhibit other properties such as scattering and polarization.

Recognize and explain the importance of ray diagrams in geometric optics.
Demonstrate an understanding of important principles of drawing ray diagrams.

Describe the location and number of images formed by two perpendicular plane mirrors.
Suggest some applications of multiple images formed by more than one mirror.

Draw and label a diagram which illustrates the way in which light behaves when it undergoes refraction.
State the three laws of refraction.
Apply Snell's Law to solve problems relating to refraction.

Explain what causes chromatic aberration.

outcomes.statement:
Expand and demonstrate understanding of inequalities including:

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: h

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for injury prevention to ensure safety in the work area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: General Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify personal protective equipment (PPE) such as eyewear, clothing, footwear and ear wear that may be needed for the work site, school or home.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply accident prevention principles and techniques, and discuss appropriate actions in case of an injury or accident, such as whom to contact, fire extinguisher locations, emergency exit routes and first-aid procedures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of ventilation in a confined environment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practice good housekeeping and avoid obvious hazards (e.g., touching live wires, extending cords over walking spaces and leaving objects on the floor).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Complete an assessment of all safety and robotics equipment and, in consultation with the instructor, perform maintenance to repair or replace defective or worn parts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

outcomes.statement: Explore ethical, moral and legal issues relevant to robotics and autonomous devices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Ethics and Laws (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how the ethics of robotic and autonomous devices have been portrayed in the media, particularly in science fiction (e.g., 2001: A Space Odyssey).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss legal and/or ethical perspectives with regards to fault when a robotic or autonomous device causes harm to a person, property or nature.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the theoretical relevance of Asimov’s Laws of Robotics to contemporary applications of robotics and artificial intelligence.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze case studies (e.g., The Case of the Killer Robot by Richard G. Epstein) or news reports of accidents involving death or injury caused by industrial robots and discuss who is considered at fault.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research current and proposed legislation involving the personal and commercial use of drones.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Hypothesize about the possibility that robots or devices with artificial intelligence will be able to make their own decisions and the potential ramifications of this ability.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss moral implications (e.g., racial profiling, choosing who lives or dies, unemployment and robot rights, the Trolley problem and unintended consequences) related to artificially intelligent robotic and autonomous devices.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate historical and contemporary impacts of robotics and autonomous devices on society.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Societal Impact (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the uses of robotics in the field of medicine for applications such as surgery, rehabilitation and remote diagnosis.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how movies (e.g., “I, Robot” and “ShortCircuit”) about robots portray the effects of robot interaction on humanity and the role of work in the future.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore societal implications of the increasing prevalence of robotic and autonomous devices in our daily lives and routines.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess potential positive and negative impacts of robotics on various industries (e.g., automotive manufacturing, agriculture and mining).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze how artificial intelligence can impact robotics and autonomous devices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the impact of a specific application of artificial intelligence.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Debate an issue related to autonomous devices such as the viability of driverless vehicles of varying levels of autonomy on public highways and private worksites.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the prevalence and societal impacts of automation.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between robotics and automation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the main advantages of automation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the use of automation in our society, including current and potential effects of automation on society and the environment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore issues (e.g., human input, mechanical wear, technical programming) arising with automation.

indicators.text: Explore potential applications for machine learning and artificial intelligence in robotics and automation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the usage of a transistor in a circuit.

outcomes.statement: Utilize schematic diagrams to guide the design and construction of electronic circuits.

indicators.text: Differentiate between conductors and insulators.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List materials that can be used as conductors.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: List materials that can be used as insulators.

indicators.label: d

indicators.text: Discuss what datasheets (or spec sheets) are and their purposes in robotics construction.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Construct a device that makes use of multiple outputs simultaneously.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Investigate computational thinking as a problem-solving process.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the extent to which computational thinking concepts were used in solving a coding or robotics and automation problem.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of following proper syntax practices for the programming language.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create internal documentation for programs.

indicators.text: Ensure proper separation of different sections of the program (e.g., main program, subroutines and variables) to enhance readability.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of integer data types in programs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 30C: Coding - Variables C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 30A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the advantages of using integer data types (e.g., int, short, long, byte) in a program.

indicators.text: Explore the constraints of integer data types.

indicators.label: c

outcomes.statement: Create programs that use conditional statements to control program flow.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use WAIT or DELAY to have a task WAIT for a conditional expression to be true or DELAY for a specified amount of time.

indicators.text: Explain how functions are called in programs.

indicators.text: Manipulate the movement of a device based on proximity of an object to the device.

outcomes.statement: Construct and program a device that can follow sound.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify different drive systems (e.g., direct drive chain/sprocket, belt/pulley, biped, 2-wheel drive, 4-wheel drive, front wheel drive, rear wheel drive, all-wheel drive, track drive and walking) for robotics and automation applications.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the attributes of different drive systems to achieve various needs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the appropriate drive system to meet a specific need.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Evaluate a chosen drive system for suitability in a specific device.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the suitability of gears, sprockets and chains and pulleys and belts for robotics and automation applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 47: Gears (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of gears, sprockets and chains and pulleys and belts in robotics and automation applications.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how gears can be used to change the direction of rotation of a drive shaft.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the suitability of different types (e.g., flat, round, Vee, and toothed) of belts for various robotics and automation applications.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Calculate gear ratios using the following formulas:
- gear ratio = # of driven gear teeth/# driving gear teeth
- gear ratio = diameter of driven pulley/diameter of the driving pulley

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Calculate torque and speed changes using the following formulas:
- output torque = input torque x gear ratio
- output speed = input speed/gear ratio

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Convert angular speed of a drive shaft (e.g., rpm) to linear speed (e.g., cm/s) using the formulas:
- revolutions per second (rps) = revolutions per minute (rpm) x 60
- Angular speed (radians per second) = 2 x pi x rps
- Linear speed = radius of wheel x angular speed

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe some of the challenges associated with using pulleys and belts, gears, or chains in robotic and automation applications.

indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

Know that the cost of modern warfare is enormous destruction, great human suffering, and heavy military and civilian casualties.
Know that the Nazi "New Order" was the basis for its moral vision of human rights.
Know that the Nazi racial imperialism meant that races were categorized according to their supposed level of humanness.
Know that the "final solution" left 6 million Jews dead by 1945.
Know that the economy of Europe was so destroyed that only massive economic aid was able to salvage it.
Learn/practise using an analytical grid to categorize and classify information so that it can be analyzed.

Practise applying the thinking skills of:
- stating propositions (hypotheses) that are testable and guide the search for data;
- collecting data in a systematic manner; and,
- presenting analyses to confirm or disconfirm hypotheses in dialectical thinking.

In considering the moral and legal behaviour of the Nazi, Soviet, and Allied leadership:
- Should the human rights concept of crimes against humanity override the laws of a sovereign state such as Germany?
- Should the concept of crimes against humanity also apply to the actions of Stalin?
- Does the concept of a defensive war justify the mass bombing of civilian targets by the Allies?
Know that at certain stages of history when enough people have concluded that a certain change or advance is necessary, then it is possible to make a significant advance.

Know that the events of the Holocaust so outraged the moral vision that world public opinion changed. Pople decided that certain behaviours constituted crimes against humanity regardless of whether they were crimes in particular countries at the time they were committed. These behaviours were considered to be crimes because they offended any reasonable moral standard and, therefore, individuals should know they were wrong and be held accountable for them.
Know that following World War II many of the leaders of Germany and Japan were charged with and found guilty of perpetrating crimes against humanity.
Know that countervailing powers are those powers that limit and hold accountable some other power that otherwise might be unchecked.
Know that world opinion had come to accept that an organization like the United Nations was necessary to act as a check on the power of the modern state.
Know that the declaration of human rights was seen as a system of impartial criteria which would serve to evaluate the laws and behaviour of nations.
Know that a paradigm of human rights is not just a list of rights, but is, rather, a mutually supporting system of complementary rights.
Practise using paradigms as the basis for defining a point of view (proposition or hypothesis) on an issue.
Practise the use of dialectical thinking to decide between points of view on an issue.

Practise applying the thinking skills of:
- stating propositions (hypotheses) that are testable and guide the search for data;
- collecting data in a systematic manner; and,
- presenting analyses to confirm or disconfirm the hypotheses in dialectical thinking.

In dealing with conflicting moral visions, how should one decide which moral vision should have precedence over the other:
- by accepting that the autonomy of the individual should be considered sacred; or,
- by accepting that the well-being of the community should be considered sacred?
Know that a right is a claim which has a special force that overrides other claims based on privilege, social and economic agreements, or legal and political agreements.
Know that claiming a right makes certain things happen within a society because individuals and society recognize that they must fulfil the obligations stemming from that particular right.
Know that human rights are a special class of rights that one has simply because one is a human being.
Know that human rights claims are claims of last resort which arise when the object of a particular right is threatened or denied and no higher rights appeal exists.
Know that human rights are more than just a demand for rights, they involve a moral entitlement to the right in question.
Know that the source of human rights is humanity's moral nature.
Know that human rights are those rights needed not for life, but for a life of dignity worthy of a human being.
Know that human rights represent a social choice of what is conceived to be the minimum requirements of a life of dignity based on a particular moral vision of human potentiality.

Practise applying the thinking skills of:
- stating propositions (hypotheses) that are testable and guide the search for data;
- collecting data in a systematic manner; and,
- presenting analyses to show how the parts are related to the whole.

In considering human rights:
- should one give priority to the rights of the individual over the rights of the group; or,
- should one emphasize the obligations of the individual to the group as being more significant than individual rights?
Discrimination:

Know that discrimination is the inequitable r rnt r rn r unr individual who usually has power and advantages. The group or individual uses its power to discriminate in order to maintain or increase its power and advantage.
Know that the concept of discrimination has a number of critical attributes:

Know that racism is the belief that people can be categorized into different groups according to certain characteristics such as skin colour and that these characteristics will determine how people will behave and whether they will be morally good or bad.

Know that sexism is the belief that individuals should be assigned specific roles in society based on their gender, that men and women are not equal, that laws should treat men and women differently, and that it is natural to discriminate on the basis of sex.

Know that a prejudice is an attitude or belief (often negative) toward a group or person which is thoughtlessly accepted (learned) by someone who either refuses to find out whether the attitude is justified or refuses to accept legitimate contrary evidence.
Practise gathering and organizing information systematically for a presentation.
State a proposition (hypothesis or solution) that is testable and guides the search for data.
Practise presenting an analysis of the data to confirm (or not confirm) the proposition.
Should a society be considered civilized when it carries on some form of prejudicial behaviour against one or more groups?

Know that stereotyping is forming a fixed mental picture about the reality of something (usually a group of people). This mental picture is rigid, often negative, and is applied to everyone in the group regardless of whether it fits or not.
Know that xenophobia is a fear of strangers which leads people to imagine unfavourable things and which distorts reality for them.
Know that ethnocentrism is the belief that one's group is superior to other groups combined with a blind loyalty to one's own group and an unreasonable dislike of some other group.
Know that scapegoating is expressing one's hostility, anger, and violence against a group for some wrong for which it is partially or totally innocent.
Know that genocide is the deliberate destruction or murder of a particular group of people.
Practise stating a proposition which is highly probable in light of established facts, or in light of a principle or theory, and which guides the search for data.
State the proposition so that it applies to most or all cases.

- describing cause-effect or other relationships; and,

Should individuals in a democracy be allowed to maintain attitudes of racism, prejudice, ethnocentrism, etc? Some people believe that the fundamental value of democracy:
- is freedom, so people must have the right to think and believe what they wish.
is the sanctity of the individual, so democratic societies cannot allow people to advocat polices which clearly hurt others within society.
Know that monism is the belief that there is a single world view which everyone should aspire to and emulate.
Know that pluralism is the belief that there is more than one world view which can be considered legitimate and to which people can aspire.
Know that people are concerned about maintaining their separate individuality so that they can express their potential in its own unique way.
Know that integration is the process of bringing separate and distinct parts into a whole.
Know that multiculturalism is the belief that different cultures can contribute to the well-being of society.
Know that justice is concerned with maintaining law and order in ways that are consistent with the moral and ethical criteria used by a particular society or culture to define fairness and rightness.
Know that a society's paradigm of human rights provides a set of criteria against which fairness and rightness can be evaluated.
Know that justice means the integration of autonomous individuals into a society according to principles which respect the ideals of the people being integrated.
Learn to consider and use consequences as a test for evaluating logical arguments.

In attempting to persuade This activity is intended to encourage someone to change who is obviously wrong, should:
- the person be told clearly that he/she is wrong and "to get his/her act together" immediately; or,
- the person be listened to, given a chance to tell his/her side, and allowed time to understand the need for change.

In a war or a fight for survival:
- do the ends justify the means; or,
- should moral behaviour apply even in this situation?
Know that the means by which change is achieved will generally determine the kind of change which is achieved.
Know that satyragraha was the belief that freedom cannot be taken by force.
Peoples' minds can only be changed by the love force of patience and sympathy.
Patience means self-suffering, so the conclusion must be that the vindication of truth occurs by inflicting suffering not on your opponent but on yourself.

Know that Gandhi believed:
- that there is something in humanity that is superior to its brute nature and that brute nature will always respond to humanity's superior nature;
- that those who are strong enough to accept this vision are satyagrahis; and,
- that this force is to violence, tyranny, and all injustice what light is to darkness.

Know that Bolshevism as defined by Lenin states that:
- workers cannot aspire to a social-democratic consciousness and that no revolutionary movement is possible without an organization of leaders to provide continuity; and,
- a revolutionary party must be a well disciplined organization run by professional revolutionaries who know how to deal with autocratic regimes.
Learn to consider and use consequences as a test for evaluating logical arguments.

In a war or a fight for survival:
- do the ends justify the means; or,
- should moral behaviour apply even in this situation?

- the person be clearly told that he/she is wrong and "to get his/her act together" immediately; or,
- the person be listened to, given a chance to tell his/her side, and allowed time to understand the need for change.
Know that full acceptance of a human right requires that a majority be prepared to accept the obligations of the moral claims made by the human rights holder.
Know that human rights claims are often perceived to be a challenge and a threat by those who will be obligated by the claim.

Know that human rights are not needed by those who already have power and status but are needed by those who lack power and who for one reason or another are unpopular and unacceptable to mainstream opinion.

Know that it is difficult to legislate human rights with instruments such as bills of rights so long as a significant part of society is unwilling to accept the moral vision on which the human rights are based.

How should a society go about identifying an appropriate set of choicesto for the future:
- by adopting a fatalistic "what will be will be" attitude; or,
- by using a variety of decision-making and problem-solving techniques to select a future course of action?
Did Martin Luther King fail in achieving his ideals because his moral vision was never accepted by a majority of Americans?
Know that power is often seen as a limited
com es e en s s ity to do what one chooses, especially in terms of protecting security and status within society.
Know that elites whose power and security are threatened in some way will often become very defensive and rigid, seeing the issue of power sharing only in win-lose terms.
to the power of an elite is often perceived as being intolerable, especially when it comes from individuals or groups who for one reason or another are not seen to merit any kind of consideration.
Know that empowerment sees the sharing of .
power as way of increasing the power of everyone within society.
Know that empowerment begins with the acceptance of others as being worthy and equal to oneself.
Know that empowerment often means an increase in security status and esteem for people within society so that they see power sharing as a win-win situation.

Practise stating the proposition so that it applies to most or all cases.

- by adopting a fatalistic "what will be will be" attitude; or,
- by using a variety of decision-making and problem-solving techniques to select a future course of action?

Know that gradualism is the belief that a group can best make social progress by contributing to society through work, getting an education, and showing everyone that they are worthy of having citizenship rights.
Know that those who favour active resistance believe that those who benefit from racism and discrimination will continue to do both until they are confronted and forced to give up these practices.
Know that the democratic political process enables groups to gain political power if they are prepared to use the sources of power effectively and creatively.
Know that nonviolent protest was a process of four basic steps.
1. Collecting facts to make sure that an injustice does, in fact, exist.
2. Negotiating with those who have the power to change the injustices.
3. Purifying oneself because those who are contemplating nonviolent direct action must be sure that what they are about to do is morally acceptable.
4. Taking nonviolent direct action if negotiation fails. This action may be necessary to create enough tension in a community to force it to confront the issues of injustice it is trying to avoid

Know that those who advocate civil disobedience do so when the majority are more concerned about order than they are about justice. They argue that:
- The majority must come to understand that the purpose of order is to facilitate justice.
- When order is used to thwart justice then a dangerous block to social progress has been created.
- This will ultimately lead to the anarchy of frustration and violence where any possibility of order and justice will be destroyed.
Practise stating a proposition that is highly probable in light of established facts, or in light of a principle or theory.

What level of conformity should a democracy be able to require:
- that all individuals ought to be free to behave according to the requirements of their conscience provided they do not hurt any other individual; or,
- there is in any civilized society, a social contract, which determines the basic standard of behaviour which is agreed upon and which everyone must obey.

Know that sexism is the belief that an individual's gender justifies different treatment in terms of rights, social roles and responsibilities, and economic and political participation within a society.
Know that there has been a long tradition of inequitable treatment of people based on and justified by gender.
Know that in most countries and particularly in developing countries, women suffer greater hardship and deprivation than do men.
A great deal of controversy remains associated with the proper role of women and men, particularly in relation to accepting responsibility for the family.
Practise stating a proposition that is highly probable in light of established facts, or in light of a principle or theory.
Practise stating a proposition that is testable and guides the search for data.

Practise presenting an analysis of the data to confirm or disconfirm the proposition by:
- describing and defining the main parts;
- describing cause-effect or other relationships; and,
- ·showing how the parts are related to each other and to the whole.

Is education a better method of eliminating inequalities than action through the court system?
Should men have equal rights to paternity leave as women have to maternity leave in the workplace?
Is one-half of humanity being enslaved?
Has technology in the form of dishwashers and clothes dryers done more for liberating women than the entire feminist movement?
Should women be guaranteed half of the political and judicial positions so as to ensure gender equality in a society?
Know that in the past century a number of changes within society have resulted in a significant shift in the accepted roles, rights, and rewards for women.

Know that in Western, developed countries there are indications that a permanent shift is taking place in the roles and responsibilities of women and men; but at the same time this shift is by no means universally accepted.
Know that over the years, in many countries, laws have been changed which have improved the lot of women.
Know that much remains to be done, because the range of opportunities, levels of pay, pensions, and family responsibilities still remain inequitable.
Practise stating a proposition that is highly probable in light of established facts, or in light of a principle or theory.

- describing and defining the main parts; and
- describing cause-effect or other relationships; and,
- showing how the parts are related to each other and to the whole.
Practise selecting and applying the abilities of problem solving and dialectical thinking to an issue.

When considering issues of systemic injustice, the democratic value/right of equality of treatment means:
- that any kind of discrimination, however good the reasons for it, cannot be accepted; or,
- that long standing systemic injustice can only be changed by giving certain groups special consideration in the short run.
A female police officer is equally as effective as a male police officer in law enforcement. Agree or disagree.
Should women automatically have the right of custody of children after a divorce?
Should a female candidate be hired automatically for a job even if male candidates have equal qualifications, so as to overcome the effects of past discrimination?
Do men have responsibility equal to women for birth control?
Is a female soldier as able to serve on the front lines in combat as a male soldier?

Know that the parties to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child have agreed that a convention is necessary:
- "Considering that ... recognition of the inherent dignity ... of all members of the human family .. is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world,
- Recalling that in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the United Nations has proclaimed that childhood is entitled to special care and assistance,
- Convinced that the family is the fundamental group of society ... for the well-being of all its members and particularly children should be afforded the necessary protection and assistance ... so it can fully assume its responsibilities ..,
- Recognizing that the child ... should grow up in a family environment ... of happiness, love, and understanding,
- Bearing in mind that .. the child ... needs special safeguards and care including appropriate legal protection before as well as after birth,
- Recognizing that, in all countries, there are children living in exceptionally difficult conditions [who] ... need special protection," and have, therefore,
- agreed to sign a convention protecting the rights of children within their jurisdiction. (adapted from: UNICEF: The State of the World's Children 1992)

Practise stating a proposition that is testable and guides the search for data.

- describing and defining the main parts;
- describing cause-effect or other relationships; and,
- showing how the parts are related to each other and to the whole. statistics youth are Practise selecting and applying the abilities of problem solving and dialectical thinking to an issue.

Should children be considered:
- creatures of the family to be shaped and moulded according to the family's dictates: or,
- autonomous individuals with the right to self-determination?
Should children have the right to sue a negligent or abusive parent?
Should children have the right to choose which parent they will live with when the parents divorce?
Should the legal driving age be raised to nineteen because according to involved in more car accidents than adults?
Is abortion a denial of a fundamental human right?
Know that the Indigenous Peoples are the descendants of the original inhabitants of lands which have been colonized by foreigners.
Know that the Indigenous Peoples are a minority in their own lands often representing less than one per cent of the national population.
Know that Indigenous Peoples are also known as the First Peoples and they have a strong sense of their own identity which is tied to their own land, language, and culture.
Know that acculturation is change that occur within a culture that is caused by the influence of another culture which results in greater similarity between the two cultures.

Practise stating a proposition that is testable and guides the search for data.

- describing and defining the main parts;
- describing cause-effect or other relationships; and,
- showing how the parts are related to each other and to the whole.

A minority culture can integrate more effectively into a society dominated by a majority which is significantly different through:
- assimilation; or,
- accommodation?
Should Native People be granted self-government which includes their own justice system and police force?
Are affirmative action programs a form of discrimination against able-bodied white males?
Indigenous Peoples worldwide have had to face the cultural collapse that accompanies the loss of their land, their language, their social and political systems, and their knowledge.
Know that racism and prejudice are used to justify inhuman treatment of Indigenous Peoples by an exploitive mainstream society.
Indigenous Peoples have never accepted the assault on their lands and culture passively.
They have fought back in every area with the weapons available to them.
Ultimately the issue for Aboriginal Peoples seems to come down to the issue of self-determination.
Practise selecting and applying the abilities of problem solving and dialectical thinking to an issue.

Based on modern conceptions of an adequate moral vision:
- Canada should be considered a just society because it does as well as any modern nation and better than many; or
- Canada should not be considered a just society so long as people are denied access to the basic necessities for a dignified life?
- The proportionally higher percentage of Aboriginals in prison populations worldwide is evidence that the justice system discriminates against Aboriginals. Agree or disagree.
Know that the rate of natural increase in a population is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate.
C Know that population growth rates vary from region to region and that regions with different population compositions make different demands on social policy.
Know that population density can be calculated in several different ways.
Know that the migration of people has had a major effect on people's histories and their relationships with other groups of people.
Know that a theory is made up of a set of definitions, assumptions, and propositions integrated into a meaningful whole and is a proposed explanation for some aspect of reality.
Learn to deduce an hypothesis from a theory and apply it to a particular situation.
Learn to devise a theory that better corresponds to current reality.

In determining social policy should a government, if it wishes to represent the interests of society ethically, make social policy:
- on the basis of rule by majority; or,
- on the basis of the greatest good for the greatest number?

Is progress achieving the goal of:
- allowing as many people as possible to live;
- giving as much wealth and power as possible to as many people as possible; or,
- learning to live in harmony with the environment?
