indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate mindfulness (e.g., take only what is needed) and gratitude (e.g., offering tobacco) when harvesting materials for shelters.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the differences between building shelters for emergency and recreational situations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore natural environmental features that provide shelter from the elements, such as depressions in the ground, holes from tree roots and lowhanging branches.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine factors that affect shelter choice (e.g., number of people requiring shelter, available materials and their cost, weather and animals).

indicators.label: e
f
g
indicators.text: Describe optimal snow conditions and construction of various snow shelters (e.g., quinzhee, snow cave and igloo).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Practise “Leave No Trace” principles by dismantling shelters when they are no longer required.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe knife skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Basic Knife Skills (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate materials (e.g., stone and bone) used by Indigenous people to create traditional knives.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Compare types of knives for safety features (e.g., locked and fixed blade).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify parts of knives, including the spine, blade and finger guard.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the use and functionality of different types of knives (e.g., bush, kitchen, hunting and filleting).

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Discuss the consequences of inappropriate or unsafe knife use, including harm to self or others (e.g., cuts and injuries) and harm to the environment (e.g., carving initials into trees and stripping birch bark for fire starter from a live tree).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how to identify a serviceable knife blade (e.g., sharp or dull).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Practise safe knife skills with basic knife craft projects (e.g., whimmy diddle, curl sticks and carving wood).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate respectful and safe basic fire-building skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9A: Basic Fire Skills (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the cultural and traditional significance of fire, including sacred fires, with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the significance of fire in other cultures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the natural environment by conserving fuel and by practicing an act of mindfulness when harvesting material to burn.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Research local fire regulations (e.g., no open fires and fire bans).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the risk of using accelerants when lighting fires.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Discuss commonly used types of household tinder (e.g., cotton ball and newspaper).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the importance of gradually increasing the size of kindling.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Practise safely lighting and maintaining fires in favourable conditions with common ignition sources, tinder and kindling.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to determine when a fire is fully extinguished.

outcomes.statement: Explore traditional and nutritional uses of local plants.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10A: Basic Plant Skills (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the cultural and traditional significance of local plants with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss traditional ethical harvesting practices (e.g., take only what is needed and leave tobacco).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how the ecozones of Saskatchewan, and their corresponding treaty territories, affected the food and shelter needs of Indigenous people.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Refer to a variety of resources (e.g., books, Knowledge Keepers and technological applications) to identify local plants.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research how vegetation can be used as a navigational tool.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the relationship between soil and vegetation (e.g., tamaracks and wet soil, birch trees and rich soil, and jack pine and sandy soil).

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Explain the risks of consuming unfamiliar plants.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe angling and fishing practices and understanding of regulations.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12B: Angling and Fishing - Safe Practices and Regulations (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 12A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss who is eligible, and how to apply, for an angling license.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe fishing practices, such as using barbless hooks, keeping hooks and lures in tackle boxes, wearing eye protection and using dehooking tools to remove hooks.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Explain proper maintenance of common fishing equipment, including:
- dry out rods and tackle when not in use;
- loosen drag tension for storage; and,
- oil the reel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how to craft fishing equipment, including a tip-up or rod.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Experiment with different angling techniques (e.g., ice fishing, open water fishing, bait fishing and fly-fishing) for different purposes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ethical fishing practices, such as catch and release, barbless hooks and lead-free tackle.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the techniques for care of table fish and trophy fish.

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of referring to the Saskatchewan Anglers Guide for information such as season dates, zones and limits.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research fishing regulations and associated legislations (e.g., protection and conservation of fish, conduct of fisherman and small vessel legislation) that provide a legal standard of conduct for game fishing.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the fishing license regulations for different user groups (e.g., First Nations people, youth under 16 and seniors).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Investigate the differences in fishing regulations (e.g., equipment and limits) in national parks and other regions.

outcomes.statement: Explore the history and types of bowhunting.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate materials (e.g., stones, wood from local trees, and sinew and bone from animals) used to make traditional Indigenous bows and arrows.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history and evolution of archery equipment (e.g., spear, atlatl, simple bows and compound bows) in different cultures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages (e.g., quiet, early season and less intrusive) and challenges (e.g., wind, limited range, required strength and necessary accuracy) of bowhunting.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the function of basic parts (e.g., limbs, riser and bowstring) of various bow styles (e.g., recurve, longbow, compound and crossbow).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the importance of matching bows and arrows.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of arrow points used for large game, small game and target practice.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how to determine appropriate draw length and draw weight.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research specific regulations for bowhunting in Saskatchewan regarding seasons, equipment and tagging requirements.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the considerations unique to crossbow hunting (e.g., restrictions in seasons and management zones).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the “rule of first blood” (i.e., ethical and sportsmanship way of determining who claims an animal shot by two hunters).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text:
Demonstrate proper use and maintenance of a bow, including:
- correct shooting form;
- tuning the bow; and,
- sighting-in a bow.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe precautions that can be taken to prevent injury to both the archer and to others.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of inspecting archery equipment prior to use.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Investigate the rules and safety practices to follow at an archery range.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Explore archery training opportunities (e.g., National Archery in the Schools Program) in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Explore the evolution and safe use of firearms.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13C: Hunting and Game - Firearms (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 13A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how the introduction of firearms affected the Indigenous way of life in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history and evolution of firearms (e.g., muzzle-loaded rifles, breech-loading rifles, repeating firearms, semi-automatic firearms, openand telescopic-sights).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Categorize commonly used hunting firearms (e.g., rifles, shotguns and black or modern powder firearms) according to their distinguishing features and purpose.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the operation of various firearms, including the types of action, ammunition and function of sights.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the basic components of rifle and shotgun ammunition.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the ethics of using the appropriate firearm calibre for the target game species.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate ammunition considerations (e.g., size of bullet, casing and gun powder in the casing).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe safe practices for storing, transporting, handling, maintaining, loading and sighting-in firearms

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how hunting and firearm use may be made available to persons with physical disabilities, including those with visual impairment.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate hunting training opportunities and firearm licensing requirements (e.g., Hunter Safety Course and Possession and Acquisition License).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain the Twelve Commandments of Firearm Safety.

outcomes.statement: Investigate traditional and contemporary trapping.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Examine federal, provincial and municipal laws governing trapping.

indicators.text: Explain the rights (e.g., furs) and responsibilities (e.g., annual fee) of owning a trapline.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline the steps to obtain a trapper's license.

indicators.label: f

indicators.text: Research the humane trapping practices (e.g., harvesting, methods and equipment) as outlined by the Agreement of International Humane Trapping Standards.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the value in harvesting fur when it is prime (i.e., December to March).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain circumstances that justify trapping outside of winter months (e.g., nuisance management, predator control, flooding and beaver activity).

indicators.text: Investigate methods to process and preserve furs, including stretching and tanning hides.

indicators.text: Investigate trapping training opportunities (e.g., Humane Trapper Education Program).

outcomes.statement: Explore human effects on wildlife species and spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Human Effects on Wildlife and Habitat (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the cultural and traditional use of natural resources with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the effects of human populations on wildlife (e.g., distribution, diversity and abundance of species) and habitat in the local area.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the diversity of wildlife and plant species in areas of high and low human population.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the contributions and goals of different stakeholder groups (e.g., hunters, conservation organizations, government, recreational users, farmers and Indigenous people) in managing interactions between wildlife and society.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore management strategies (e.g., migration corridors, bounties, euthanasia and relocation) that enable wildlife and humans to coexist.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the role of protected spaces (e.g., parks, wildlife and wilderness areas, migratory bird sanctuaries, ecological reserves, world heritage sites, private land and grazing reserves) in managing ecosystems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the role of public (e.g., government) and private (e.g., industry) organizations in managing and protecting wildlife and ecosystems.

indicators.label: h

outcomes.statement: Investigate wildlife rescue and rehabilitation practices in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the purpose and function of wildlife rescue and rehabilitation organizations in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define “capture myopathy” and identify its symptoms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Outline steps that can be taken to prevent capture myopathy from occurring in wildlife.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the negative impact of imprinting on young wildlife and the risks (e.g., no fear of humans, territorial behaviour and difficulty interacting with their own species) when young wildlife imprint on humans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Explore humane ways of coping with “nuisance” wildlife, such as:
- deterring or hazing the animals with unpleasant smells (e.g., cider vinegar), sounds (e.g., music, air horn) or bright lights;
- sealing off any denning areas; and,
- using repellants.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Explain why relocation of wildlife is an ineffective method for dealing with “nuisance” wildlife, including:
- wild animal babies left orphaned when their mother is trapped and removed;
- danger to the relocated animal in other animals' territory; and,
- difficulty finding food, water and shelter in unfamiliar areas.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how seeking alternatives to euthanizing an injured animal is an act of stewardship.

indicators.text: Discuss the importance of land acknowledgements (e.g., naming the traditional peoples of the area, identifying the treaty and partnerships with local Indigenous people) when participating in overnight excursions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon the traditional stories of the land where the overnight excursion will take place.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Explain and demonstrate use of the principles of layering clothing, including:
- base layer (i.e., wicks moisture away from the skin);
- mid layer (i.e., insulates to preserve body warmth); and,
- outer layer (i.e., protection from weather).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select and collect appropriate equipment for the excursion.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Conduct an equipment check prior to excursion to ensure functionality, including:

- erecting tents; and,
- verifying stock in First Aid kit.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of carrying a personal survival kit (e.g., compass, personal medications, knife and emergency blanket).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise communication routines (e.g., whistle commands and satellite phone) in emergency situations both within and outside of cell phone range.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Establish plans for emergency situations such as extreme weather conditions, fire, injury, illness, becoming lost or animal threats.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify factors (e.g., pain, cold, hunger, fatigue and fear) that affect the ability to cope with emergency conditions in the outdoors.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Plan appropriate menus for the excursion and group.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop a budget for the menu and other excursion costs.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the risks of consuming untreated water and methods (e.g., filters, chemical treatment and boiling) of water purification.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Prevent food from spoiling and attracting wildlife by using safe food storage practices (e.g., appropriate containers, bear-proof containers and hanging food).

indicators.text: Plan and prepare a meal cooked over a fire or gas stove.

indicators.text: Compare preservation (i.e., protect endangered areas and species) and conservation (i.e., proper use of areas and species) as they relate to wildlife and habitat.

d

indicators.text: Investigate the agencies responsible for managing Saskatchewan’s game animals.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how organizations use “community science” (i.e., applications to record observations) to assist in monitoring wildlife.

indicators.label: g
h
i

outcomes.statement: Investigate characteristics of specific careers in the field of wildlife and habitat management.

indicators.text: Examine how wildlife contributes to the economy of an area.

indicators.text: Investigate aquaculture facilities in Saskatchewan.

Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: c

outcomes.statement: Extend and apply understanding of surface area, volume, and capacity using concrete and pictorial models and symbolic representations (SI or imperial units of measurement).

indicators.text: Observe, analyze, generalize, and explain using examples including nets, the relationships between area, surface area, and volume.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe, analyze, and compare volume and capacity using examples.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement: "Volume and capacity represent the same attribute to measure so the same units of measure can be used for either volume or capacity".

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations in which given SI or imperial volume or capacity units would be used.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Justify and compare the choice of personal referents for surface area, volume, and capacity measurements in both SI and imperial units, (e.g., The bottom half of a two-litre carton of milk has a capacity of one litre, a surface area of 500 cm² or if a top was added to make a prism it would have a surface area of 600 cm² and a volume of about 1000 cm³, or the volume of a box for hockey helmets is approximately 1 ft³ [1800 in³] and the surface area is about 6 ft² [900 in²]).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Justify and apply strategies including use of personal referents to estimate the surface area and volume of 3-D objects, and the capacity of containers.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Solve situational questions that involve:
- the volume of 3-D objects and composite 3-D objects in a variety of contexts
- the capacity of containers.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Convert given volume, surface area, and capacity measurements:
- expressed in one SI unit to another SI unit (including units squared and units cubed)
- expressed in one imperial unit to another imperial unit (including units squared and units cubed).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine the surface area and volume of prisms, cones, cylinders, pyramids, spheres, and composite 3-D objects, using a variety of measuring tools such as rulers, tape measures, callipers, and micrometers and explain the strategy used including the manipulation of formulae.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the capacity of prisms, cones, pyramids, spheres, and cylinders, using a variety of measuring tools and methods, such as graduated cylinders, measuring cups, measuring spoons, and displacement and explain the strategy used.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text:
Analyze and generalize the relationship between the volumes of:
- cones and cylinders with the same base and height
- pyramids and prisms with the same base and height.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze and illustrate, using examples, the effect of dimensional changes on area, surface area, and volume.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text:
Solve using a variety of strategies, including the manipulation of formulae, situational questions that involve:
- the surface area of 3-D objects, including spheres
- the volume of 3-D objects, including composite 3-D objects
- the capacity of containers.

indicators.text: Describe conditions under which a slope will be either 0 or undefined and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Employ appropriate formality (e.g., “du” vs. “Sie”).

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text:
Produce sentences using the following verb conventions:
- present tense;
- modal verbs in the past perfect tense (e.g., “Ich kann im Winter Eislaufen gehen.”, “Ich bin im Winter Eislaufen gegangen.”); and,
- auxiliary verb in the past perfect tense.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compose sentences using “two way” adjectives (e.g., “Ich gehe in die Klasse.”, “Ich gehe zu der Tafel in der Klasse.”).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use conjunctions such as “weil”, “damit”, “dass”, “als”, and “wenn” to add subordinate clauses (e.g., “Wenn die Kekse braun sind, nimm sie aus dem Ofen.”).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply adjective endings in the accusative and dative case, using both strong and weak ending patterns and definite and indefinite articles (e.g., “Ich trage ein weißes Hemd mit meinem blauen Rock.”).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Practise using the following types of pronouns to clarify communication:
- relative pronouns to supply additional information (e.g., “Ich trage meine neue Hose, die ich in den tollen Laden gestern gekauft habe.“); and,
- dative pronouns such as “mir”, “dir”, “ihm” and “ihr” when using dative verbs such as “gehören”, “gefallen”, “passen”, “stehen”, “helfen” (e.g., “Deine neuen Schuhe gefallen mir sehr.”).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text:
Enhance communication with the following types of prepositions:
- dative prepositions (e.g., aus, bei, mit, nach, von, seit, zu), followed by the appropriate adjective endings and/or pronouns (e.g., “Samuel geht gern mit seinem neuen Freund ins Kino”); and,
- accusative prepositions (e.g., durch, für, gegen, ohne, um), followed by the appropriate adjective endings and/or pronouns (e.g., “Sanjida geht durch die offene Tür in den Flur”).

- ‘工人gōngrén’ means ‘worker’ (noun); and,
- ‘工gōng作zuò’ means ‘work’ (noun).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Comprehend common sight words:
- Standard Chinese characters that sound alike, such as (音yīn 似shì 字zì) (e.g., 目mù，木mù，墓mù ；鸡jī 机jī，肌jī); and,
- Standard Chinese characters that look alike, such as (形xíng似sì字zì) (e.g., 人rén，八bā，入rù ; 士shì，土tǔ ；千qiān，干gàn).

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text:
Discuss differences in formal and informal Mandarin, such as:
- the number “1” is pronounced differently by some; instead of pronouncing “1” as “yī” like in pinyin, it is read as “yāo”. The reason is to clearly distinguish “1” from “7” because “7” in pinyin is “qī”, which may sound alike over the crackling of a telephone conversation.
